text:
WASHINGTON – On Friday, United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Commissioner Rodney Scott toured a cargo processing facility in Arizona, seeing firsthand how CBP keeps harmful contraband from entering the United States.

At the cargo inspection facility at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, CBP personnel inspect imported goods for illegal drugs, fraudulent labeling, and other national security threats. Among the items that were seen during the visit were baseball jerseys that were labeled as being manufactured in Mexico, but were actually manufactured in China.

“The hardworking men and women of CBP look at almost every package that comes in, so that dangerous drugs, counterfeit products, and other harmful contraband does not come into our country,” said Secretary Mullin. “The patriots at CBP understand these criminals’ patterns, how the traffickers and cartels try to get around the duties and customs, and the way they try to ship things into our country. That’s why experience matters.”

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil asked the Supreme Court on Monday to let federal judges quickly determine the legality of immigration-related detentions so that individuals cannot be held for months or years without judicial oversight.

In papers filed with the high court, Khalil asked it to overturn a ruling earlier this year by the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia that found federal courts do not have jurisdiction to review the legality of the detentions until immigration courts had fully considered each case.

Khalil, a lawful permanent U.S. resident, was detained by immigration authorities last year because of his participation in pro-Palestinian demonstrations at Columbia University in the spring of 2024.

The U.S. government argued at the time that Khalil's presence in the U.S. was harmful to the country's foreign policy interests.

As a result, the former Columbia graduate student spent over three months in detention before a federal judge in New Jersey ordered him freed after finding that the federal government had acted unconstitutionally.

READ MORE: Mahmoud Khalil lawsuit says Columbia University failed to protect pro-Palestinian activists

In a statement Monday, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said: "It is a privilege to be granted a visa or green card to live and study in the United States of America. The Trump Administration acted well within its statutory and constitutional authority with respect to Khalil, as it does with any alien who advocates for violence, glorifies and supports terrorists, harasses Jews, and damages property. We would encourage him to use the CBP Home app and self-deport."

The 3rd Circuit has put its ruling on hold so that Khalil could appeal to the Supreme Court. He remains free.

Although the Supreme Court typically agrees to grant only a small percentage of appeals requests, the U.S. government has already asked the high court to overturn a federal appeals court decision that upheld a judge's decision to release Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri. That ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, Virginia, directly conflicted with the 3rd Circuit decision in the Khalil case.

Sometimes, conflicting appeals court rulings can increase the chances that the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case. If it does, oral arguments before the justices would likely occur sometime next year.

text:
Former Columbia grad student and pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil, whom the Trump administration detained and sought to deport from the U.S. on foreign policy grounds last year, has appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, seeking to sue the government for allegedly violating his First Amendment rights.

A divided federal appeals court ruled earlier this year that Khalil, a green card-holder married to an American citizen, could not litigate his claims before a judge unless and until immigration proceedings against him had been completed.

He was arrested by federal agents in New York City in March 2025 and held more than 100 days in ICE custody ahead of deportation after Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed an unusual determination that Khalil's pro-Palestinian activities "compromise a compelling U.S. foreign policy interest."

Khalil, who has not been charged with any crime, contends that he was deliberately targeted by Trump as part of a scheme to crackdown on pro-Palestinian protests and debate over Israel’s war in Gaza that had swept college campuses shortly after the president took office.

After a legal challenge, Khalil was released from custody pending the outcome of his petition.

"This fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country," Khalil said during a remote press conference Monday. "It’s about whether anyone in this country can speak out for Palestinians without being punished for it."

Asked for comment on Khalil's appeal, a White House spokeswoman said the executive branch has the authority to take actions that protect the country and the immigration system.

"Khalil obtained his visa by willfully and intentionally failing to accurately report information relevant to his background. Those who lie to the government to obtain entry into the United States will face justice,” spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

The legal question at the heart of the case involves the writ of habeas corpus, the legal procedure that allows a person detained by the government to challenge his confinement before a judge.

If the high court takes up the case -- and says Khalil can access the procedure -- his case alleging targeted retaliation by the government over disfavored speech can go forward. If the court denies the appeal, Khalil could be deported before getting the chance to make his case.

"It’s clear and conceited that Mahmoud has never committed a crime and that his detention and removal are only because of the speech the government dislikes," said Khalil's attorney Baher Azmy. This is "unprecedented weaponization of immigration power ... The question is whether the federal courts can address this egregious action."

Khalil has a separate legal challenge pending in the 5th Circuit Court of appeals focusing on U.S. immigration law.

"It's way bigger than me," Khalil said. "I can afford to lose … unlike the thousands of immigrants in this country who really cannot lose this fight. Whatever I’m going through is a drop in the sea of what other families are experiencing."

The justices are likely to consider the petition during a formal private meeting in January. If they agree to hear Khalil's case, it would likely be set for oral argument sometime in the spring and decided by the end of June.

text:
Masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents broke the arm of a U.S. citizen during a detention attempt Saturday in Long Beach, California, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., said Sunday.

Ricardo Gonzalez, a former Long Beach city employee, was found handcuffed, bleeding and being detained by several ICE officers when local authorities arrived at the scene, according to a statement from the Long Beach Police Department.

Videos of the encounter taken by bystanders appeared to show Gonzalez lying face down in a gutter while several ICE agents kneeled on his back. In several videos, Gonzalez is heard yelling repeatedly, “Help me, my arm is broken,” and “Call a paramedic.”

Gonzalez’s daughter, Leslie Gonzalez, said her father was “struck by an unmarked vehicle of federal agents while riding his E-Bike.” He was then tased twice and pinned to the ground, according to her description on a GoFundMe page created to help with her father’s medical expenses.

“ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen,” Garcia, whose district includes Long Beach and parts of Orange County, wrote in a statement Sunday posted to X. “The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country.”

Long Beach police said in a statement Monday to MS NOW that officers arrived after receiving a request for emergency assistance from the ICE officers due to “vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid.”

According to police, officers saw “a large group disturbance involving the ICE agents” and a man in handcuffs who was bleeding.

“First responders from the Long Beach Fire Department took the man to a nearby fire station,” according to the statement. There, Gonzalez’s handcuffs were removed, and he was taken to a hospital.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to MS NOW’s requests for comment Monday.

Police officers cleared a crowd of protesters who had gathered near the scene Sunday.

Gonzalez is believed to have been one of several community members who called 911 when he “saw a circumstance escalating,” Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson told CNN in a statement Sunday.

More articles

“When the police arrived, we know that he was detained. He was on a curb. He was injured,” Richardson said.

The incident drew outcry over the federal agency’s frequent use of force, which has often turned violent.

In a statement released on social media, Richardson said, “ICE doesn’t belong in our city and this activity undermines community safety and public trust.”

The situation involving Gonzalez is among the latest in a series of violent incidents and high-profile killings that have roiled the federal immigration agency. An ICE agent was placed on leave earlier this month after striking an undocumented immigrant with his vehicle in Houston.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit on Oct. 15 alleging ICE agents were unconstitutionally taking people into custody near state courthouses. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani demanded ICE end its operations in the city after an agent shot and wounded a Dominican man earlier this month while trying to arrest him as his 5-year-old child sat in the backseat.

Scores of high-profile national Democrats have demanded that the immigration agency be abolished in the wake of the deadly shootings of two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis earlier this year.

“I’m proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE,” Garcia wrote in his statement Sunday. “Donald Trump and his inhumane and illegal deportation machine must be stopped. Long Beach stands with our community and our immigrant families. ICE is not welcome in Long Beach. Abolish ICE.”

text:
The Trump administration is shifting its strategy for building out a nationwide network of immigration detention facilities, and litigators say challengers may have a harder time blocking them from opening under environmental law.

The US Department of Homeland Security is acquiring private prisons and working with contractors to bring previously shuttered facilities online while scaling back efforts to convert commercial warehouse properties into detention centers.

States, local governments, and environmental groups successfully blocked immediate renovations to the warehouses under the National Environmental Policy Act, securing preliminary injunctions and agreements with DHS to compel months-long environmental reviews.

Now, bolstered by a $45 billion detention center allocation from last year’s budget reconciliation bill, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement is signing contracts to reopen dormant private prisons across the country.

By paying for space in an existing incarceration infrastructure, the Trump administration can argue its contract “doesn’t really have any environmental effects, or the environmental effects are a lot smaller,” said Justin Pidot, a law professor at the University of Arizona and former counsel for the White House Council on Environmental Quality.

“It certainly makes NEPA claims more complicated than when it’s the federal agency doing something directly that changes the physical built environment,” Pidot said.

Acquisition Shield

Earlier lawsuits over the warehouses hinged on infrastructure restrictions at the properties ICE acquired. Warehouses built to store commercial goods didn’t have the sewage and water systems to meet the agency’s own standards for detaining hundreds, if not thousands of people, environmental groups and local officials argued in court filings.

The agency has since pivoted to purchasing or leasing what the agency’s bid proposal called “turn-key facilities,” or prison properties with existing beds and security infrastructure. DHS bought prisons operated by CoreCivic and The GEO Group Inc. in California, Minnesota, and Kansas, and now leases a facility in Colorado.

The agreements outline companies maintaining the day-to-day operations of such facilities, a caveat similar to Florida’s role in constructing the detention facility dubbed Alligator Alcatraz, according to Pidot.

The US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit ultimately ruled DHS didn’t need to prepare a NEPA review for the makeshift detention facility because it was Florida’s decision to put up the funds and construct the center in the first place.

In this kind of contract, “the state or the prison company is on its own building or rebuilding a facility, so any environmental effects from that are not related to the federal decision to enter into a contract,” Pidot said.

Courts will have to examine the timeline of when companies decided to reopen prisons or undergo renovations to determine if the environmental effects of a prison operation are far enough removed from the contracts DHS signed, according to Laurel Jobe, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity.

“They’re going to have to really be careful and look really closely at the communications and the directives between, for example, GEO and DHS,” Jobe said.

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said ICE complies with NEPA, and the agency “maintains a robust, multi-layered compliance program” to promote “contractually obligated detention standards.”

Only one contract has drawn lawsuits so far. Colorado and environmental groups challenged the $500 million five-year contract DHS signed with The GEO Group Inc. to renovate and operate a prison that hasn’t housed anyone for approximately 13 years. The lawsuit alleged the agency should have considered how reopening the facility would nearly double the population of Hudson, Colo., and strain local resources and infrastructure.

“What will be interesting to see is how courts respond is that when you have a facility that has been sitting vacant and has been dormant for the amount of time that these facilities have been empty, you almost reset to zero,” said Carmen Iguina González, deputy director for immigration detention at the ACLU’s national prison project. “For a long time you haven’t had that facility be a burden on the water system or the sewer system or the emergency response system or roads.”

DHS’s legal response is due in federal court Monday. In the statement the agency spokesperson said opposition to the agency adding detention capacity “isn’t about the environment.”

For the outright prison acquisitions, states have a lot less ground to challenge ICE detention expansions or provide oversight for prison conditions, according to Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council.

“The supremacy clause is a very big issue here,” Reichlin-Melnick said, referring to the priority of federal law in the US Constitution.

“States have very limited ability to tell the federal government how to operate facilities that the federal government owns,” he said.

ICE Portfolio

DHS remains close-lipped about its detention strategy and its current holding numbers, according to several immigration advocates, but the agency hasn’t entirely shrugged off its initial warehouse real estate portfolio. Former acting director of ICE Todd Lyons said at a Phoenix border security conference in 2025 that he envisioned the agency running its deportation process like Amazon “Prime, but with human beings,” according to the Arizona Mirror.

The department has told courts it continues environmental reviews for several warehouses, and the latest filings in New Jersey’s lawsuit against the agency suggest one warehouse has been used “in connection with immigration enforcement” in possible violation of a court order. San Antonio filed a NEPA lawsuit last week to compel an environmental review for a proposed detention warehouse in its jurisdiction after ICE awarded a $17 million contract to GardaWorld Federal Services to renovate the property.

According to a Government Accountability Office report issued last month, ICE is selling seven of the 11 warehouses acquired in the last year, a move the auditing agency said has resulted in millions in unnecessary costs.

The same report said ICE hasn’t developed a “comprehensive strategy plan,” and the agency “has not assessed the long-term affordability of facilities it purchased or the risks and benefits of using facilities with high operating costs.”

text:
A 56-year-old Mexican man held at a federal immigration facility in Laredo was found dead in his cell Saturday morning, his daughter and U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Laredo, confirmed to The Texas Tribune.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unresponsive by staff at the Rio Grande Processing Center during a security check at around 10 a.m. Saturday, Cuellar said. Staff performed CPR and called emergency services.

Andrade-Covarrubias is the seventh person to die while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas this year - the first being Geraldo Lunas Campos, whose death was ruled a homicide by the El Paso Medical Examiner's office in January.

He's also the second to die in an ICE facility in Laredo this year. Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, a 63-year-old Mexican who was being held at Webb County Detention Center, died on June 19 after being found unresponsive, according to the agency.

GEO Group and officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent Sunday.

Andrade-Covarrubias' daughter, Estefani Andrade, told the Tribune that her family has not yet been contacted by federal agencies. Instead, she said, they heard about his death on Saturday through the Webb County Medical Examiner, which is performing his autopsy.

Estefani Andrade, 29 and a U.S. citizen, said the family is going to visit the detention facility on Monday to get his belongings.

Andrade-Covarrubias lived in Dallas for decades, had three adult children who were all born in the country and worked as a contractor painting apartments and townhomes, his daughter said. He wanted to eventually return to Mexico and had been travelling back and forth to build a house there, his daughter added.

She said her dad was detained in June at the border after coming back from Mexico by bus. She added that during his months in detention, "he lost weight because he didn't look the same as when we were doing, like, the video calls with him."

Cuellar said he planned to visit the facility Sunday afternoon.

"I'll ask the basic questions: What happened?" he said. "What were the conditions? [Was] there medical? Is there anybody ill? I'm gonna talk to the medical folks there."

Estefani Andrade said her dad had a heart condition, along with diabetes and high blood pressure. He had medicine with him when he was detained, but she said staff at the center wouldn't "give him his medications."

She also said her dad was sick at the detention facility. He had a cough - which she said was concerning since he was hospitalized for COVID-19 in 2021 and that took a lasting toll on his health - and told her that he wasn't feeling good. He sought help from the facility's medical staff but he told her that "they would just ignore him."

She said her dad told her that he felt like medical staff at the center was brushing off his concerns, even when he told the staff that he was having trouble breathing and feeling tightness in his chest.

Estefani Andrade said she is now trying to be strong for her mom, who is devastated.

"When she got the news, she wasn't all there," she said. "It's hitting her really hard."

text:
Congressional Democrats sent a letter to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Monday, urging him to rescind a new policy they say violates the rights of unaccompanied immigrant children and makes them vulnerable to deportation.

Under the policy, unaccompanied minors would be represented in court by HHS lawyers instead of independent attorneys, a change the lawmakers say creates a conflict of interest, given the administration’s desire to deport as many immigrants as possible and the health department’s role in detaining the children.

“The immigration judge works for the Trump administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable,” wrote Sens. Tammy Duckworth and Dick Durbin (Ill.), Elizabeth Warren and Edward Markey (Mass.), Adam Schiff (Calif.), and Ron Wyden (Ore.).

As I reported earlier this month, HHS had quietly announced the creation of a new division, the Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division, to perform this legal work. Kennedy’s agency also oversees the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is responsible for placing kids in shelters after they cross the border alone and deciding when to release them to relatives in the United States.

Under President Trump, ORR is holding kids significantly longer than it had under Biden—about six months on average; it also is sharing information with ICE. “HHS holds these children in custody, decides where they live, and shares information about them and their families with immigration enforcement. HHS cannot also be their lawyer,” the lawmakers wrote.

Federal law gives unaccompanied minors a right to an attorney, and HHS’ own regulations stipulate they should receive a legal orientation from an independent provider. Historically, that’s been done by a network of experienced nonprofits, led most recently by the Acacia Center for Justice. But the Trump administration let the network’s contract expire over the summer. It then awarded the job to Burke Law Group, a small firm with far less experience in these matters, but greater ties to Trump: One of Burke’s co-founders served in the first Trump administration and one of its founding partners works for the second.

Facing backlash, Burke Law Group pulled out. Next, the contract went to Our Rescue, a nonprofit founded by a former ICE agent. A court put that deal on hold after the Acacia Center filed a protest against it. In the meantime, the administration gave a temporary contract to the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, whose personnel, according to court filings, often sit silently in court and have only represented 12 children so far; by contrast, the nonprofit network had been representing more than 20,000.

The network’s advocates doubt the government’s lawyers will have their clients’ best interests in mind if they take over the cases. “The idea that HHS, the same agency that’s detaining the children, would be able to provide the kind of child-centered, zealous and trauma-informed, independent legal services that were mandated by Congress is frankly absurd,” says Shaina Aber, the Acacia Center’s executive director. Aber questions whether HHS attorneys would help children who are wrongly detained or abused or mistreated while in government custody.

“It’s a major conflict of interest and ethical concern,” adds Adina Appelbaum, an attorney with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, part of the nonprofit network.

Some independent attorneys have continued representing kids without pay, but they can’t afford to pick up new cases and say the administration is hampering their work in other ways. For one, immigration judges in the Justice Department are fast-tracking children’s cases, requiring them to attend hearings with little time for counsel to prepare, according to a lawsuit filed this month. “They’re just ordering everybody removed—even good asylum claims where the kids are genuinely going to be killed” if they return to their countries of origin, says Laura Smith, an attorney at the Children’s Legal Center in Illinois.

In recent weeks, the administration has also transferred children’s cases to courts far from where they are living, their attorneys say, thus forcing the children and their lawyers to appear virtually, even when there is courtroom space in the jurisdiction where they are located, where they could otherwise attend in person. Meanwhile, the Department of Homeland Security lawyers seeking to deport the children can often show up at the new location, putting the children at a disadvantage.

Attorney Lauren Fisher Flores, who represents kids at the American Bar Association ProBAR in Texas, says she and a young client logged into one hearing but could not see the judge on the screen, which made it difficult for the child to follow what was happening.

“Part of due process is having to look at the child they’re deporting and explain things to that child, and have the child be able to ask questions,” she says. “When you have a child looking at an empty court room, and you have no real ability for all the parties to be in the same space, it’s contrary to child-friendly best practices, and it means children are just churned through this deportation machine.”

When I reached out to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, the Justice Department office that handles immigration cases, it said it was not “fast-tracking” cases but rather working efficiently, and it defended the virtual hearings. The office “prioritizes the timely completion of all cases and makes scheduling adjustments as needed to ensure cases do not languish,” a spokesperson said. HHS did not respond to my questions about its lawyers representing unaccompanied minors, but told the Associated Press that the lawyers would “give the Department an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families.”

The senators who sent the letter on Monday aren’t buying it. They are calling on the administration to restore independent counsel for the kids. “Unaccompanied children deserve lawyers whose only loyalty is to them,” they wrote. “We demand that you rescind this harmful policy before a single HHS attorney stands beside a child in immigration court.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández credited ProPublica’s reporting as the catalyst for the bill, the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act.
Earlier this month, we revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been detained in warrantless arrests during the second Trump administration.

text:
What Happened: A New Mexico Democrat in the House introduced a bill last week that would make it easier for U.S. citizens to sue immigration agents and the federal government over wrongful detentions and arrests.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández credited ProPublica’s reporting as the catalyst for the bill, the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act. Earlier this month, we revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been detained in warrantless arrests during the second Trump administration.

Leger Fernández said the legislation would roll back the protections from lawsuits that agents and the federal government currently have. It would also establish a minimum level of compensation for people who win their suits, and extend the statute of limitations for such cases.

The legislation would also take back any unspent Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding from President Donald Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Leger Fernández’s bill was introduced with co-sponsor Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, a New Jersey Democrat.

Why It Matters: It can be difficult to sue federal officers for wrongful arrests or excessive force, or for local prosecutors to bring charges. Federal agents can claim immunity in response to civil lawsuits or to state charges and can move their cases to federal court.

People who accuse immigration agents of wrongdoing can currently only sue in a narrow set of circumstances, and previous Democratic bills aiming to change that have not passed.

Some local prosecutors have announced investigations into the wrongful arrests of U.S. citizens or prosecuted federal agents accused of wrongdoing during immigration enforcement actions.

What They Said: In an interview with ProPublica, Leger Fernández emphasized that accountability could not only address past wrongs, it may also help head them off in the future. “We know that when there are consequences, bad actors start behaving better because they don’t want to face those consequences,” she said.

Without legislation, Leger Fernández said, agents “will continue to violate the law, to violate their own policy, and to violate the Constitution without any consequences.”

Asked about the legislation, the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, repeated claims that it is not arresting U.S. citizens and defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.”

Background: The federal government denies that there is any pattern of immigration agents detaining U.S. citizens, but according to ProPublica’s count, more than 100 citizens were held after agents questioned their citizenship. At least 70 children and teens were also detained.

description:

text:
The mayor of Long Beach says Immigration and Customs Enforcement must answer pressing questions about why its agents seriously injured a U.S. citizen and then denied him medical attention until local police arrived.

Ricardo Gonzalez was riding an e-bike in his North Long Beach neighborhood on Saturday when agents blocked him in with their car and knocked him to the ground, according to video from the scene.

Neighbors told the Long Beach Post that agents then pinned him to the ground and tased him twice while he yelled that his arm was broken.

Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson is now demanding those agents be pulled off the streets immediately. He wants the Department of Homeland Security, which supervises ICE, to explain why agents stopped Gonzalez, whether he was racially profiled and why he wasn’t immediately given any medical aid.

“ICE should not be operating in our communities, and it should be abolished,” Richardson said in an interview Monday.

Richardson said he is sending a written complaint Monday to the DHS Office of Inspector General and Long Beach’s congressional representatives.

“We want a public report out,” Richardson said. “We want acknowledgement of this complaint. We don’t want this to just be received and filed. … We want to make sure they preserve evidence. All of those things, because our community shouldn’t allow a paramilitary force to simply roam our streets and harass and commit violence without any accountability in the United States of America.”

DHS so far has not answered the Long Beach Post’s questions about what happened.

Since the Trump administration ramped up immigration enforcement, Long Beach has pushed back by joining a lawsuit accusing agents of racially profiling, and, earlier, it broadened its sanctuary city law to ban city contractors — not just employees — from participating in most immigration enforcement.

Rep. Robert Garcia, who represents Long Beach in Congress, said ICE needs to be reined in and, ultimately, dismantled.

“ICE and DHS are completely out of control,” he said at a news conference Monday. He pledged to lead oversight efforts if Democrats win back the House in November.

Neighbors who witnessed Gonzalez’s detention said ICE agents in unmarked cars had been hanging around their neighborhood in North Long Beach for hours on Saturday morning.

Multiple neighbors, including Gonzalez, called police about the unmarked vehicles, according to Richardson. One neighbor told the Post that she wanted police to come move the cars that were blocking streets. Richardson said Gonzalez seemed worried about the tense situation and hoped police could de-escalate it.

Soon, Gonzalez was on he ground. A neighbor, who asked to be identified only by his first name, Joe, said agents knocked Gonzalez off his bike and accused him of throwing something at their car.

A crowd of about 50 people formed around them. Neighbors demanded agents let Gonzalez go and began blocking their cars. The standoff, neighbors said, lasted about an hour.

At some point, agents also called 911 “due to vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid,” police said in a statement.

When police arrived, “they saw chaos taking place,” according to Richardson. Video shows ICE agents letting officers take Gonzalez after looking at his wallet and finding identification. Richardson said police drove Gonzalez to a local fire station where paramedics then took him to the hospital.

Gonzalez is still recovering, according to an online fundraiser.

Richardson said Gonzalez is a father who works with his hands to support his family. The mayor called him recently to see how he was doing and offer help. He said Gonzalez’s biggest request was for privacy.

“What he really shared with me is that he doesn’t really want the attention, and that he’s mostly concerned about his children seeing him detained,” Richardson said.

Reporter Jacob Sisneros contributed to this article.

text:
Welcome to Court Crawl, Colorado Politics’ roundup of news from the third branch of government.

The state Supreme Court will return this week for oral arguments, plus the judicial discipline rulemaking body has proposed more new policies.

Recommended Stories

▶

In Supreme Court news

• Starting tomorrow, the Colorado Supreme Court will hear five oral arguments. Two of them will happen on Thursday at Overland High School in Aurora, as part of the long-running “Courts in the Community” program:

Brassill v. People: Do trial judges lose the ability to impose crime victim restitution on defendants if the prosecution hasn’t made a reasonable effort to bring the necessary details to a defendant’s sentencing hearing?

Solano v. People: Does the answer to the question in Brassill change if the defendant didn’t object or ask the prosecutor to explain whether the restitution details were available at sentencing?

People in the Interest of A.T.S.: Did the Court of Appeals correctly uphold a juvenile defendant’s sex assault adjudication even after it found the victim’s testimony by CCTV was improper?

Spectrum Retirement Communities, LLC et al. v. Continental Casualty Company: Did an operator of senior living facilities adequately show it should receive insurance coverage for the parts of its property that were unusable during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic?

People v. Ruiz: Did a trial judge correctly conclude that the legislature unconstitutionally requires in motor vehicle theft cases that a defendant only “reasonably should have known” that the car was stolen?

• The Supreme Court largely reversed a Larimer County judge’s decision blocking prosecutors from using certain evidence that police obtained against a defendant.

• The justices intervened in two ongoing cases to answer whether a lawsuit should be paused while a civil defendant appeals an order denying arbitration and whether a criminal defendant is facing a double jeopardy violation with two separate prosecutions.

• While the Supreme Court decided to answer whether insurance agents have a duty to accurately inform customers about insurance coverage in one case, it inexplicably turned down a second case raising the same issue with the same trial judge involving a home loss from the same natural disaster.

Heard on appeal

• After a Denver judge gave an incorrect statement of the law to jurors in an attempted murder case, the Court of Appeals ordered a new trial.

• The Court of Appeals revived a Montrose County man’s defamation claim against his son.

In federal news

• The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit concluded that three people could be deported after FedEx never delivered their appeal paperwork to the court within the legal deadline.

• A woman and her son will receive a new asylum hearing because an immigration judge never asked her whether she desired legal representation, as regulations require.

• A federal judge declined to get involved in Colorado’s garnishment of a Larimer County man’s veterans’ benefits for child support.

• A Jefferson County SWAT officer is immune from liability after he shot a suspect in the stomach as the man opened the door.

• Aurora officers may be sued for unconstitutionally detaining a man who looked nothing like what a 911 caller reported, a judge ruled.

• A former Salida employee failed to adequately allege she was subjected to discrimination or retaliation.

• Jurors will decide whether corrections officials violated an incarcerated plaintiff’s constitutional rights by failing to protect him from another inmate nicknamed “Stabby,” a judge decided.

• Douglas County sheriff’s deputies may be sued for detaining a teenager who was not violating the curfew ordinance.

Judicial discipline

• The Judicial Discipline Rule-Making Committee has announced 10 proposed rules for public comment. Written feedback is due by Oct. 21 and there will be a virtual comment session on Oct. 26.

• Among the proposed changes is a provision encouraging stipulated settlements between judicial discipline authorities and accused judges.

• “If you couldn’t have settlements in civil cases or criminal cases or other professional licensure cases, things would grind to a halt. It would almost be like no justice because you wouldn’t get there very quickly,” the committee’s vice chair, Nancy Cohen, told lawyers during a presentation.

In immigration news

• Readers are likely aware that Colorado’s U.S. District Court has been facing a flood of “habeas corpus” petitions from those in immigration detention. The most common allegation is that the government is improperly denying bond hearings to people who are eligible by law, and the 10th Circuit recently ruled that the government’s mandatory detention position is incorrect.

• But petitions are still being processed, and there are some interesting developments.

• Magistrate Judge N. Reid Neureiter is pondering sanctions against Immigration Judge Robyn Ross after she violated his order by holding a second bond hearing for a Venezuelan woman despite Neureiter’s directive that another judge take over the case.

• Magistrate Judge Cyrus Y. Chung observed that an immigration judge appeared to comply with his previous order to conduct a new bond hearing, but the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to defend the decision in a response to a habeas petitioner’s continued challenge. Therefore, Chung had no choice but to order release from custody:

• Neureiter ordered a petitioner’s release because the evidence “uniformly weighed against a finding” that the man was likely to flee, but Immigration Judge Meghan Buhl-Madsen decided he was a flight risk anyway:

• Chung also noted that Buhl-Madsen initially denied a petitioner the opportunity to testify at his bond hearing and invoked evidence not presented by either side when deciding to deny bond. That created a perception she was “looking to rationalize a preordained decision to deny bond”:

• Senior Judge John L. Kane agreed with Senior Judge William J. Martínez (as has Senior Judge R. Brooke Jackson) that there is “mounting evidence” of immigration bond hearings having “preordained outcomes”:

• Judge S. Kato Crews wrote that “the cruelty appears to be the point,” after the government gave a habeas petitioner a notice to appear with completely incorrect information, an immigration judge dismissed the deportation case, but the government continued to detain him. Also, the government blew past its deadline by one week to respond:

Vacancies and appointments

• There are three finalists to succeed retiring Arapahoe County District Court Judge Bonnie McLean: Jefferson County Magistrate Bryce David Allen, Arapahoe County Magistrate James Christopher Boeckx, and Patrick E. Thompson.

• There are also three finalists to succeed former Gunnison County Court Judge Ashley Burgemeister, who resigned this month: Kyle Ipson, Hinsdale County Court Judge James McDonald, and Jon Schumacher.

• Applications are due by Oct. 26 to succeed former Crowley County Court Judge Jeremy P. Boyce, who resigned rather than face voter retention after his performance commission unanimously found he does not meet the standards for a judge. The position is part-time and doesn’t require a law degree.

Miscellaneous proceedings

• The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments about whether to let Boulder County and the city of Boulder proceed with their lawsuit seeking climate change-related damages against fossil fuel producers.

• Colorado judges spoke with lawyers about how to handle ethical and professional dilemmas, including questionable uses of artificial intelligence.

• A lawsuit alleges Rep. Sheila Lieder, D-Littleton, directed a staff member to perform campaign work during legislative hours.

title: Ilhan Omar denies any fraud, blasts probe as a political hit job as scrutiny widens - KOKH

"In the case of Ilhan Omar, if she's going to be denaturalized, more likely it would be under the civil context," Fahey said.
He pointed to the potential statute of limitations affecting criminal naturalization fraud charges.

text:
A federal investigation involving Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is raising questions about whether a naturalized American citizen could lose citizenship if immigration fraud is proven, as investigators reportedly examine allegations involving the congresswoman's immigration history and financial disclosures.

Federal authorities are reportedly reviewing Omar's citizenship records and possible discrepancies in documents connected to her immigration history, along with separate questions about financial information disclosed during her time in Congress.

Omar has denied wrongdoing and accused the Trump administration of politically targeting her.

Former federal prosecutor and former acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement Director Jonathan Fahey joined The National News Desk to explain the legal standards investigators would need to meet and how federal law distinguishes between criminal and civil proceedings to revoke naturalized citizenship.

Fahey said the government has two primary legal avenues for pursuing denaturalization, the process of revoking citizenship obtained through naturalization.

"In the criminal context, the crime of naturalization fraud, if you're convicted of that crime, denaturalization is automatic," Fahey said. "It's part of the consequences in the statute."

Under federal law, a conviction for knowingly procuring naturalization contrary to law can result in citizenship being revoked.

The government can also pursue denaturalization through a civil lawsuit, although it must meet a demanding evidentiary standard.

"On the civil grounds, the government would need to go in front of a judge in an Article III court and prove by clear and convincing evidence that there was naturalization fraud, to then revoke someone civilly," Fahey said.

Federal courts have held that citizenship cannot be revoked based on minor mistakes or immaterial inaccuracies. The government must establish legally sufficient grounds for denaturalization, and the evidence must satisfy the applicable standard.

Fahey said the distinction could be particularly important in Omar's case because of how long ago she became a naturalized citizen.

"In the case of Ilhan Omar, if she's going to be denaturalized, more likely it would be under the civil context," Fahey said.

He pointed to the potential statute of limitations affecting criminal naturalization fraud charges.

"She was naturalized in 2000, I believe. So the statute of limitations is ten years," Fahey said.

Fahey suggested that a criminal prosecution based solely on conduct from that period could face significant timing obstacles unless prosecutors identified legally applicable exceptions or additional conduct.

"That would have already run on that case, absent a few considerations like an ongoing conspiracy," he said.

Civil denaturalization proceedings are not subject to the same general criminal limitations period, although the government must still establish that citizenship was unlawfully obtained or procured through material misrepresentation or concealment.

Fahey said the circumstances surrounding any alleged false information would be central to determining whether the government could successfully pursue a case.

One question raised during the interview involved what would happen if incorrect information originally came from a parent rather than the person who was naturalized.

Fahey said age, knowledge and participation could become important factors in evaluating the evidence.

"If she was like three years old at the time and was a total unwitting, I think she would have a better chance of remaining naturalized," Fahey said.

He cautioned, however, that the legal consequences could depend on whether the individual was legally eligible for citizenship in the first place.

"You could still denaturalize someone because they shouldn't have been naturalized," Fahey said.

The discussion then turned to allegations that Omar may have been older than certain immigration documents indicated when she became a citizen.

Fahey said that if investigators established a false date of birth, they would need to examine whether Omar knew about the alleged discrepancy or knowingly relied on it.

"Here, I think it's quite different because, you know, she was either, if it was fraud, she was 18 at the time. She was an adult and she presumably knew what was going on," Fahey said.

The allegation that Omar falsified her age has not been established in court, and the interview did not provide documentary evidence proving the claim.

Fahey said investigators would likely look for records showing whether any allegedly incorrect information continued to be used after the naturalization process.

"That's why the search warrant's so important," Fahey said.

"Because if they find documents that then went with the continued use of a false date of birth, assuming it's false, that would show she was complicit in the earlier naturalization or if she adopted that fraud," he added.

Fahey emphasized that such conclusions would depend on whether investigators could first establish that the underlying information was fraudulent.

"So I think that's a harder part for her because she may show, if it was fraud, she was actually an adult at the time and not a child," he said.

A judicially authorized search warrant requires a finding of probable cause, but it does not establish that the subject of an investigation committed a crime.

The government would still need to prove the relevant legal elements in court before citizenship could be revoked.

The investigation has also reportedly expanded into questions about Omar's financial disclosures.

Members of Congress are required to file periodic financial disclosure reports identifying certain assets, liabilities, income sources and financial transactions.

The disclosures are intended to provide transparency about lawmakers' financial interests and potential conflicts of interest.

Fahey said prosecutors examining possible false statements would need to determine whether any inaccuracies were material, meaning they were significant enough to affect a government function or decision.

"They would have to show that there was a material false statement, meaning a statement that could make a difference, essentially," Fahey said.

He pointed to reported changes in Omar's financial disclosures as an issue investigators might examine.

"On these financial disclosures, when she was going from large swings of money upwards of tens of millions of dollars back to almost nothing, those are certainly significant changes," Fahey said.

"So if false, meaning they would be material," he added.

Changes in reported financial holdings do not, by themselves, establish fraud. Congressional disclosure forms often report assets within broad value ranges, and changes can result from business valuations, transactions or other legitimate financial developments.

Fahey said investigators would need to establish that any inaccurate statements were knowingly and materially false rather than the result of a reporting mistake.

He referenced 18 U.S.C. 1001, the federal statute prohibiting certain knowingly and willfully false material statements in matters within federal jurisdiction.

"It's a federal felony," Fahey said.

He argued that significant discrepancies, if proven to be intentionally false, could provide a stronger basis for prosecutors to pursue charges.

"These statements are not the type of things that would be sort of a clerical error or a mistake," Fahey said, referring to the magnitude of the changes he described.

"They're massive changes. So if they are false, it would be a very, very strong argument that they were materially false."

The applicable criminal penalties would depend on the specific offense charged and the facts established. The ordinary maximum penalty under Section 1001 is generally five years in prison, with a higher maximum applying in certain specified circumstances.

Omar has denied allegations of wrongdoing, and no criminal conviction or judicial finding establishing that she falsified financial disclosures was presented during the interview.

The conversation also addressed Omar's claim that the investigation is politically motivated.

Fahey said members of Congress are subject to federal criminal laws like other Americans, but prosecutors must ensure that an investigation is driven by evidence rather than political considerations.

"Federal prosecutors are required to prosecute, you know, if they find these, are required to investigate," Fahey said.

He argued that elected office should neither shield someone from a legitimate investigation nor serve as the basis for targeting that person.

"This shouldn't be a shield and shouldn't give her immunity, nor should it be, you know, she shouldn't be targeted simply because of it," Fahey said.

Fahey also criticized Democrats who have raised concerns about political prosecutions, arguing that Republicans have made similar accusations about previous investigations involving President Donald Trump.

"It's certainly ironic that the Democrats are now saying this after years of not only targeting President Trump, but everyone in his orbit suffered at the hands of sort of political prosecutions," Fahey said.

That characterization reflects Fahey's political assessment rather than a legal finding about those earlier cases.

The Justice Department's handling of politically sensitive investigations has remained a subject of debate, particularly when investigations involve elected officials or individuals closely associated with the president.

Legal experts generally emphasize that prosecutors must apply the law consistently, avoid selective enforcement and base charging decisions on admissible evidence.

Fahey said the ultimate outcome of the investigation involving Omar will depend on whether federal authorities can establish sufficient evidence to support a legal proceeding.

"But again, the facts will be what they are," Fahey said.

He emphasized that allegations alone are not enough to establish criminal liability or justify revoking someone's citizenship.

"If they go in front of the court, a judge or jury will decide," Fahey said.

The investigation remains a developing matter, with significant questions about the underlying evidence, the nature of the allegations and whether prosecutors will pursue any charges or civil proceedings.

For now, Omar remains a naturalized U.S. citizen and a sitting member of Congress, and the allegations discussed in the interview have not been proven in court.

title: Federal prosecutors charge 28 California green card holders with voting violations
description:
Twenty-eight immigrants from across California are facing federal charges alleging they illegally registered to vote or voted in California elections, federal prosecutors announced Monday in the Trump administration’s latest effort to imply California election rolls are riddled with fraudulent voters.
“Twenty-eight out of 23 million registered voters in California is just … a drop in the bucket numerically,” Bonta said.
Federal prosecutors said all of the 28 foreign nationals who face charges are lawful permanent residents, otherwise known as green card holders.
Essayli said that in the last two months, federal prosecutors have charged around 113 noncitizens in 20 states with illegal voting and registration offenses.
Federal prosecutors also sought information on registered voters in San Diego County, the news outlet inewsource reported, as well as Orange County, according to records obtained last week by CalMatters.
text:
Twenty-eight immigrants from across California are facing federal charges alleging they illegally registered to vote or voted in California elections, federal prosecutors announced Monday in the Trump administration’s latest effort to imply California election rolls are riddled with fraudulent voters.

The charges come days after federal authorities filed a lawsuit against state and Los Angeles County election officials that seeks to force elections officials not to count up to 20,000 registered voters’ ballots because federal prosecutors suspect those voters could be non-citizens.

“Today’s charges demonstrate why that lawsuit is so important,” Acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told reporters. “It’s about preventing voter fraud that cancels out the votes of U.S. citizens. Enforcing federal law increases the integrity of elections.”

McCotter said federal prosecutors filed a motion urging the judge overseeing the lawsuit in federal court in Los Angeles to order state officials to segregate the ballots that prosecutors suspect may have already been mailed to noncitizens.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta told reporters at an event Monday that voter fraud is wrong. If the suspects are guilty, they should be held accountable, he said.

But Bonta noted that the charges are hardly proof that California’s elections are filled with fraudulent voters as President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed.

“Twenty-eight out of 23 million registered voters in California is just … a drop in the bucket numerically,” Bonta said. “It’s 0.0001% of all the registered voters, and it makes the point that there is no widespread voter fraud.”

The announcement comes just 15 days before the Nov. 3 election in which Californians are already deciding on a new governor, 14 statewide ballot measures and several competitive races that will be key to which party controls Congress.

It’s part of a national push by the Trump administration to find examples of noncitizens voting illegally in elections. Independent experts and state election officials say that voter fraud is exceedingly rare, despite claims from Trump and his allies that it happens on such a massive scale as to sway elections in Democrats’ favor.

Federal prosecutors said all of the 28 foreign nationals who face charges are lawful permanent residents, otherwise known as green card holders. That means they are legally allowed to stay in the country but they are not citizens and are not allowed to vote in elections.

The defendants live in cities around the state from Los Angeles County to Sacramento. Of them, 22 are accused of voting in at least one election including as recently as the June primary; five only registered to vote and one submitted a provisional ballot in 2020, prosecutors say.

Essayli said that in the last two months, federal prosecutors have charged around 113 noncitizens in 20 states with illegal voting and registration offenses.

The arrests represent just a miniscule fraction of registered voters. For example, more than 9.4 million Californians cast ballots in the June primary election.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who oversees prosecutors in Los Angeles, said the federal government may charge state election officials with crimes if they allowed noncitizens to vote.

“They are being complicit in noncitizens voting in our elections,” Essayli said. “And as they were warned last week, not only is it a civil violation, but they could also face criminal consequences for that conduct if they knowingly process ballots from noncitizens once we’ve informed them who the noncitizens are.”

The charges come weeks after federal investigators issued grand jury subpoenas to Los Angeles elections officials seeking information on registered voters.

Federal prosecutors also sought information on registered voters in San Diego County, the news outlet inewsource reported, as well as Orange County, according to records obtained last week by CalMatters.

The Department of Homeland Security recently claimed that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls; they sent the state the names of only 185 voters. Nevada officials confirmed they were all U.S. citizens.

Gov. Gavin Newsom last week called the Trump administration’s voter fraud hunt “a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day.”

He said the prosecutors’ request to throw out ballots “should scare the hell out of every American.”

“We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook,” Newsom said in a statement.

KQED’s Christopher Alam contributed to this report.

text:
Home security video captured three U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents cornering and questioning a man Monday morning in SoMa. One, a plainclothes officer in a red flannel and a baseball cap, drew his gun on the man, who appeared unarmed.

Juan Carlos, a financial analyst who asked that his last name be withheld for privacy, said he witnessed the incident from his 6th Street apartment. When he heard yelling around 8:45 a.m., he looked out his front door and saw the plainclothes officer with his gun out. He didn’t immediately see the badge around the officer’s neck and couldn’t tell he was law enforcement.

“I was like, ‘Am I about to see someone get murdered?’” Juan Carlos said. “I said, ‘Hey, you’re being recorded.’ They didn’t give a fuck.”

Footage captured by Juan Carlos’ security cameras shows a man in a navy-blue suit and brown leather shoes running across the street toward the cameras, with the plainclothes officer just behind him. Soon, two other officers in green ICE uniforms catch up, and the pursued man stops. “Get on the ground!” one of them yells.

The suited man continues to stand and asks what the officers are doing. One asks why he ran. “I don’t know who you guys are,” he responds, adding that he was on his way to work. “You’re violating my rights as a U.S. citizen,” he says.

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) introduced a bill to restore temporary protected status for Yemen, which the Trump administration officially terminated in July, following a legal battle. Conditions in countries designated for TPS are too dangerous for people to return safely. Those who qualify for TPS are allowed to remain in the U.S. temporarily.

Yemen is facing one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises amid an ongoing civil war and foreign siege and military intervention, including the Trump administration’s bombing of the country last year. The Department of State has placed Yemen under a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory, citing violence, kidnapping, landmines and unexploded ordinances, as well as the re-emergence of diseases like cholera, polio, and measles.

Michigan, especially Rep. Tlaib’s district, is home to large Yemeni communities.

“The Trump administration is threatening our Yemeni neighbors, and I will not stand for it. DHS unjustly terminated temporary protected status for Yemen without care for the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe and escalating armed conflict facing the country,” said Rep. Tlaib. “The Trump administration was bombing civilians in Yemen as recently as last year and is currently trying to give the Saudi monarchy billions of dollars in bombs and jets to continue the devastation. The State Department explicitly warns against any travel to Yemen, and yet, this president wants to send our neighbors back as part of his racist mass deportation agenda. I am proud to represent one of the most Yemeni districts in the country. These are our family members, coworkers, friends, and neighbors. They belong here, and I will not turn my back on them.”

In April, Rep. Tlaib led 23 Members of Congress in urging the Trump administration to halt its planned termination of TPS for Yemen. Conditions in the country have only deteriorated since then.

The Yemen TPS Act is cosponsored by 14 Members of Congress: U.S. Reps. André Carson (IN-07), Jim Costa (CA-21), Jesús “Chuy” García (IL-04), Jonathan L. Jackson (IL-01), Henry C. “Hank” Johnson, Jr. (GA-04), Timothy Kennedy (NY-26), Gwen Moore (WI-04), Seth Moulton (MA-06), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-at large), Ilhan Omar (MN-05), Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Lateefah Simon (CA-12), Shri Thanedar (MI-13), and Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12).

text:
Recent federal immigration actions and proposed rule changes affecting Optional Practical Training, Curricular Practical Training and Duration of Status can raise questions and uncertainty for international students. Ohio State continues to closely monitor federal rules, legal developments and guidance, assess how they may affect our international community, and share timely information and resources as they become available.

Ohio State’s international students contribute greatly to enhancing the Buckeye experience for all students, faculty and staff. The Office of International Affairs and the broader Ohio State community remain committed to providing international students with clear guidance, timely resources and compassionate support as they navigate changes that may affect their academic and personal journeys.

Optional Practical Training

On October 8, 2026 the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a proposed rule that would require all schools, including Ohio State, to pay fees for all Optional Practical Training (OPT) applications. The rule would impose a $70,000 fee on initial OPT applications, pre-completion and post-completion, and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT applications.

Ohio State intends to submit a public comment outlining the basis for its opposition to the proposed rule by the November 9 deadline.

Action taken by Ohio State

Sent a message to all international students notifying them of the proposed rule.

Updated the OPT webpage to include information about the proposed rule; while the proposed rule is under review, current OPT application procedures remain unchanged.

Curricular Practical Training

The Student and Exchange Visitor Program issued guidance on August 24, 2026 specifying that Curricular Practical Training (CPT) may be authorized only when the practical training is an integral and required part of an established curriculum.

Based on this recent guidance the Office of International Affairs can only approve CPT for students whose academic program requires an internship as a mandatory requirement for graduation. Ohio State must follow the guidance set by federal authorities to ensure students and the university remain in compliance with the federal guidance.

Action taken by Ohio State

Sent a message to all international students and Ohio State’s University Career Services Committee notifying them of the CPT guidance.

Updated the CPT webpage to reflect the eligibility requirements and guidance, including application procedures.

Duration of Status

On July 17, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published the final rule in the Federal Register that ended “duration of status,” which previously allowed those on F or J visas to remain in the United States as long as necessary to complete their academic program, practical training or research activity provided they continue to meet all immigration requirements.

Just before the government’s scheduled implementation, a federal court issued a nationwide preliminary injunction blocking the rule from taking effect on September 15. As a result, the immigration regulations for F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors remain unchanged while litigation continues.

description:
Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil on Monday asked the US Supreme Court to overturn a ruling that opened the door for President Donald Trump's administration to re-arrest and deport the Palestinian activist.
His lawyers say the Supreme Court should make clear immigration law does not prevent noncitizens from pursuing cases arguing they have been detained to punish them for speech that is protected by the US Constitution's First Amendment.
Khalil faces possible re-arrest and deportation pending Supreme Court ruling If the 3rd Circuit's decision is allowed to stand, Khalil faces the prospect of arrest and deportation, after the Board of Immigration Appeals in April rejected his challenge to an immigration judge's order that he be removed to Algeria or Syria.

text:
Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil on Monday asked the US Supreme Court to overturn a ruling that opened the door for President Donald Trump's administration to re-arrest and deport the Palestinian activist.

Khalil's lawyers asked the justices to take up his case after the Philadelphia-based 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that federal immigration law barred a lower-court judge from ordering his release from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.

Khalil was among the most prominent foreign students to be arrested last year as the ​Trump administration pursued a campaign to detain and deport noncitizens who ⁠engaged in pro-Palestinian activism on college campuses.

His lawyers say the Supreme Court should make clear immigration law does not prevent noncitizens from pursuing cases arguing they have been detained to punish them for speech that is protected by the US Constitution's First Amendment.

"If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech," Khalil told reporters on Monday.

Khalil faces possible re-arrest and deportation pending Supreme Court ruling

If the 3rd Circuit's decision is allowed to stand, Khalil faces the prospect of arrest and deportation, after the Board of Immigration Appeals in April rejected his challenge to an immigration judge's order that he be removed to Algeria or Syria.

A lower court order barring him from being re-detained remains in place for now until the Supreme Court rules. A separate appeal of the immigration judge's order remains pending.

Khalil, a prominent figure in pro-Palestinian protests against Israel's war in Gaza, is an Algerian citizen who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria.

Immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 in the lobby of his university residence in Manhattan despite being a lawful permanent resident, or green-card holder. His wife and their 1-year-old son are both US citizens.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio had invoked an obscure provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act to deem Khalil removable, citing his involvement in "antisemitic protests and disruptive activities" at Columbia in 2024 the government said fostered a hostile environment for Jewish students.

He was released from a Louisiana detention center in June 2025 after the New Jersey-based US District Judge Michael Farbiarz, an appointee ​of former Democratic President Joe Biden, ordered ​the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, to ⁠release him.

Federal appeals court overturns ruling that secured Khalil's release

In January, a 2-1 panel of the 3rd Circuit overturned Farbiarz's decision, saying that under the Immigration and Nationality Act, Khalil's claims could not be addressed through a district court and instead could be ​raised in an appeal of a removal order from an immigration judge.

After the full appeals court declined to reconsider the case, Khalil turned to the Supreme Court.

Federal appeals courts are split on whether district judges may hear challenges like Khalil's or whether such claims must proceed first through immigration courts, which are not part of the federal judiciary but are instead run by the US Department of Justice.

text:
San Diego, CA. — Today, U.S. Representative Scott Peters (CA-50) led members of the San Diego Congressional delegation, Reps Juan Vargas (CA-52), Sara Jacobs (CA-51), and Mike Levin (CA-49), and U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-CA) and Adam Schiff (D-CA) in a letter to U.S. Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Markwayne Mullin on recent reports of increased immigration enforcement activity in San Diego and elsewhere in California. This comes a month after San Diego Unified School District (SDUSD) and San Diego City College both informed the Congressman's office of multiple U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests outside their schools.

The Members cited more frequent reports and videos online of a growing presence of agents detaining individuals throughout San Diego. They stated that these practices are actually more harmful, as the “presence of ICE officers destabilizes the sense of safety schools offer and places an additional burden on school staff and local communities.”

The Members added that the “fear among students and families that these incidents cause can also negatively impact a student’s educational engagement, mental and physical health, academic performance, and developmental trajectories. Parents should be able to bring their children to class and return to pick them up without fearing that a routine school day could end in family separation. Teachers should be able to focus on teaching and students on learning.”

They also outlined how federal agents have been noted at other sensitive locations, such as hospitals, places of worship, and courthouses, which threatens the very safety these places are supposed to offer.

“When people are afraid to seek medical care, attend religious services, or appear in court, the consequences reach well beyond any individual arrest. These are places where people turn for help, and enforcement practices that discourage access leave entire communities less safe,” the Members added.

To address their concerns, the members demanded a response to the following questions;

Has DHS authorized an “Operation Safe California” or similar immigration enforcement operation for California? If so, what is the scope of the operation? Who authorized it? And when was it authorized?

Has DHS authorized enhanced immigration enforcement in San Diego, and, if so, how long is it expected to last? How many agents are involved?

Who are the intended targets, and what criteria govern whom officers or agents stop or detain?

Have officers or agents been directed or authorized to conduct enforcement at or near schools or other sensitive locations?

“San Diegans deserve a clear explanation of the federal activity being reported in our communities,” the Members concluded.

See the full letter here.

Background: As unregulated ICE activity has heavily increased throughout the second Trump Administration, Rep. Peters has called out DHS for allowing federal agents to terrorize communities without notice or consequences, leaving communities less safe.

Shortly after the arrests at San Diego schools, Rep. Peters hosted a virtual training event with Rep. Juan Vargas (CA-52) to ensure community members understand how to safely interact with federal law enforcement officers, what to do if they or their loved ones are detained by agents, and what resources are available to San Diego’s immigrant community.

And last year, Rep. Peters led the Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act, which would establish stronger standards for immigration agents' use of force. The bill would also restrict the use of crowd munitions like tear gas and create greater transparency in enforcement by requiring the use of body cameras and strictly limiting the use of masks. Rep. Peters has pushed Republicans to pass these commonsense reforms, but they have continued to block this bill from a vote.

name: Litigation
title: Mahmoud Khalil asks US supreme court to review his deportation case - The Guardian
description:
If the supreme court takes the case, lawyers expect arguments to take place in the spring.
If it declines, or if it upholds the third circuit’s decision, Khalil could immediately be redetained and deported, and may continue to make his case from overseas.
In Khan Suri’s case, an appeals court in Virginia upheld a lower court’s order to release him, splitting from the court that ruled on Khalil’s case.
The government has asked the supreme court to review that decision, and the court might decide to review the cases jointly.
“This administration knows all too well that its baseless allegations and smears against me cannot survive the slightest scrutiny in federal court,” Khalil said on Monday.
text:
Attorneys for Mahmoud Khalil, the former Columbia University student who has become the symbol of the Trump administration’s crusade against pro-Palestinian speech, have petitioned the US supreme court to review his case – the final chapter in a months-long legal saga that could determine countless foreign citizens’ ability to challenge their detention by US immigration authorities in federal court.

Khalil, a US permanent resident who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, was arrested in his Columbia housing in March 2025, the first of several foreign students and scholars the Trump administration targeted over their advocacy for Palestinian rights. He was detained for more than three months in an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Louisiana before a federal judge in New Jersey, where he had been briefly held before ICE moved him, ordered him released while his immigration process proceeds.

“This fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country, it’s really about whether anyone in this country can speak out for Palestinians without being punished for it,” Khalil said during a press conference on Monday.

The US departments of state, justice and homeland security did not respond to requests for comment.

The government has cited an obscure McCarthy-era law to argue that Khalil and the other scholars’ pro-Palestinian expression posed a threat to US foreign policy objectives. So far, no court has fully weighed in on the constitutionality of the law, with legal arguments instead focused on whether district courts have the authority to order people released from immigration detention while their immigration cases are under way. Khalil’s attorneys and immigrants rights advocates warn that if the supreme court rules the district courts lack such authority, that would effectively result in people the government has detained unconstitutionally to languish in immigration detention with no recourse, potentially for months or years.

“It’s terrifying,” said Baher Azmy, the legal director of the Center for Constitutional Rights, which is part of Khalil’s legal team. “What’s particularly dangerous about this decision is the idea that you can be in detention based on some arbitrary executive diktat – and there is nothing you can do to challenge it.”

The New Jersey judge who ordered Khalil’s release had done so on the basis that his detention was likely to be found unconstitutional on first amendment grounds, because Khalil was targeted over constitutionally protected speech. In a related case, a federal judge in Boston ruled last year that those protections apply to noncitizens.

But a federal appeals court in Pennsylvania reversed the New Jersey judge’s decision that freed Khalil in January, with an expanded panel upholding that reversal in a 6-5 split decision. In a dissenting opinion, three of the judges who voted against argued that the ruling flouted legal precedent and “imperil[ed] the civil liberties of [Khalil] and similarly situated noncitizens”.

If the supreme court takes the case, lawyers expect arguments to take place in the spring. If it declines, or if it upholds the third circuit’s decision, Khalil could immediately be redetained and deported, and may continue to make his case from overseas.

Mohsen Mahdawi and Badar Khan Suri, two other foreign scholars detained by the administration after Khalil, are also challenging their detention through the federal court system. In Khan Suri’s case, an appeals court in Virginia upheld a lower court’s order to release him, splitting from the court that ruled on Khalil’s case. The government has asked the supreme court to review that decision, and the court might decide to review the cases jointly. In Mahdawi’s case, the second court of appeals in New York initially sided with the government but has since ordered the case to be reheard.

Should the supreme court rule against Khalil, the decision would affect scores of people in immigration detention who would effectively be unable to challenge their detention through the judiciary – which has traditionally been more isolated from political interference than immigration courts, which are overseen by the executive branch.

“This administration knows all too well that its baseless allegations and smears against me cannot survive the slightest scrutiny in federal court,” Khalil said on Monday. “That’s why it’s doing everything it can to keep the federal courts away from looking at my case and they’re trying to channel it into their kangaroo immigration courts, because they can control the outcome.”

“We want to be in a constitutional court, a real court, while they want us to be in the president’s courts,” Azmy said of the jurisdictional dispute.
