text:
When more than 200 federal, state, and local agents descended on a rural horse-racing event in Wilder, Idaho in a sweeping immigration raid, what was supposed to be a Sunday family activity quickly turned into a nightmare. The agents violently detained around 400 people, including U.S. citizens, children, and grandparents.

At La Catedral Arena, children watched as their parents were thrown to the ground, zip-tied, and abused by masked agents. Mothers told us they couldn’t feed their babies, even as their children cried. People had guns pointed in their faces, had rubber bullets fired at them, and were forced to urinate in public.

Along with our partners, Cooley LLP and Stoel Rives LLP, the ACLU is representing three Latino families, who are U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, including children ages 3 to 16, and a proposed class of people who were at La Catedral Arena on October 19, 2025 in a lawsuit against the federal, state, and local officers that coordinated the unlawful and discriminatory raid. The lawsuit argues that those officials violated the Constitution by conspiring to abuse narrow criminal warrants to unlawfully detain hundreds of Latino event attendees in violation of their Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable detentions, and their right to equal protection regardless of ethnicity .

Wilder, Idaho, is a small, agricultural community in southwest Idaho. It is also a majority-Latino town. Wilder and the surrounding communities are home to a variety of Mexican cultural events, including dances, concerts, horse races, and rodeos. La Catedral Arena hosts horse races, food and toy vendors, and local businesses.

The raid at La Catedral is part of a broader pattern under the second Trump Administration of federal agencies colluding with local law enforcement to abuse narrow criminal warrants for mass immigration fishing expeditions targeted at Latinos. Our documentary provides a glimpse of how this pattern played out in Wilder.

Ivan Popoca, 40, is a lawful permanent resident who has lived in Idaho for most of his life. He has five children with his partner. Popoca is a plaintiff in our lawsuit, as well as his then-16-year-old son and then-10-year-old daughter who are both U.S. citizens. They enjoy attending the races as a family.

“I realized something was happening when I was talking with my friends, and I saw a helicopter flying above us,” Popoca said. “That’s when I thought something’s not right.”

An officer told Popoca’s son to put his hands up and turn around, while they tied his hands. Then, they escorted him and other teens to the horse track at gunpoint, ordering them on their knees at one point to shoot at a nearby SUV. Another agent grabbed Popoca’s daughter by the neck as she was trying to reunite with her father.

“They didn’t care that there were children there,” Popoca said.

Juana Rodriguez, then-30, is a U.S. citizen and mother of four children born and raised in Idaho. She has worked with bilingual children and their families to ensure they feel welcome and secure. Rodriguez is a plaintiff in our lawsuit along with her then-3-year-old son, who loves to attend horse races with his mother. On the day of the raid, Rodriguez and her son were denied food and water, and officers zip-tied Rodriguez.

“I was like, why? I have my son with me. I have to take care of him. I was scared. If I overreacted, I felt like they were going to hurt me,” Rodriguez said. “For the longest time, my son begged me for food. He begged me for water… I wish I could have done more in the moment, but I couldn’t. I think that’s what really gets to me till this day.”

Not only is Leo Morales the executive director of the ACLU of Idaho, he also grew up in Wilder. He first learned about the raid while he was on a run. He immediately drove to Wilder where a fence separated him from the people whose rights he sought to protect — and more than 200 armed agents in military-style gear.

“There’s a possibility that what the administration was trying to do is go to a rural community, where no one is paying attention, while there is like 1500 people at most,” Morales said. “But what they got wrong is that the ACLU is in every single state of the union, and our job is to protect the constitutional rights of every person, regardless of whether that’s in a large city or whether that’s in rural America.”

text:
MIAMI — More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire Monday.

Temporary Protected Status was set to end Oct. 19 for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But DHS said an announcement "will be made at the appropriate time." Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the U.S. covered by those temporary measures "retain protection." The Department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.

DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.

The decision Monday marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.

The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the U.S.

Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.

Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.

The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive U.S. administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.

The decision Monday comes two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Trump's hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.

The U.S. Congress created TPS in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.

It allows people already in the country to remain and work, for renewable periods if the homeland security secretary determines conditions are unsafe for their return. But it doesn't give them a pathway to permanent residency.

Supporters say that using this tool protects people from being returned to dangerous situations and that uprooting people covered by TPS after years of living in the U.S. is cruel. Critics, especially in the Trump administration, say successive administrations have extended these protections for years regardless of what has happened in the home countries.

Federal rules say TPS is automatically extended for six months if the secretary doesn't make a determination at least 60 days before the designation expires.

"We're grateful for an extension, however temporary, for TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan," said Myal Greene, president and CEO of World Relief, an organization that has provided humanitarian assistance in both countries. "We encourage the administration and Congress to consider longer term relief for women, men and children trying to carve out stability while their countries of origin remain in upheaval."

Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, noted Ukraine and Sudan are not safe and meet the legal conditions for TPS to be extended.

"Russia's war on Ukraine is nearing its fifth year, and Ukrainians are bracing for another winter under drone and missile strikes, driving civilian casualties and devastating critical infrastructure. Sudan remains locked in a brutal civil war marked by famine, widespread human rights abuses and the hallmarks of genocide," Vignarajah said. "It is not safe for these families to go home."

About ICE Flight Monitor ICE Flight Monitor uses publicly available aviation data to track U.S. immigration enforcement flights operated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and partner agencies.

text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, ICE Flight Monitor, housed at Human Rights First, released its latest monthly report, which reveals that the Trump administration conducted at least 331 removal flights to 38 countries in September, slightly more than the totals over the previous two months. This continued increase is largely driven by removal flights to Mexico, making up 35% (116 flights) of September’s removal flight total. These flights are separating families across the country and making it harder for people to secure legal counsel; many of these flights are taking place without due process and pose serious safety and security risks for the people being removed.

Additionally, ICE Flight Monitor has noted a dramatic increase in ICE Air domestic shuffle flights under the second Trump administration, with both the scale and reach of these flights expanding in September. Shuffle flights take people between detention centers across the U.S., often isolating them far away from their communities, their loved ones, and their legal counsel. These flights often take people thousands of miles away from their home, often without notifying their lawyer, or updating their location in ICE’s public tracking system. Several U.S. states are now seeing a growing number of these flights across multiple cities.

In September, ICE Flight Monitor tracked nine flights carrying third country nationals to six countries, including to the Dominican Republic and Guyana for the first time, as well as repeated flights to Ghana, Costa Rica, Panama and Paraguay. These flights forcibly transfer people—including those who were already granted protections by U.S. immigration judges—to places where they have no connection and they are at risk of persecution, harm, and even refoulement to the very places they escaped.

“Community members across the country, many of whom are in ongoing immigration processes, live with the debilitating fear that at any moment, they could be taken from their loved ones, and forced onto a plane taking them to a detention center thousands of miles away, or to a country they have never set foot in,” said Savi Arvey, Director of Policy, Refugee and Immigrant Rights at Human Rights First. “The Trump administration’s cruel deportation campaign subjects people to egregious harms—horrific conditions in detention centers, shuffle flights in the middle of the night to destinations unknown, removal to places where their lives are at imminent risk, and separation from their families. It is a policy that is designed to instill terror in the lives of our neighbors, friends and loved ones.

Key Findings from September Include:

In September, the Trump administration conducted 331 removal flights to 38 countries, a 48% increase from September 2025, largely driven by a continued increase in removal flights to Mexico, as well as flights to Guatemala and Honduras together accounting for roughly a third of all removal flights.

Removal flights to Haiti have increased to once per week (four times more than their previous pace of once/month) after the end of Temporary Protected Status for 350,000 Haitians living in the United States, despite U.S. State Department and UNHCR warnings against returns due to severe security and humanitarian risks. Removal flights to Venezuela have also increased to twice per week, despite recent natural disasters that have exacerbated the insecurity and instability of the country

This month, the administration carried out nine forced third country transfer flights to six countries – including the first-time transfers to the Dominican Republic and Guyana, as well as repeated transfers to Ghana, Costa Rica, Panama and Paraguay. September saw an 11-day pause in forced transfers of third country nationals due to a federal court ruling deeming the practice unlawful on September 18. However, such transfers have resumed following the U.S. Supreme Court stay, with ICE flights continuing to forcibly carry third country nationals to destinations across Latin America and the Caribbean and Sub-Saharan Africa, to places where people are at imminent risk of persecution, harm, arbitrary detention, or refoulement to their country of origin.

Domestic ICE Air transfer (“shuffle”) flights have expanded in scale and geographic reach under the second Trump administration, with airports in 10 new Florida cities now serving shuffle flights, in addition to Miami and Jacksonville. Major increases were also seen in the DMV region (+300%), Pennsylvania (+365%), Alabama, and California, reflecting broader escalations in the Trump administration’s cruel mass deportation and detention agenda.

Under the Trump administration, Alexandria, Louisiana remains the primary hub for removal flights taking people to places where they face harm and persecution– with over 400 flights in September – including 316 domestic shuffle flights and 122 deportation flights through the deportation hub. Advocates, Louisiana residents, and child welfare experts have raised the alarm about a new detention facility that is slated to open adjacent to the airport to hold children and families. Such a detention facility would inflict further trauma on children and families, expose them to contamination from chemicals detected at the site, and violate due process rights.

Read the September 2026 report here and explore the dashboard here.

About ICE Flight Monitor

ICE Flight Monitor uses publicly available aviation data to track U.S. immigration enforcement flights operated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and partner agencies. Founded on the methodology pioneered by researcher Tom Cartwright, the project provides transparent, data-driven reporting to strengthen accountability and inform the public about the human and democratic costs of mass deportation policies. Our public interactive ICE Flight Monitor Dashboard enables users to visualize common routes and patterns, track historical deportation flight trends, and look up recent deportation flights to specific countries.

text:
America's first Black president warned that targeting elected officials over their political views threatens a basic principle of American democracy.

Former U.S. President Barack Obama slammed the Trump administration's current investigation of Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, calling the immigration probe "appalling."

"It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can't selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say. But that's exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota," Obama wrote in a lengthy social media post. He added, "To understand why this is so appalling, it's important to know the facts."

As theGrio previously reported, federal agents raided Omar's home in Washington, D.C., in connection with the investigation into whether the congresswoman violated immigration laws prior to becoming a U.S. citizen.

Obama noted that Omar, a U.S. representative for Minnesota's 5th Congressional District, immigrated to the United States with her father at age 12. When she turned 17, Omar's father became a naturalized citizen, which gave Omar automatic citizenship by descent.

"Congresswoman Omar went on to graduate from college, work as a community organizer, become the first Somali-American legislator elected to public office in the U.S., and win a seat in Congress," noted America's first Black president, who pointed out that as a sitting member of Congress since 2019, Omar has been one of the Trump Administration's "fiercest critics."

"[It] has led the president to repeatedly single her out as someone who he believes does not belong in this country," said Obama.

He continued, "Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen. Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone — all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case."

Tom Homan, Trump's "border czar," recently claimed that he believed the administration had a "strong" case against Omar and suggested that she could be denaturalized as a result.

"I'm not going to get ahead of the bureau or HSI, but I've been told they have a strong case, and we'll let the evidence lead where it leads," Homan told Fox News.

But Obama said the probe is the result of the Trump administration using the "full weight of the federal government" against a "law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president." The former president noted that it's not the first time the Trump Justice Department has gone after his perceived political enemies, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook, and former FBI Director James Comey.

The Trump administration is also prosecuting U.S. Congresswoman LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) over her role in conducting an oversight visit at an immigration detention center in Newark. The unprecedented case has repeatedly been slammed as politically motivated and an attempt to intimidate other members of Congress. McIver, who just gave birth to her second child, faces 17 years in prison if convicted.

"In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case," said Obama. "But not before Congresswoman Omar's life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she's been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota."

President Obama continued, "The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar's political views." He added, "Because if this becomes the new normal, there's no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."

Among the cases to watch are Anderson v. Intel Corporation Investment Policy Committee, No.

text:
With summer behind us and fall underway, the Supreme Court’s 2026–2027 term is here. Twenty-five cases spanning civil, criminal, and administrative topics will occupy the Justices’ docket; several may capture the nation’s attention.

Among the cases to watch are Anderson v. Intel Corporation Investment Policy Committee, No. 25-498 (Jan. 16, 2026); Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, No. 25-352 (Mar. 30, 2026); and Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, No. 25-183 (Dec. 8, 2025).

Anderson v. Intel Corporation Investment Policy Committee

Anderson v. Intel Corporation Investment Policy Committee comes from the Ninth Circuit and concerns the fiduciary duties associated with managing retirement savings under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (“ERISA”). In Anderson, the plaintiffs commenced a putative class action under ERISA against the trustees of their employer’s (“Intel”) proprietary retirement funds. The plaintiffs relied on 29 U.S.C. § 1109(a), which imposes personal liability on ERISA plan fiduciaries for any losses associated with their breach of fiduciary duty, and alleged two fiduciary duties were breached: (1) the duty of prudence which was allegedly breached by investing retirement funds in private equity funds and hedge funds; and (2) the duty of loyalty which was allegedly breached by routing funds to companies in which Intel’s venture-capital arm had previously invested. In support of their duty of prudence claim, the plaintiffs claim “that hedge funds and private equity pose challenges and risks beyond those posed by ‘traditional investments’ such as mutual funds” and “do not increase diversification of asset classes.”

The district court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding the plaintiffs did not plausibly allege breaches of the duty of prudence or duty of loyalty, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed. For purposes of the Supreme Court review, the Ninth Circuit’s imprudence analysis is most pertinent. First, the Court rejected the plaintiffs’ argument that the trustees were imprudent by investing the plans’ assets in hedge funds and private equity—effectively dismissing the contention that these investment vehicles are categorical underperformers. It explained that a risky investment decision is not per se imprudent but must be measured against the portfolio as a whole and against comparable plans. Indeed, courts “evaluate prudence prospectively, based on the methods the fiduciaries employed, rather than retrospectively, based on the results they achieved[.]” As such, the Ninth Circuit explained that the plaintiffs’ theory that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently in like circumstances must be gauged by drawing a factually sound comparison—a “meaningful benchmark”—not merely an assertion that the “costs are too high, or returns are too low.”

To enable plaintiffs to present a “meaningful benchmark,” the Court noted the plan administrators, as ERISA requires, made extensive disclosures that sufficiently equipped the plaintiffs with detailed information about the plan’s assets to find a comparable plan and sufficiently plead that a prudent fiduciary in similar circumstances would have taken a different course of action. Instead, the plaintiffs did not use this information to strengthen their pleadings and, thus, the Court granted dismissal at the pleading stage. As it currently stands in the Eleventh Circuit, this decision serves as a practical reminder of what is needed at the pleading stage to cross the threshold “between possibility and plausibility.”

In October 2026, the Supreme Court will hear arguments on the following issue: “Whether, for claims predicated on fund underperformance, pleading that an Employee Retirement Income Security Act fiduciary failed to use the requisite ‘care, skill, prudence, or diligence’ under the circumstances and thus breached ERISA’s duty of prudence when investing plan assets requires alleging a ‘meaningful benchmark.’”

Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia

In Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, the Supreme Court will analyze whether a defendant may assert an affirmative defense as the basis for a summary judgment motion where the affirmative defense was not raised in a pleading, the defendant did not seek to amend the pleading, and amending the pleading could have been barred by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(b)(4).

This question arises in a pregnancy discrimination matter brought under Title VII. In April 2019, Plaintiff-Petitioner Jasmine Younge was hired as Deputy Chief of Staff and Director of Policy and Programs at the Fulton County District Attorney’s Office (the “DA’s Office”) by Fulton County District Attorney Paul Howard, Jr. In this position, Younge was third-in-command, supervised more than thirty employees, and worked closely with Howard. Approximately two months after starting, Younge told Howard that she was pregnant. Upon learning this information, Howard allegedly stopped meeting with Younge, reassigned some of her work duties, and two weeks later, fired Younge.

Younge sued the DA’s Office for pregnancy discrimination in violation of Title VII. In answering the complaint, the DA’s Office asserted several affirmative defenses, but did not assert that Younge was “personal staff” of an elected official exempt from Title VII’s protections. The DA’s Office later raised the personal staff exemption defense at summary judgment, and Younge opposed that motion, arguing that the DA’s Office could not belatedly raise the affirmative defense absent good cause. The district court allowed the DA’s Office to raise the personal staff exemption defense and granted summary judgment, and Younge appealed to the Eleventh Circuit. The Eleventh Circuit held that Younge was not unfairly surprised or prejudiced by the argument, noting that she never moved to reopen discovery, despite the magistrate judge’s willingness to do so. The Supreme Court will be asked to decide whether allowing the affirmative defense to be raised at summary judgment, rather than at the pleading stage, is permissible without amending or seeking to amend the answer, even where adding the affirmative defense would be barred by Rule 16.

Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia

Lastly, in Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, the Supreme Court will address: “Whether Title IX provides employees of federally funded educational institutions a private right of action to sue for sex discrimination in employment.”

This inquiry arrives before the Supreme Court as a consolidated appeal involving two separate cases decided by the Eleventh Circuit: Joseph v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, No. 23-11037, and Crowther v. Board of Regents, No. 23-12475. The common throughline is the Eleventh Circuit’s construction of Title IX as “an express remedial scheme for withdrawing federal funding,” not a vehicle for a private cause of action. The Court explained that unlike Title VII, which confers a private cause of action for victims of discrimination, Title IX serves to protect individuals from discriminatory practices by federally funded institutions. The one nationwide exception is that students are awarded an implied right of action to sue under Title IX because they would otherwise have no comparable statutory right unlike employees under Title VII. The Eleventh Circuit’s narrow interpretation of Title IX, however, is not uniformly applied throughout the nation and, therefore, the Supreme Court will have the opportunity to opine on the circuit split.

The Fall 2026 term began on October 5, 2026, and the Court will hear arguments in these and other cases throughout it. If you have any questions about these matters or topics, please reach out to the authors of this article or the EBG attorney with whom you normally coordinate.

text:
Since taking office on January 20, 2025, the Trump administration has pursued an unprecedented mass deportation agenda. U.S. officials have adopted a range of new tactics, many of which are unlawful, and undoubtedly cruel, to achieve this objective, including expanding the use of expedited removal, sending people from the United States to offshore detention facilities at the U.S. Naval Base in Guantanamo Bay, terminating protected legal statuses, disappearing people without due process, ramping up interior enforcement, and forcibly transferring individuals to other countries of which they are not citizens, where they have experienced grave human rights abuses. Federal courts have determined many of these actions to be unlawful and carried out with little to no transparency, while thousands of people’s lives are uprooted from communities across the country, families separated, and their rights systematically violated.

ICE Flight Monitor responds to this lawlessness and lack of information by using publicly available aviation data to monitor and document flights conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including deportation flights and domestic transfers between U.S. detention centers and deportation staging facilities. To date, the project has tracked 66,000+ flights since 2020. ICE Flight Monitor publishes monthly reports, tracks critical flights in real time, and provides updates on new developments through social media (@ICEFlightM; @iceflightmonitor.bsky.social). Additionally, our new public interactive ICE Flight Monitor Dashboard enables users to visualize common routes and patterns, track historical deportation flight trends, and look up recent deportation flights to any country.

text:
In Brief

Supreme Court reviews Trump administration immigration detention policies

Justices consider Boulder, Colorado, climate change lawsuit against ExxonMobil

Court to hear challenge to assault-style rifle bans in Illinois and Connecticut

Arguments scheduled on voting restrictions in Arizona backed by Republicans

The U.S. Supreme Court is hearing a series of important cases during its current nine-month term involving issues such as President Donald Trump’s immigration policies, asylum, assault-style rifle bans, race, Big Oil’s role in climate change, Republican-backed voting restrictions, LGBT rights and more.

Here is a look at some of the cases being argued during the term, which runs to about the end of June.

Big oil climate suit

The justices wrestled with complex questions over whether to let local governments try to hold oil companies liable for the harms caused by climate change during October 5 arguments in a bid by ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy to thwart a lawsuit by officials in Boulder, Colorado. The companies appealed after Colorado’s top court allowed Boulder’s lawsuit accusing them of violating state law and seeking unspecified monetary damages. The Trump administration backed the companies. The justices voiced concerns about unduly limiting the authority of states to pursue climate-related litigation, as well as the potential to unleash chaos if local governments across the country were permitted to sue these companies. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Trump’s mandatory immigration detention

The court will decide the legality of Trump’s policy that subjects millions of immigrants in the US illegally to mandatory detention during deportation proceedings. The policy is part of ​Trump’s pursuit of mass deportation. The justices took up the Trump administration’s appeal of a lower court’s ruling against the policy in a case involving a Brazilian national. The administration abandoned the US government’s longstanding interpretation of federal law that immigrants already living in the US could be released on bond while their cases play out in immigration court. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Trump’s third-country deportations

The justices will hear arguments in December over the Trump administration’s policy of deporting migrants to nations other than their own — so-called “third countries” — without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face. The court on September 29 let the administration continue the policy for the time being, putting on hold a federal judge’s ruling that removing migrants to third countries is unlawful. More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy, according to human rights groups. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Asylum and terrorism

The court will hear the Trump administration’s bid to deny asylum to a ​man who was forced to prepare meals for an apparent separatist group in Nigeria — a case that could expand what officials ‌may deem terrorist activity under American immigration law. The Justice Department appealed a lower court’s ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba. He was denied US asylum due to his work cooking for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen that US officials considered to be a terrorist organization. The lower court ruled that cooking did ​not qualify as “material support” for terrorism under the immigration statute. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Ban on assault-style rifles

The justices will hear arguments on Dec. 2 in a challenge to the legality of state prohibitions on assault-style rifles, giving them another chance to expand gun rights in a case that ​involves a type of weapon often associated with mass shootings. Lower courts upheld bans in Cook County, Illinois, and Connecticut on powerful ‌semiautomatic rifles such as AR-15s. The lower courts rejected arguments that the measures violate the US Constitution’s Second Amendment right to “keep and bear arms.” Gun rights groups and other challengers have said that Supreme Court precedents concerning the ​Second Amendment protect these firearms, which they described as in “common use.” A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Voting rights

The justices will hear arguments on Dec. 8 in a Republican-led bid to revive voter restrictions in Arizona that would stiffen proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registrants ‌and purge state voter rolls of alleged non-US citizens. Republicans appealed after a lower court halted provisions of Arizona’s law because they were found to violate a federal voting registration statute. President Donald Trump’s administration has backed key elements of the appeal. Critics have said the Arizona measure adds extra mandates for voting ​that unfairly target Latino, Native American and student voters. Those groups tend to favor Democratic candidates. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Race in student admissions

The justices will consider whether to revive a lawsuit against a Maryland county’s lottery admissions policy for four elite public middle ​schools that some parents claim unlawfully discriminates against Asian American applicants. The case has the court delving again into the contentious issue of race in student admissions. A coalition of parents appealed a lower court’s decision rejecting their claim that Montgomery County’s policy violates the US Constitution’s 14th Amendment guarantee of equal protection under the law. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

LGBT rights

The justices will hear arguments on Nov. 3 in a bid by the Archdiocese of Denver ​and other Catholic entities to be exempted from a Colorado preschool funding program’s ‌nondiscrimination requirement. A lower court found that Colorado’s program did not violate ​the religious rights of the Catholic plaintiffs under the US Constitution’s First Amendment. The program provides ​state funds for preschools. The Catholic plaintiffs objected to the state’s requirement ⁠that schools receiving funding under the program give all children “equal opportunity” to enroll in preschool regardless ​of certain characteristics, including the sexual orientation or gender identity of students or their family members. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

DOGE transparency

The justices will decide whether the Trump administration can avoid handing over records to a watchdog group about its Department of Government Efficiency, an initiative aimed at slashing agency budgets and workers spearheaded last year by the president’s former adviser Elon Musk. The administration appealed a judge’s order for DOGE to respond to requests by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington for information about its operations. The judge found that DOGE likely is a government agency covered by the federal Freedom of Information Act, or FOIA. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Federal ban on home distilling

The court will decide the legality of a federal ban on ​the home distilling of alcoholic spirits that was enacted in 1868 after the US Civil War ‌to crack down on liquor tax evasion. The dispute pits the Trump administration, which is defending the law, against challengers who argue that the home-distilling prohibition exceeds the authority of Congress under the US Constitution. More than a dozen Republican-led states have backed the legal challenge ​to the statute. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Epic Games suit against Apple

The justices will hear Apple’s bid to escape being found in contempt ​in its legal fight with “Fortnite” maker Epic Games after the iPhone maker was deemed in violation of a ‌judicial order mandating sweeping changes to its lucrative App Store in the antitrust litigation. Apple appealed a lower court’s ruling upholding a decision by an Oakland, California-based federal judge finding Apple in contempt in Epic’s 2020 lawsuit contesting App Store fees. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Pepsico trademark case

The court will hear arguments in a bid by ​canned-coffee maker Rise Brewing to hold PepsiCo liable for alleged trademark infringement ‌concerning Pepsi’s morning energy drink “Mtn Dew Rise.” Rise appealed a lower court’s ruling rejecting the company’s claim that the product name “Mtn Dew Rise” infringes its trademarks and creates customer confusion with ​its coffee brand. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

text:
Former U.S. President Barack Obama slammed the Trump administration’s current investigation of Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, calling the immigration probe “appalling.”

“It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say. But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota,” Obama wrote in a lengthy social media post. He added, “To understand why this is so appalling, it’s important to know the facts.”

As theGrio previously reported, federal agents raided Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., in connection with the investigation into whether the congresswoman violated immigration laws prior to becoming a U.S. citizen.

Obama noted that Omar, a U.S. representative for Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District, immigrated to the United States with her father at age 12. When she turned 17, Omar’s father became a naturalized citizen, which gave Omar automatic citizenship by descent.

“Congresswoman Omar went on to graduate from college, work as a community organizer, become the first Somali-American legislator elected to public office in the U.S., and win a seat in Congress,” noted America’s first Black president, who pointed out that as a sitting member of Congress since 2019, Omar has been one of the Trump Administration’s “fiercest critics.”

“[It] has led the president to repeatedly single her out as someone who he believes does not belong in this country,” said Obama.

He continued, “Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen. Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone — all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.”

Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar,” recently claimed that he believed the administration had a “strong” case against Omar and suggested that she could be denaturalized as a result.

“I’m not going to get ahead of the bureau or HSI, but I’ve been told they have a strong case, and we’ll let the evidence lead where it leads,” Homan told Fox News.

But Obama said the probe is the result of the Trump administration using the “full weight of the federal government” against a “law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.” The former president noted that it’s not the first time the Trump Justice Department has gone after his perceived political enemies, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook, and former FBI Director James Comey.

The Trump administration is also prosecuting U.S. Congresswoman LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) over her role in conducting an oversight visit at an immigration detention center in Newark. The unprecedented case has repeatedly been slammed as politically motivated and an attempt to intimidate other members of Congress. McIver, who just gave birth to her second child, faces 17 years in prison if convicted.

“In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case,” said Obama. “But not before Congresswoman Omar’s life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she’s been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota.”

President Obama continued, “The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views.” He added, “Because if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.”

text:
Student attorneys in the Immigration Clinic at GW Law helped a 72-year-old client avoid deportation by successfully obtaining a writ of coram vobis, which vacated shoplifting convictions from over a decade ago.

The Immigration Clinic, led by alumna Paulina Vera, B.A. ’12, J.D. ’15, professorial lecturer in law, is one of 15 clinics currently offered through GW Law’s Jacob Burns Community Legal Clinics Program. Student attorneys in the clinics provide free legal services to both individual and organizational clients in the Washington, D.C., area.

The client in this case is a grandmother and green card holder, originally from Hong Kong, who has lived in the U.S. for decades. About 10 years ago she was convicted for various shoplifting-related offenses and entered guilty pleas for all of them. The convictions were considered “crimes involving moral turpitude” and placed the client in removal proceedings in immigration court.

However, the client was never advised in her native language of Fuzhou when she was facing the shoplifting offenses. At the time, she relied on the help of her adult children, who were able to provide only amateur interpretation, and attorneys who spoke to her in Mandarin, which is linguistically very different from Fuzhou, Vera said. Because of the language barrier, the client did not understand the immigration consequences of her guilty pleas.

“Our client has no family left in Hong Kong and was facing a situation of going back to a place she had not lived in for decades, without any familial support,” Vera said. “In the U.S., she has all her adult children, as well as her grandchildren, who she spends her days caring for. When she entered the pleas, she did not understand the gravity of the situation she was facing because no one explained it to her in her native language.”

Vera and her predecessor, Alberto Benitez, professor emeritus, who led the Immigration Clinic for over two decades, worked with student attorneys to petition for a writ of coram vobis for the client. The coram vobis is a common law writ of error that allows a court to “correct its own record with reference to a vital fact not known when the judgment was rendered, and which could not have been presented by motion for a new trial, appeal or other existing statutory proceeding.”

The coram vobis is rarely granted, Vera said. Even so, the student attorneys in GW Law’s immigration clinic successfully obtained it, with the help of pro bono counsel at Paul Hastings, on August 12. With the writ in hand, the clinic was able to halt their client’s removal from the country. Their motion to do so was granted on September 16.

“This victory is a testament not only to the value of clinical legal education, but also to the quality of advocacy and instruction by Professor Vera, and our clinics as a whole,” Associate Dean for Experiential Programs and Clinic Director Carmia Caesar said.

The clinic worked with Sam Thomas, J.D. ’20, an associate in the litigation department at Paul Hastings, to represent the client in Virginia state court. Thomas represented the client alongside other Paul Hastings attorneys on the firm’s pro bono team, including Chris Brewer, Marguerite Harris and Faven Getahun, along with a team of student attorneys from the clinic.

“Creativity goes a long way in the law,” Thomas said. “The team at the clinic deserves so much credit here. They came to us with the idea of filing a coram vobis petition, which is a pretty unique procedural mechanism and form of relief.”

The support from Thomas and the other Paul Hastings attorneys was immensely valuable, Vera said.

“We attempted to get pro bono support for the post-conviction relief from a few firms before Sam and his team agreed to take on our client,” Vera said. “From working with our clinic students to draft the arguments, to doing the oral arguments to survive a motion to dismiss, to negotiating with the Virginia office of the attorney general to stipulate to facts, the Paul Hastings team advocated zealously to get our client this amazing result.”

An ‘only at GW’ experience

The Immigration Clinic’s success in this case was not only life-changing for the client; it also provided an intensive learning experience for the 14 students and alumni who worked on the case.

“Being a student attorney in the Immigration Clinic, specifically under Professor Vera’s direction, has been the highlight of my legal education,” said Mary O’Brien, the student attorney who filed the motion to terminate proceedings on behalf of the client. “Each student attorney that touched this case, each professor—from Professor Benitez to Professor Vera—all of them zealously fought for our client. I wouldn’t have had the honor of meeting and representing our client without those who came before me."

Thomas said he encourages every law student he meets to work for a clinic.

“The clinic gave me the opportunity to work hard on something that I care about, while also gaining experiences and developing skills as a law student that often only become available to lawyers later in their careers—things like arguing in court, individually counseling a client, and making substantive filings under your own signature,” Thomas said.

The lessons students learn from working in clinics prepare them to be practicing lawyers immediately after graduation.

“This case was won because of an idea that originated with a group of law students,” Caesar said. “Clinics contribute critical legal work to the clients that they serve. Their victory underscores for our students that it is never too early to be an outstanding advocate.”

title: Behind the Headline: Pulling Back the Curtain on Immigration Court
description:
Amelia Frank-Vitale: One of the things we've learned by being in court is just how much we don't know about what happens in immigration court.
Unlike other court proceedings, the decisions are often rendered immediately orally, and there's no court reporter.
Immigration court proceedings are starting to take place in unmarked office buildings and out of public view.
AFV: Immigration proceedings are civil, and immigration judges are technically attorney employees of the Department of Justice.
Taking immigration court out from under the DOJ, out from under the executive branch, is essential so that there is independence built into the court.
text:
For the past two years, researchers have been observing immigration court proceedings to better understand how the asylum process is evolving under the second Trump administration. A new report (external link) details their findings, based on more than 1,300 hours of courtroom observation across 107 courtrooms in 13 states and Puerto Rico.

Amelia Frank-Vitale, assistant professor of anthropology and international affairs at Princeton University and the report’s co-author, explains what her team found, why asylum law even matters, and how the system can be improved to ensure it is fair and transparent.

You and your team have spent hundreds of hours monitoring immigration court proceedings around the country and in Puerto Rico over the last two years. What did you learn?

Amelia Frank-Vitale: One of the things we've learned by being in court is just how much we don't know about what happens in immigration court. Unlike other court proceedings, the decisions are often rendered immediately orally, and there's no court reporter. Often the written record doesn't get made, and so there's so much, about how questions have been asked and who has said what in the courtroom to whom, that we really only know by being there.

These proceedings have changed under the Trump administration. What are some of the patterns you observed?

AFV: We've seen a lot of different ways that people are being rerouted or coerced into not having a final hearing on the merits of their claim. We're seeing procedural maneuvers being implemented to get rid of cases before they ever get to a hearing, so that a judge isn't actually hearing the specifics of a person's reasons for why they should not be deported.

One is the rise of “in-absentia” removal orders, people who are being ordered removed after they fail to appear for a hearing. In-absentia rates have historically been low, and they have skyrocketed in the last year and a half in the wake of courthouse arrests and people being scared to show up for their hearings.

Another one is this idea of pretermission. This is a new invention where, before a hearing actually happens, judges look at the paper filing and say this case is likely not to meet the legal threshold of the grounds for asylum. Another form of pretermission happens now because the U.S. has signed agreements with different countries with the idea that people should go there to seek asylum instead. These are countries from which people are also fleeing, often countries with dismal human rights abuses like Guatemala, Ecuador, Honduras, Uganda, and South Sudan.

So, cases are being pretermitted – they're being canceled before a hearing – and people are being sent to places they've never been to, sometimes where they don't speak the language, but most importantly, places where they don't have a real functioning justice system. Congress did make a provision that people's cases don't necessarily have to be heard in the U.S. if they could be heard in another safe third country, but this makes a mockery of that by assigning agreements with countries that, under no independent adjudication, could be considered safe or to have a functioning asylum system.

Why does it matter if the United States provides due process to asylum seekers?

AFV: This is still the country that a lot of people believe to be the place where they are going to find safety and possibility, and that is part of the strength and the beauty of the U.S. The laws that we have about asylum come out of a particular history. They come out of the recognition that we turned people away and sent them back to Hitler during the Holocaust and the Second World War. That is a shame that the U.S. carried with it, despite winning the war, despite all the sacrifice that U.S. servicepeople made to fight fascism in Europe.

The idea of asylum is that there are some people whose security, whose safety, whose needs for protection, supersede the otherwise restrictive nature of immigration laws, and that as a community of democratic nations, we recognize those rights. That is a foundational principle of how the community of democratic nations decides to work with one another, and we enshrined it into U.S. law in 1980. U.S. law says that people have a right to seek asylum in the U.S., and if they show up on U.S. soil, it does not matter how they got there – that we have a process for adjudicating them.

Immigration court proceedings are starting to take place in unmarked office buildings and out of public view. What are the implications of that?

AFV: There are reports in a couple different jurisdictions of people being sent to places that are not within the roster of immigration court, so a different floor in the federal building in New York City or an unmarked office building that you have to go through a fast-food restaurant to get into in Washington D.C. I think it's part of a general attempt to make things happen faster and with less review. It makes it easier to short-circuit the limited but important universe of due process rights that people have in immigration court if no one's there to watch, if no one can access the space to observe.

Although these hearings are traditionally held in a courtroom, they are not actually independent like criminal court, right?

AFV: Immigration proceedings are civil, and immigration judges are technically attorney employees of the Department of Justice. Their conditions of employment are more similar in many aspects to the rest of the civil service than to an independent judiciary, and we can see this as the Trump administration fired one out of every seven judges in its first year. Judges are employees who have to perform in a certain way for their boss, which is the DOJ. They then also have to make sure that their decisions hold up to review. At the appellate level, cases can eventually get appealed to the Circuit Court, and that is where the federal judiciary has some oversight.

But people in immigration court have no right to representation at government expense, and the rules of evidence are different. Judges don't have the power to hold parties in contempt, and in some ways, both the prosecutor and the judge have the same boss. They're both appointed by executive agencies because of the sort of structural choices that Congress made.

What can policymakers do to ensure that the asylum process is fair and transparent?

AFV: Congress decided to give the attorney general a lot of power over immigration court, and that's something that Congress could change. Taking immigration court out from under the DOJ, out from under the executive branch, is essential so that there is independence built into the court. There's precedent for other kinds of administrative law courts under the federal system that immigration court could be modeled after.

It also doesn't have to be a court. We already have a system through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services that is less adversarial, where people have their cases reviewed by a trained asylum officer. We could expand that process. There are many other countries that don't have an adversarial court process with a prosecutor present, but instead a review by specialists in the law. Something that allows for independent review, that is less politicized than the current system, would be a really important first step.

Headshot courtesy of Amelia Frank-Vitale. Background image by Shutterstock.

text:
Originally published in the Mercury News (link is external)

By Grace Hase

Silicon Valley Rep. Sam Liccardo’s bill to make Afghan immigrants once again eligible for temporary protected status has gone nowhere since it was introduced this summer, leaving more than 8,000 refugees nationally at risk for deportation. Now, the first-term congressmember plans to leverage an obscure procedural rule to advance the legislation.

Liccardo, who co-authored the “Afghanistan TPS Act of 2026” with Reps. Jason Crow, D-Colo., Don Bacon, R-Neb., and Maria Salazar, R-Fla., told the Bay Area News Group that he plans to file a discharge petition when Congress returns from recess on Nov. 9. The bill would offer Afghan refugees a shield from deportation as their immigration cases move forward, a status they held previously until the Trump administration ended the protection in 2025.

The legislative mechanism is a way for congressmembers to buck House leadership, which controls what bills proceed out of committee. If a discharge petition receives at least 218 signatures, it will force a vote on the bill.

Long considered a seldom-used tool with very little success, discharge petitions are finding new utility in the Trump era as House Speaker Mike Johnson holds a razor-thin majority that’s at risk in the upcoming midterm election.

Donna Crane, a lecturer in San Jose State University’s Department of Political Science, said that Republicans, who are facing dire reelection prospects, have used discharge petitions this year as a way to distance themselves from President Donald Trump. But for the minority party, she said, it’s also been an incredibly powerful instrument.

“This can be pretty much the only way of getting any control over the House floor schedule because the majority controls the entire schedule,” she said. “If you can hold your own group together and pick a few members off from the other side, then your bill is going to go to the floor.”

Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Santa Clara, and Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, famously used a discharge petition last year to bypass House leadership in their quest to pry loose investigative records related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The discharge petition could mark a critical step in Liccardo’s efforts to reinstate TPS for Afghan nationals. The Trump administration has halted protections for immigrants from 13 countries as it looks to dismantle the program, which guards from deportation individuals who can’t safely return to their homes due to ongoing conflict or other disasters.

The Biden administration granted TPS to eligible Afghans in 2022 after the United States ended its military presence in the country the year prior.

“Regardless of political differences, we ought to be able to agree on the critical importance of keeping our promises as a country,” Liccardo said about his bill. “America promised thousands of Afghans who risked their lives as interpreters, as informants, as other support roles to our military; they risked their lives with the expectation that we would not betray them and put them in harm’s way for doing so.”

Joseph Azam, a Berkeley resident and the board chair of the Afghan-American Foundation, said that the end of TPS for Afghan nationals has “shaken people’s belief that protecting this population is a bipartisan priority.”

The decision, along with other moves by the Trump administration to ban Afghans from entering the U.S., has sent shockwaves throughout the Bay Area(link is external) — especially in Fremont, which is home to one of the largest concentrations of Afghan immigrants in the country(link is external).

Azam said that it’s been “frustrating” to see Liccardo’s bill stall and applauded his plans to file a discharge petition.

“I think people who care about this population and care about the integrity of America’s word should use every tool in their toolbox,” he said. “Once it’s opened, I think that’s when the real pressure can start. Members of Congress need to step up and be counted on this issue, and they’ve gotten a pass for a while now, particularly under this new administration. I’m looking forward to people being held accountable and having to be on the record on where they stand.”

Whether Liccardo and his co-sponsors have enough signatures remains to be seen; however, the congressman said that having “five Republican co-sponsors is certainly a very strong indication.” There are 214 Democrats serving in the House of Representatives.

The success of a discharge petition filed earlier this year to force a vote on a bill that would extend TPS for Haitian immigrants could also be another positive indicator for Liccardo’s bill — four Republican congressmembers signed the discharge petition alongside Democrats, to reach the 218 threshold.

A spokesperson for Johnson did not respond to a request to comment about the discharge petition, but told reporters last year(link is external) that “I am not a fan of discharge petitions. It is typically used as a tool against the majority.”

Regardless of who wins control of the House on Nov. 3, Liccardo said that Republicans up for reelection might be more emboldened to sign on.

“After Election Day,” he said, “I’d like to believe we’re going to have a lot more interest from a lot of those Republicans, particularly a lot of the veterans who served in Afghanistan, who understand what a betrayal this has been to essentially abandon our promise to protect Afghans who risked their lives alongside U.S. troops.”

text:
October 19, 2026 9:00 am

NEW YORK – The American Civil Liberties Union premiered Wilder Raids, an original short film telling the story of two families whose lives were upended by a violent immigration raid at a horse-racing event in Wilder, Idaho, one year ago today. The film follows the families as they reckon with the lasting trauma of the raid and details the ongoing lawsuit brought by the ACLU, ACLU of Idaho, Cooley LLP, and Stoel Rives LLP seeking accountability.

One year ago today, more than 200 federal, state, and local law enforcement officers descended on an otherwise peaceful family event at a horse-racing track in Wilder, Idaho. Law enforcement arrived in armored trucks and a helicopter with flashbang grenades and guns drawn and detained approximately 400 spectators – including U.S. citizens and children – for four hours in inhumane conditions before subjecting everyone to suspicionless immigration interrogations.

Through interviews with the families and an inside look at the ongoing legal fight, Wilder Raids explores the lasting impact of the raid on those who experienced it and the broader Wilder community. Juana Rodriguez, one of the lead plaintiffs and featured storyteller in the film, is a U.S. citizen who was at the event with her 3-year-old son. After being violently rounded up with hundreds of other families, Rodriguez was placed in zip ties and detained for several hours without food or water. Law enforcement instructed her toddler to hold onto her pocket while Rodriguez remained zip tied and unable to comfort her son.

“I was like, why? I have my son with me. I have to take care of him. I was scared. If I overreacted, I felt like they were going to hurt me,” Rodriguez said. “For the longest time, my son begged me for food. He begged me for water ... I wish I could have done more in the moment, but I couldn't. I think that's what really gets to me till this day.”

The families featured in the film filed a lawsuit last February that argues that federal, state, and local law enforcement used criminal warrants as a pretext for a sweeping immigration dragnet at an event where they knew attendees would be predominantly Latino. The complaint further alleges that the agencies conspired to deprive those detained of their Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable seizures and their right to equal protection regardless of ethnicity. The lawsuit invokes federal civil rights laws enacted after the Civil War to protect people from racialized government violence and provides a potential avenue for holding federal actors accountable for constitutional violations.

“Defendants continue to characterize what happened in Wilder as an ordinary warrant execution, but there was nothing routine about the terror they inflicted on hundreds of people trying to spend a Sunday with their families,” said Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy director on policing at the ACLU. “This film makes it impossible to ignore what our clients and their families experienced that day and puts a human face on the reckless violence and cruelty inflicted on the community. One year later, we will not let the government rewrite what happened in Wilder and we will continue fighting to hold those responsible accountable.”

“The violent raid in Wilder has had significant ripple effects across many communities in Idaho, which can still be felt today, a year later,” said Leo Morales, executive director of the ACLU of Idaho. “The film reminds us of how critical it is for every American to rise to the challenge of protecting civil liberties. It also highlights how personal and fragile our rights can be if left unprotected from government action. Families cannot simply shake off and ignore the abuse; it is our collective responsibility to seek justice, take action, and make things whole.”

The lawsuit is ongoing as the families await a decision on the defendants’ motions to dismiss. On Sept. 8, 2026, plaintiffs filed an opposition brief urging the federal court to allow the lawsuit to proceed.

Additional statements from co-counsel are below.

Jade Ford, an attorney at Cooley LLP:

“This film sends a clear message: the Wilder community will not stand idly by in the face of constitutional violations. Every person in this country is entitled to freedom from unlawful seizure and freedom from discriminatory targeting. Those are not hollow promises—they are vital constitutional guarantees, and the Wilder community intends to see them enforced.”

Wendy Olsen, an attorney at Stoel Rives LLP:

“All Idaho families should be able to enjoy community and cultural events without fear that their rights will be violated, that their children will be traumatized or that they will be targeted based on their perceived color or national origin. This film bravely tells that story on behalf of the Wilder community.”

text:
PHOTO: Mainers protest outside Sen. Susan Collins office for supporting ICE funding in August. Photo by Channa Steinmetz, Maine Beacon.

Monday is the three-month anniversary of the ICE killing of 25-year old delivery driver Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford and his murderer still has not been brought to justice. In U.S. Senate debates last week, Sen. Susan Collins was forced to defend her votes to provide over $100 billion to supercharge ICE without any guardrails to protect civil liberties and prevent more murders of innocent people.

Collins strongly opposes dismantling the lawless agency that functions like President Trump’s personal paramilitary force. That isn’t surprising since she has received over $130,000 from top ICE contractors —including Palantir Technologies, CoreCivic and the Geo Group — that are profiting off Trump’s vicious mass deportation policies. Before the second Trump administration, Collins received just $2,850 from ICE contractors, their employees and PACs.

Executives from the tech company Palantir, best described as the “surveillance backbone” for ICE, have donated $117,000 to PACs supporting Collins, including $100,000 from Palantir executive Alex Karp to the pro-Collins super PAC Pine Tree Results one month after she voted in 2025 to advance an eye-popping $70 billion for immigration enforcement, more than most foreign military budgets. In fact, according to campaign finance reports, Collins received the fourth most money from Palantir executives and its PAC out of all Senators between 2006 and 2026.

Co-founded by pro-Trump billionaire Peter Thiel in 2003, Palantir received a $30 million contract from the Trump administration to use artificial intelligence and data mining to identify, track, and deport suspected noncitizens. Civil liberties groups have raised serious concerns that Palantir’s automated “Immigration0S” surveillance platform uses flawed data to make enforcement decisions, bypassing traditional due process and disproportionately targeting Black and brown people.

ICE has even been dumping photos of protestors and legal observers into their Palantir-supported data database to track and intimidate people exercising their First Amendment rights. Newly unsealed court documents just revealed that ICE agents added eight Mainers to a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database in January during ICE’s so-called “Operation Catch of the Day” enforcement surge. Maine resident Caryln Williams was added to the DHS Investigative Case Management (ICM) after agents spotted her car at a location where people were filming immigration officers in South Portland. However, Williams was not driving the car, her spouse Plyxenia Pantos was.

A DHS agent later called Williams to warn Pantos, “not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist,” according to court documents. Two months later, Williams and Pantos were detained for an hour by U.S. Customs and Border Protection at the Canadian border after their names were flagged in the ICM system. They have since joined two other Maine residents in filing a lawsuit asking a federal judge to prohibit immigration agents from entering people legally exercising their First Amendment rights into the “domestic terrorist” database. It’s bone chilling that the President and his minions can target anyone as a potential “domestic terrorist” for legally observing federal agents and using their free-speech rights.

In addition to Palantir, executives and board members of the private prison company CoreCivic contributed over $9,500 to Susan Collins. Last year, CoreCivic reported record profits after receiving billions of dollars from the Trump administration to run detention facilities to house detainees seized in ICE raids. In an earnings call, the company called the mass incarceration of immigrants to be a “significant growth opportunity,” thanks to a $45 billion budget Senator Collins voted to advance in the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill. In February, CoreCivic CEO Patrick Swindle assured investors that Trump’s immigration crackdown would pick up, bringing in more revenue to warehouse men, women and children. More than half of the 3,500 detainees that have been housed in CoreCivic’s Dilley Immigrant Detention Center in South Texas were minors.

In August, Texas Monthly reported that the Dilley facility has been routinely holding migrant kids five times longer than court orders allow. Psychology Professor Maryam Tahmasebi, her husband, Seyed Eissa Hashem, and teenage son were all detained by ICE after the U.S. government revoked their green cards because her husband’s mother was a translator for the Iranian hostage takers in 1979. They have been reportedly detained at the Dilley facility for over six months “with swarms of cockroaches, spiders and mosquitoes”

“We have been put through hell for the past four months, and our physical and mental health have deteriorated in ways that might not be reversible for years,” Tahmasebi wrote in the Nation in August. “We are only allowed to speak with my husband for 10 minutes every two weeks, under supervision.”

Less than a month after the murder of Johan Sebastián Guerrero, Collins took $3,500 from the private prison company Geo Group, which operates 19 ICE detention centers housing roughly one-third of all immigrant detainees. With $2.6 billion in revenue in 2025, GeoGroup has profited handsomely from billions of dollars in funding that Collins advanced in the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill. The company also has a horrible human rights record, detaining a record 600 immigrant kids for an average of six months in 2025.

At Geo Group’s Folkston facility in Georgia, 73 people recently launched a mass hunger strike to protest abhorrent conditions including substandard medical care, lack of air conditioning, threats by GEO Group guards, routine collective punishment, moldy food and a lack of due process. Many of them came to America fleeing persecution and violence in their home countries and are fighting to obtain asylum in immigration courts.

“Many of us have been separated from our families,” reads their open letter signed by 45 detained immigrants. “We have missed births, funerals, years of our lives while sitting behind fences without having committed any crime.”

In June, a Geo Group detention facility in Newark, NJ put down a separate hunger strike of immigrant detainees protesting inhumane conditions, including inedible food and poor treatment by guards. The facility transferred a number of detainees out of the jail to punish them for dissenting and threatened to put others in segregation to break the strike.

Susan Collins has made a lot of excuses for ICE as it continues to murder, abuse and jail people without due process. She claims that without ICE we wouldn’t be able to deport dangerous criminals, despite the fact that more than 70 percent of ICE detainees do not have a criminal conviction. As her opponent Troy Jackson has pointed out, we also have plenty of other law enforcement agencies like Customs and Border Protection that handled the job before ICE was created in 2003.
