title: Imran Khan Leave India Notice: Bombay High Court Challenge
authors: Zeynep Mukherjee, Adv. Tarun Choudhury, Legal Service India Editorial Team, Legal Service India
description:
What Is the Imran Khan Leave India Notice Case About?
This is where the Imran Khan Leave India Notice dispute could assume wider significance.
Why the Imran Khan Leave India Notice Case Matters Beyond One Actor The public interest in this dispute is understandable.
Key Takeaways: Imran Khan Leave India Notice Bombay High Court challenge: Actor Imran Khan Pal has reportedly approached the Bombay High Court challenging a Leave India Notice issued by immigration authorities following his alleged participation in an anti-Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) protest in Mumbai.
Separate OCI cancellation proceedings: Any reported show-cause notice concerning cancellation of OCI registration must be distinguished from the challenge to the Leave India Notice.
text:
Imran Khan Leave India Notice: Bombay High Court Challenge Raises Questions About Immigration Powers and Natural Justice

Introduction: When Immigration Powers Meet Constitutional Accountability

Can the government direct a foreign national who has lived in India since early childhood to leave the country after his alleged participation in a political protest? The answer cannot be determined by looking at the person’s nationality alone. It requires a closer examination of the statutory power exercised, the grounds on which it was invoked and the procedure followed by the authorities.

That is the central legal question raised by the Imran Khan Leave India Notice controversy.

Actor Imran Khan Pal, a United States citizen and Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, has reportedly approached the Bombay High Court challenging a notice issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO), Mumbai, directing him to leave India by 28 October 2026. The notice reportedly followed his presence at a demonstration held near August Kranti Maidan in Mumbai on 10 October, where protesters demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

According to media reports, Khan’s petition describes the notice as arbitrary, inadequately reasoned and issued without giving him an opportunity to be heard. He is reported to have sought its quashing, an interim stay and disclosure of the material on which the authorities relied. The FRRO has also reportedly initiated separate proceedings concerning the possible cancellation of his OCI registration.

These developments must be approached with care. The actor’s allegations are not judicial findings, and the government’s complete reasons for its action have not been independently established from the original administrative record. Nor should the filing of a writ petition be mistaken for a court ruling in the petitioner’s favour.

As of 18 October 2026, the immediate significance of the case lies in the legal questions it places before the High Court. It concerns the limits of immigration discretion, the procedural safeguards available to foreign nationals and the distinction between a government’s power to take action and the lawful exercise of that power in an individual case.

What Is the Imran Khan Leave India Notice Case About?

The dispute arose after a demonstration in Mumbai on 10 October 2026 connected with demands for the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner.

Media reports state that Khan, who holds United States nationality and OCI registration, was present at the gathering and was detained by the police. Reports also indicate that a complaint concerning his participation was made by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya and that the matter was subsequently brought to the attention of the immigration authorities. The precise contents and evidentiary basis of the underlying complaint have not been independently verified from the original record.

The reported sequence of events is significant.

On 14 October 2026, the FRRO issued a notice directing Khan to leave India by 28 October. Reports quoting the notice state that the authority relied on the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, including Sections 7(2)(c) and 29, along with a Ministry of Home Affairs notification dated 1 September 2025. The notice reportedly warned of prosecution in the event of non-compliance.

Khan subsequently approached the Bombay High Court. According to reports published on 17 October, his petition challenges the legality of the notice and seeks urgent protection against its operation.

The petition is reported to argue that the authorities did not identify the specific immigration provision allegedly breached, explain how his conduct constituted that breach or provide him with a prior opportunity to respond. It also reportedly disputes the suggestion that his presence at the protest, by itself, established an immigration violation. These remain the petitioner’s contentions unless and until examined and determined by the Court.

The reported issue is therefore narrower—and legally more important—than the question of whether a foreign national may participate in a demonstration.

The Central Legal Question

The central issue is whether the statutory power invoked by the FRRO was lawfully exercised on the facts of this case.

The Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025: What Must Be Examined?

The Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, provides the statutory framework governing matters concerning foreigners and immigration in India. The official text is available through the Government of India’s .

The reported notice invokes Sections 7(2)(c) and 29 of the Act. Their precise wording, the relevant rules or orders made under the Act, and the applicable Ministry of Home Affairs notification must be read together before drawing a definitive conclusion about the scope of the FRRO’s authority.

It would be a mistake to decide the case merely by pointing to a statutory provision that permits the government to regulate the presence of foreign nationals. Equally, it would be incorrect to assume that every direction requiring a foreign national to leave India is unlawful because it was issued without a conventional criminal trial.

The proper questions are these:

Did the authority have the legal power to issue the particular notice?

Were the statutory conditions for exercising that power satisfied?

What conduct was treated as the alleged violation?

Was there material connecting that conduct to the legal ground relied upon?

Did the authority consider relevant facts, including the person’s immigration status and any applicable conditions?

Was the procedure followed consistent with the statute and the requirements of fairness that applied in the circumstances?

Was the direction proportionate to the lawful purpose for which the power was exercised?

These questions cannot be answered conclusively from media reports alone. The complete notice, the underlying administrative record and the applicable statutory instruments are needed.

A Power to Remove Is Not the Same as an Unrestricted Power

The State has substantial authority over the entry, stay and departure of foreign nationals. A person who is not an Indian citizen does not enjoy an unconditional right to remain in India indefinitely. Immigration authorities may take action where the governing law permits it.

But the existence of a power does not settle whether its exercise is lawful in a particular case.

An administrative order must be traceable to the authority conferred by law. If the statute makes specified conditions relevant, the decision-maker must act within those conditions. If the order rests on an alleged breach, the nature of that breach and its connection with the statutory power may become important to judicial review.

This is where the Imran Khan Leave India Notice dispute could assume wider significance. If the original notice merely recites that the Act has been contravened without identifying the relevant conduct or legal basis, the Court may have to examine whether that formulation was legally sufficient in the circumstances.

However, the conclusion must follow from the actual notice and statutory text, not from a newspaper paraphrase. A short notice is not automatically invalid, just as the citation of a statutory provision does not automatically establish that the authority applied it correctly.

Does OCI Status Give Imran Khan a Right to Remain in India?

One of the most important aspects of the controversy is Khan’s reported status as an Overseas Citizen of India cardholder.

OCI status is often misunderstood. Despite its name, it does not confer Indian citizenship. An OCI cardholder remains a foreign national and does not acquire all the rights reserved exclusively for Indian citizens.

Under Section 7B of the Citizenship Act, 1955, OCI cardholders are not entitled to certain rights available to citizens, including the right to vote and the constitutional rights under Article 19 that are expressly guaranteed to citizens.

OCI registration nevertheless has a legal framework of its own. The applicable provisions of the Citizenship Act, registration conditions and government notifications must be considered when determining the rights and obligations of an individual OCI cardholder.

Khan’s reported long residence in India may be relevant to the factual context and the practical consequences of removal. It does not, by itself, convert OCI status into citizenship or create an absolute right to remain in the country.

The legally sound position lies between two extremes.

It would be wrong to argue that OCI registration makes a person immune from immigration law.

It would be equally wrong to treat the existence of foreign nationality as sufficient, by itself, to answer every question concerning the legality of a particular administrative decision.

The authorities must act under the law applicable to the person and the action they seek to take.

Can an OCI Cardholder Participate in a Political Protest?

This is one of the most sensitive questions raised by the controversy, and it requires a distinction between political expression, immigration compliance and the conditions attached to OCI registration.

Article 19 of the Constitution guarantees specified freedoms to citizens. A foreign national cannot claim those rights on the same footing as an Indian citizen. It would therefore be legally inaccurate to argue that Khan’s foreign nationality is irrelevant simply because the demonstration concerned a matter of public interest.

That does not mean, however, that the presence of a foreign national at a protest automatically establishes an immigration offence.

The legal analysis must identify the applicable restriction, if any, and determine whether the person’s conduct violated it. The nature of the gathering, the individual’s actual participation, the conditions applicable to the person’s immigration status and the precise statutory ground relied upon may all be relevant.

Distinguishing Attendance at a Protest from Prohibited Conduct

There is also an important distinction between attending a demonstration and engaging in conduct independently prohibited by law. The two should not be treated as interchangeable without examining the evidence.

According to media reports, Khan’s petition disputes the basis for the immigration action and denies the alleged connection between his conduct and the violation asserted by the authorities. Those claims require examination against the record.

The question before a court is not whether a person’s political views are popular or unpopular. It is whether the action taken against that person is authorised by law and can withstand the applicable standard of judicial review.

Articles 14 and 21: Constitutional Protections for Foreign Nationals

Although Article 19 is restricted to citizens, Articles 14 and 21 use language that extends their protection to persons. Foreign nationals are not outside the protection of these provisions merely because they do not hold Indian citizenship.

The distinction matters in the present controversy.

Article 14 and the Prohibition Against Arbitrary State Action

Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. In administrative matters, it is also relevant to the requirement that State action must not be arbitrary.

If the Imran Khan Leave India Notice was issued without a legally relevant basis, relied on irrelevant considerations or failed to address material facts required by law, Article 14 may become relevant to the challenge.

But a claim of arbitrariness must be demonstrated through the facts and the applicable legal standard. A petitioner cannot establish a constitutional violation merely by describing an order as unfair or unreasonable.

The Court would need to consider the statutory authority invoked, the reasons for the decision, the material before the authority and the explanation, if any, offered by the government.

Article 21 and the Protection of Personal Liberty

Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

The Supreme Court’s decision in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, (1978) 1 SCC 248, is a leading authority on the constitutional scrutiny of procedures affecting personal liberty. It established that the procedure contemplated by Article 21 cannot be treated as a purely formal requirement divorced from constitutional fairness.

For a foreign national, the constitutional position must also be understood in light of Louis De Raedt v. Union of India, (1991) 3 SCC 554. The Supreme Court recognised that foreigners are entitled to protection under Article 21, while making clear that they do not possess a fundamental right to reside and settle in India under Article 19(1)(e).

These principles must be read together.

Article 21 does not create an unconditional right for a foreign national to remain in India. At the same time, the State cannot avoid constitutional scrutiny simply by characterising an action as an immigration measure.

The relevant question is whether the action is authorised by law and whether the applicable legal and procedural requirements have been observed.

Was a Prior Hearing Legally Necessary?

The reported allegation that the FRRO issued the notice without first hearing Khan is central to the dispute. It is also an issue that requires careful legal analysis rather than a categorical answer.

The rule of audi alteram partem—the principle that a person should have a fair opportunity to present their case before an adverse decision—is an important component of natural justice. Its application depends on the governing statute, the nature of the decision, the circumstances in which it is made and any legally recognised exception.

It does not follow that every administrative direction affecting a foreign national must invariably be preceded by a full oral hearing. Nor does it follow that immigration authorities may dispense with fairness whenever they invoke a statutory power.

The first task is to identify what the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, and the relevant rules or orders require. The next is to determine whether the nature of the action and the circumstances of the case required notice, an opportunity to respond, reasons or some other procedural protection.

A further distinction may arise between the decision to issue a direction to leave and the procedure for challenging that direction. The availability of a subsequent remedy is relevant, but it does not automatically cure every procedural defect.

The Importance of Reasons

A person affected by an adverse administrative decision should ordinarily be able to understand the substance of the case they must meet, subject to any lawful limits on disclosure.

In this case, media reports indicate that Khan’s petition argues that the notice did not identify the particular provision allegedly violated or explain how his conduct attracted the statutory power.

If the original notice is as broadly worded as reported, the High Court may need to consider whether it sufficiently communicates the legal basis for the direction. The answer will depend on the statutory framework, the notice read as a whole and the administrative record.

The distinction is important: a notice may be brief without being legally defective, but an authority cannot necessarily cure the absence of a legally required foundation by relying on reasons that were never part of its decision.

The Separate OCI Cancellation Notice: Why It Matters

Reports also indicate that the FRRO issued a separate show-cause notice concerning the possible cancellation of Khan’s OCI registration under Section 7D(e) of the Citizenship Act, 1955. That provision addresses specified grounds on which OCI registration may be cancelled, including matters relating to sovereignty and integrity, security, friendly relations with foreign countries and general public interest.

The reported show-cause notice is significant because it appears to initiate a distinct legal process.

A direction requiring a foreign national to leave India and a proceeding to cancel OCI registration are not necessarily the same decision. They may have different statutory foundations, procedural requirements and consequences.

The validity of the departure notice therefore should not be conflated with the outcome of the OCI cancellation proceeding. Each must be examined under the legal provision governing it.

The distinction also matters for procedural fairness. Where the statute expressly requires a reasonable opportunity of being heard before cancellation, the authority must comply with that requirement. The person concerned must have a meaningful opportunity to respond to the proposed action in accordance with the applicable law.

The precise allegations and material supporting the reported OCI show-cause notice have not been independently verified from the original document. It would therefore be premature to say that the cancellation proceeding is justified, unjustified or destined to succeed.

For the same reason, the issuance of a show-cause notice should not be described as a cancellation of OCI status. A notice initiates a process; it does not, by itself, establish that the proposed action has been completed.

Key Legal Distinctions

The Calcutta High Court Precedent: Kamil Siedczynski v. Union of India

The controversy has drawn attention to Kamil Siedczynski v. Union of India, reportedly decided by the Calcutta High Court on 18 March 2020 in W.P. No. 4432(W) of 2020.

The case is described in secondary accounts as involving a Polish national who received a notice directing him to leave India after attending a protest against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act. Reports and commentary have drawn comparisons between that matter and the present controversy.

The comparison is worth examining, but it must not be overstated.

Before relying on Kamil Siedczynski as authority for a particular proposition, the complete judgment should be obtained and checked. The exact factual findings, statutory provisions, reasoning and operative directions matter. A summary of a judgment cannot safely substitute for the judgment itself, particularly where the proposed article makes claims about the scope of immigration powers or the requirement of a prior hearing.

There are also obvious questions of distinction. The applicable immigration legislation, the terms of the notice, the person’s status and the material relied upon by the authorities may differ from case to case. The 2020 dispute arose under the legal framework then in force, whereas the present notice reportedly invokes the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025.

Even where an earlier decision is factually similar, it does not automatically determine the outcome of a later case under a different statutory framework.

The sound approach is to use Kamil Siedczynski as a potentially relevant precedent after verifying its text, explaining the principle actually decided and identifying any material differences. It should not be presented as conclusive proof that Khan’s notice must be quashed.

What Could the Government Argue?

A balanced legal analysis must consider the possible position of the Union of India and the immigration authorities, even though their complete response to the petition has not been independently verified.

The government may contend that foreign nationals do not have an unrestricted right to remain in India and that the statutory framework gives the competent authorities substantial powers to regulate their presence. It may also argue that the action was taken under the relevant provisions of the 2025 Act and that the decision must be assessed in light of the administrative record and the applicable immigration conditions.

If the authorities rely on security, public order or a specific breach of immigration requirements, the legal and evidentiary basis for that position will matter. The government would be entitled to place its reasons and supporting material before the Court, subject to the law governing disclosure and judicial scrutiny.

It may further argue that courts should exercise appropriate restraint in reviewing decisions involving immigration administration, particularly where the legislature has conferred decision-making powers on designated authorities.

These are potential arguments, not confirmed submissions. The government’s actual position must be taken from its pleadings, affidavits or statements made in court.

There is, however, a limit to the general proposition that immigration decisions are matters for the executive. Statutory discretion does not ordinarily mean discretion without legal boundaries. Where a decision is challenged as ultra vires, arbitrary or procedurally unlawful, the Court may examine whether the authority acted within its powers.

The legal contest is therefore not simply between a foreign national and the government’s power to control immigration. It concerns the relationship between that power and the legal conditions governing its exercise.

What Relief Has Imran Khan Sought?

According to published reports, Khan’s writ petition seeks to challenge the departure notice and obtain urgent interim protection against its operation. Reports also indicate that the petition asks the authorities to produce the records on which the decision was based.

The precise prayers must be confirmed from the filed petition. Based on the available reporting, the relief reportedly sought includes:

Quashing the Leave India Notice.

Interim protection against enforcement of the notice while the challenge is considered.

Production of the relevant administrative record.

Protection against consequential immigration action, to the extent sought in the petition.

These are reported prayers, not reliefs already granted by the Court.

The distinction between interim and final relief is particularly important. An interim stay, if granted, would temporarily restrain enforcement of the challenged direction in accordance with the terms of the order. It would not necessarily amount to a final determination that the notice was unlawful.

Likewise, the filing of a writ petition does not automatically suspend an administrative order. The legal effect of any protection depends on an actual judicial order and its terms.

As of 18 October 2026, available reporting indicated that the matter was expected to be mentioned for urgent consideration on the following Monday. An official case number, cause-list entry and court order should be checked before publication of any subsequent update.

What Could the Bombay High Court Examine?

If the matter is taken up, the Court could be asked to consider several connected but distinct questions.

1. Statutory Authority

Did the FRRO possess and properly exercise the power relied upon in the notice? This requires examining the relevant provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, the applicable rules and orders, and the notification cited in the notice.

2. The Basis of the Decision

Did the authority identify a legally relevant ground for directing Khan to leave India? Was the decision supported by material capable of sustaining the action under the applicable law?

3. Procedural Fairness

Was Khan entitled to an opportunity to respond before the direction was issued? If so, was that opportunity provided, or did a legally recognised exception apply?

4. Constitutional Scrutiny

Does the challenged action withstand the applicable requirements of Articles 14 and 21? The analysis would have to respect the distinction between rights available to all persons and rights reserved for citizens.

5. Interim Relief

Is there a legal basis to suspend the operation of the notice while the Court considers the challenge? The answer would depend on the pleadings, the material presented, the applicable principles governing interim relief and the consequences of granting or refusing it.

6. The Separate OCI Proceeding

What is the legal relationship, if any, between the departure notice and the reported show-cause notice concerning OCI cancellation? Each action must be assessed under its own statutory requirements.

None of these questions should be treated as having been decided merely because the petition has been filed.

Why the Imran Khan Leave India Notice Case Matters Beyond One Actor

The public interest in this dispute is understandable. It involves a recognisable actor, a politically sensitive demonstration and a direction that could require a person who has lived in India for much of his life to leave the country.

But its legal significance does not depend on celebrity.

Immigration decisions affect people who may have lived in India for years, maintained family relationships here, established professional lives and developed substantial personal ties to the country. At the same time, the State has a legitimate responsibility to administer immigration law and enforce the conditions applicable to foreign nationals.

The law must accommodate both realities without treating either as absolute.

A long period of residence does not itself confer citizenship or eliminate immigration restrictions. Conversely, foreign nationality does not make every administrative decision immune from scrutiny. The relevant statutory power must be identified, the facts must be assessed under the correct legal standard, and the prescribed procedure must be followed.

The case also illustrates why public commentary should distinguish political disagreement from legal adjudication. A complaint by a political figure, an allegation of immigration non-compliance and an administrative direction are different events. None, by itself, proves that the legal requirements for removal have been met.

Equally, the fact that a person attended a protest does not, without more, establish that the resulting immigration action was politically motivated. That allegation would require evidence and judicial assessment.

The Court’s role, if called upon to decide the dispute, is to examine the legality of the impugned action—not to endorse a political narrative in advance.

Conclusion: The Question Is Whether the Law Was Properly Applied

The Imran Khan Leave India Notice controversy raises a serious question about the exercise of immigration powers, but a responsible legal assessment must stop short of predicting the result before the relevant records have been examined.

The government has authority to regulate the presence of foreign nationals in India. OCI registration does not confer Indian citizenship or an unrestricted right to reside in the country. Those propositions are not in dispute.

The more difficult question is whether the particular direction issued to Khan was supported by the statutory provisions invoked, based on legally relevant material and issued in accordance with the procedure required by law.

If the notice fails to satisfy the applicable statutory or procedural requirements, the High Court may be asked to intervene. If the authorities demonstrate that the decision was lawfully made under the governing framework, the petition will have to be assessed against that record. Neither outcome should be assumed in advance.

The separate OCI cancellation proceeding must also be treated independently, with due attention to the requirements of the Citizenship Act and the actual contents of the show-cause notice.

For now, the case remains a pending legal challenge, not a judicial finding that the government acted unlawfully. The next meaningful development will be the Court’s consideration of the petition and any order it may pass.

In immigration law, the State’s power to act is important. So is the requirement that it act within the law. The ultimate issue in this case is not whether immigration control is legitimate, but whether the particular power exercised against the petitioner can be legally justified.

text:
At least 21 people have been shot by federal immigration agents during the second Trump administration, according to an ABC News count.

The most recent shooting was on Sunday, when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin, Texas, shot Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a Venezuelan man who was making deliveries for DoorDash.

Eight of those shootings, which included three U.S. citizens, were fatal, according to an analysis based on ABC reporting, statements from lawmakers, and government press releases. ABC News found at least 15 other incidents in which federal immigration agents fired shots but did not injure people.

The latest shooting has continued to raise questions among lawmakers and immigrant advocates about the Trump administration's deportation campaign.

"There was hope that ICE would abandon the physical brutality and inhumanity of its tactics on the streets," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said on Tuesday. "There was hope that there would be accountability. That hope has been vanished. Most recently, just days ago in Austin, Texas."

In response to the incident in Texas, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said on Tuesday that the agency is "tasked with enforcing the laws passed by Congress" and that ICE "will not be slowing down or leaving Austin."

"We will continue to enforce our nation's laws," the agency said.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin also pushed back on calls by Austin officials and some House Democrats that ICE leave Austin in the wake of Sunday's shooting of Garces Perez, who DHS alleged was in the country illegally and had a final order of removal.

"If sanctuary politicians like the Mayor of Austin had their priorities straight, they'd stop putting the needs of illegal aliens over the safety of the American people," Mullin said in a social media post on Tuesday. "The men and women of @ICEgov have arrested some of the most heinous criminal illegal aliens in Texas, including terrorists, pedophiles, drug traffickers, and fugitives wanted for murder."

Garces Perez's attorney, Kat Lincoln-Goldfinch, said her client was in the country legally and had applied for asylum.

Law enforcement sources have told ABC News the ICE officer involved in the shooting of Garces Perez was not wearing a body-worn camera at the time of the incident.

"DHS will NEVER apologize for removing these criminals from our communities, because deporting illegal aliens saves lives," Mullin said in his post on X.

On Tuesday, the mother of Renee Good, the 37-year-old Minneapolis, Minnesota, woman fatally shot by an ICE agent in January, spoke out at a congressional hearing in Washington, D.C.

Good's mother, Donna Granger, told the joint hearing of the U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations and the U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform that she voted for President Donald Trump.

The lawmakers held a hearing on Tuesday with families impacted by deadly ICE-involved shootings after the Austin shooting.

"I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States, innocents like our family and the others here, against terrorists," Granger said. "Certainly not to accuse those of us here of being terrorists and take precious lives. This is madness."

The ICE agent who shot Good has not been charged with any crime connected to the shooting of Good, who was an American citizen.

The family of Lorenzo Salgado, a 52-year-old Mexican man fatally shot by an ICE agent in Houston in July, said at the joint hearing that they have received no answers from the government on the death.

"It's been two and a half months, and we still don't have my dad's belongings back," Lorenzo Salgado Jr. told the lawmakers. "Aside from some change that he kept in his pocket, we don't have his wallet or his phone. We have no idea where his things are or who might have them."

During a news conference on Monday in Austin, Roman Palomares, president of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), also evoked Salgado's death while calling for an independent investigation of Garces Perez's shooting.

"Seventy-five days after Houston, Texas, we still do not know who pulled the trigger, and we're still counting," Palomares said, referring to Salgado's shooting.

Sulma Franco, director of the Grassroots Leadership Immigration Campaign, issued an emotional statement at Monday's news conference in Austin, saying, "I'm one of many, many voices of people that are being terrorized right now by ICE."

"We have a community hotline where community members have been reporting the abuses," Franco said. "We ask the community to not fall asleep, to not go back to business as normal, and to get involved. Migration is not illegal. It's part of nature. And we're here to say today, we want ICE out of Austin."

ABC News' Ely Brown and Luke Barr contributed to this report.

text:
Homan said ICE had repeatedly broken its records for arrests during the summer, with September recording the agency's highest monthly number of removals, according to his remarks. He said additional personnel would help expand enforcement operations, while arguing that deportations involve legal procedures that prevent authorities from removing everyone immediately after an arrest.

“I think President Trump is keeping his promise because we're arresting more people now than ever before,” Homan said.

Also read: Trump govt plans tougher US worksite crackdown, targets employers hiring undocumented workers

“It's not as simple as, 'Let's go arrest them and deport them,'” he said, explaining that many people arrested by immigration authorities have a right to an immigration hearing.

He also claimed that more than 100 nationwide injunctions and class-action lawsuits were preventing the administration from carrying out some deportations. These were figures cited by Homan and were not independently verified in his remarks.

Homan further said authorities were dealing with approximately 85,000 habeas cases. Habeas corpus petitions allow detained people to challenge the legality of their detention in court.

Homan complained that court orders sometimes require authorities to release detainees, forcing officers to locate them again if they are subsequently pursued for removal.

Also read: More US universities may face J-1 visa probes as nine, including Harvard, face scrutiny: Trump govt

He said ICE personnel were continuing to make arrests despite these constraints and defended the administration's broader approach to immigration enforcement.

The addition of 3,000 agents would strengthen the administration's enforcement capacity, although Homan's remarks did not provide a specific deployment schedule or a revised annual deportation target.

The expansion comes as the Trump administration continues to pursue its mass deportation agenda. The scale of future removals will depend not only on staffing and detention capacity but also on immigration court proceedings and the outcome of legal challenges to federal enforcement policies.

text:
Hundreds of demonstrators carrying handmade signs lined streets in Ferndale and Troy on Saturday, Oct. 17, as part of the latest wave of “No Kings” events focused on getting people to vote early.

Demonstrators waved signs reading, “If you’re not angry, you’re not paying attention,” “No kings in America,” and “We don’t bow, we vote!” Some signs were simply crossed-out crowns.

Their concerns ranged from the cost of living and immigration to civil rights, political influence and what they see as threats to democracy.

Among those joining the demonstrations was Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist, the Democratic candidate for Michigan secretary of state, who spoke in Troy alongside other Democratic candidates and officeholders.

"The 'No Kings' movement has been a really important assertion of people power, saying that you know democracy is worth organizing for," Gilchrist told the Free Press. "It's important that people speak out and have their voices heard, and as you can hear by the all the horns blowing in solidarity — that we're not alone."

The Detroit Free Press reached out to the Michigan Republican Party for comment on the latest "No Kings" events on but did not receive a response before publication.

The Saturday events in Ferndale and Troy were among at least 100 taking place across Michigan. While organizers have shifted the latest "No Kings" mobilization toward encouraging voter participation and early voting, opposition to President Donald Trump and his administration remained prominent among the crowd.

Individual events varied. In Ferndale, the theme was “Voting Is Your Superpower — Use It,” with a Captain America cutout for photos outside the post office. In Troy, attendees could get voter information, meet candidates or sign up to text voters and canvass ahead of Michigan’s Nov. 3 election.

Huntington Woods resident Michael Majewski, 46, brought his 7-year-old daughter, Jane, to the Ferndale demonstration. She made her own "No Kings" sign, drawing a crown and crossing it out.

Jane said she was excited to participate, “because I want to help our country.”

Her father, Majewski, said he worries about political influence overshadowing science and environmental concerns, and he wants human rights, women's rights and LGBTQ+ rights protected.

“We want human rights in general to matter again. We want women's rights to matter again. We want the queer community's rights to matter again,” Majewski said. “We want environmental issues being addressed and not being sold off.”

“Money is being prioritized over a lot of things, right, and we’re here to fight against that,” he added.

'Make that make sense'

Debbie Elliott, 71, of Royal Oak said she thinks about what today's political decisions could mean for her grandchildren, citing economic concerns, job losses, and the spread of misinformation.

“I want them to have opportunities, and I want them to feel safe, and I want them to feel free, and I want them to be who they want to be and not be prosecuted for it,” Elliott said. “I’m hoping that the people who voted for him will change their mind and realize that we’re here to show love and do good for the country.”

Detroiter Tracey Traylor, 59, who said she has attended several "No Kings" events around Metro Detroit, said she worries about the effects of Trump administration policies on Black communities, particularly changes involving diversity and equity programs, education and civil rights.

The Trump administration has taken several steps targeting DEI initiatives, including rescinding a decades-old equal-opportunity requirement for federal contractors. In Michigan, the University of Michigan announced in March 2025 that it would close its DEI office amid pressure from the Trump administration over DEI programs.

Traylor said she believes those changes could make it harder for Black students and workers to access opportunities.

“Make that make sense,” she said. "I would say in the last 10 years, we've been terrorized by someone who claims to love America, but he has done every single thing to show that he hates America and what we truly should stand for,” Traylor said.

'Get out and vote'

The Troy Democratic Club combined its street demonstration with election organizing.

Justine Galbraith, 47, of Troy, the club's vice chair, said organizers sold signs, provided voter information and set up tables for texting voters and canvassing. She said half of the proceeds from $10 sign sales went to the ACLU of Michigan.

“It’s time to vote for people who will stand up for human rights and our democracy and our constitution,” Galbraith said.

She cited the Trump administration's treatment of immigrants, tariffs and rising gas and grocery prices among her concerns.

At the Troy event, Tom Turner, the Democrat challenging Republican state Rep. Thomas Kuhn in Michigan's 57th House District, said affordability has consistently emerged as a top concern in his conversations with voters.

“Number one, first and foremost, is cost of living. Every single conversation starts with it's just way too expensive right now,” Turner said.

Turner urged participation regardless of voters' choice of candidate.

“Whoever you vote for. Make sure you get out and vote.”

Gilchrist on protecting voter information

Gilchrist, who is running against Republican Anthony Forlini, criticized the Trump administration's efforts to obtain Michigan voter information and said protecting voters' personal information would be a priority if elected secretary of state.

In 2025, the Trump administration sued Michigan in 2025 seeking voter data, but a federal appeals court in June upheld the dismissal of the case.

“I won't let him or big tech get their hands on the private information that people give the Secretary of State. Privacy matters to people, and that transcends partisanship,” Gilchrist said. “I know how to protect data really well. I'm a software developer. I'm the only software developer elected statewide in this country.”

Forlini could not be reached for comment as of Saturday evening.

Gilchrist also touted Proposal 2, the "money out of politics" initiative appearing on Michigan's Nov. 3 ballot.

The proposal would prohibit regulated electric and gas utilities, government contractors receiving more than $250,000 annually in government contracts, and certain affiliated people and organizations from making some campaign contributions. It would also expand disclosure and regulation of certain political communications, including online communications, according to a Michigan House Fiscal Agency analysis.

"The Michigan 'money out of politics' initiative (will) get dirty and dark corporate money out of our politics," Gilchrist said. "As Secretary of State, I'll oversee campaign finance law. I'll be the one to administer that, to bring transparency, so we can see that money, where it goes, to be able to go after the bad actors with my authority, and to close the loopholes that allow them to create an unlevel playing field for the people of Michigan."

Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

text:
Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar is fighting back against the Trump administration’s search of her home earlier this week – disputing its legality and demanding the return of her property seized by federal agents.

Omar’s attorneys sent a letter Friday, obtained by CNN, to prosecutors at the Justice Department, saying, “This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers.”

The administration pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Omar’s Washington, D.C.-area house in an immigration fraud probe that targets the congresswoman, possible false statements made on government documents, and a potential conspiracy, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday after a federal magistrate judge signed off on the warrant, while limiting how the Justice Department could access her documents. Omar has been the persistent target of ire from President Donald Trump’s administration.

Omar sought to dismantle the basis of the probe, saying she became a lawfully naturalized citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia in 1995.

“There is no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status,” Omar’s attorneys, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, wrote in the letter to federal prosecutors. They also demanded that all video and audio recordings made by federal agents during the search be preserved.

A Justice Department spokesperson told CNN in a statement that the letter from Omar’s attorneys was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies.”

“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” the spokesperson said in the statement to CNN. “Leaking a letter to the press right after sending it is not good faith. It is a publicity play.”

Omar’s attorneys pointed out a number of issues with how the search of Omar’s home was conducted. They said the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel was not notified about the search until after it was publicly reported. The judge in Washington had mandated special procedures about giving notice to the House and to Omar and her attorneys about her Constitutional protections as a member of Congress, the letter said. Omar’s defense attorneys indicated the investigators may have infringed on the congresswoman’s rights by not following the judge’s parameters.

There also was no one from the US attorney’s office or the Justice Department at the search to read Omar her privileges under the Speech or Debate Clause, according to the letter, and instead Omar was presented with a waiver that she did not sign. Omar’s attorneys also alleged they did not have the opportunity to identify or segregate materials that were protected under the clause.

The search “arose from a years-old, tired conspiracy theory,” Omar’s attorneys wrote, also pointing out the search was conducted less than three weeks before Election Day.

“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions. But the political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day. For the reasons given above, this search was neither justified nor lawful,” they wrote in the letter, first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

Jeffress and Matz noted that Omar was repeatedly referred to by her first name in the search warrant paperwork and called on the agents to respect the congresswoman with her proper title going forward.

text:
Local activist groups are protesting the sale of Boston Dynamics’ robot dogs to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, demanding, among other things, that the Waltham-based company pull the software license that would allow ICE to operate the machines.

Don’t Mourn Organize and De-ICE Action Network are spearheading two protests outside Boston Dynamics headquarters this month. One was held Oct. 15, with another planned for Oct. 20.

“It’s just shocking that they would do something so likely to result in human rights violations,” said Betsy Leondar-Wright, a member of both Don’t Mourn Organize and De-ICE Action Network.“This just seems to go against everything that Boston Dynamics says that it stands for,” she said.

In addition to revoking the software license, Don’t Mourn Organize also wants the commonwealth of Massachusetts to rescind a $25 million tax credit awarded to Boston Dynamics in June, according to a petition with signatures from more than a dozen local organizations. The tax credit is part of a $100 million expansion of the Boston Dynamics manufacturing facility in Waltham, according to the company website.

“We cannot claim to protect our residents while at the same time we provide a subsidy to create weapons used against them,” the petition reads.

These local activist groups are targeting any company doing business with ICE, but felt a special responsibility to protest Boston Dynamics because it was so close to home.

Elizabeth Hoffecker, founder of activist group Indivisible Waltham, said IW’s goal in joining these protests is preventing businesses like Boston Dynamics from collaborating with or selling to ICE, and making it “as economically painful” as possible for them to continue doing so.

“A lot of corporations have been willing to sell out on community values to make a buck at participating in the infrastructure of dismantling democracy,” Hoffecker said.

A contentious contract

The contract for the robot dogs is between ICE and Connecticut company RADeCO, which modified Boston Dynamics’ original machines, called SPOT dogs, to include a robotic arm, thermal camera and sensors for explosive materials. ICE spent about $1.3 million on four such modified versions, called Cerberus, according to a federal contract document.

Although Boston Dynamics is not named as a contractor in the recent sale, the company has long partnered with RADeCO, especially for “government-related applications,” according to a Boston Dynamics spokesperson. They added, however, that Boston Dynamics’ ethics code applies to all sales of their products like SPOT, even when officially sold by RADeCO.

The company’s robots are “legally prohibited from being weaponized or used for purposes of harm or intimidation,” the spokesperson said. Boston Dynamics also published an open letter against the weaponization of general use robots like SPOT.

Boston Dynamics has previously said that if ICE misused the robots, it would void the warranty, terminate the license for the SPOT software, and take legal action. The company has also said that it has not recorded any instances of misuse in the time that it has contracted with law enforcement agencies.

RADeCO declined to comment.

A different call to arms

So far, Cerberus has been used for tasks like “hazardous gas detection, unexploded ordnance inspection, suspicious package investigation, search and rescue, subterranean or confined space exploration and structural assessments following fires, disaster events and other hazards,” according to the Boston Dynamics representative.

“Even if they’re not like Boston Dynamics is saying, they’re not going to physically attack humans, they can aid and abet the harm that ICE does. It just seems really, really outrageous,” Leondar-Wright said.

Even if Boston Dynamics didn’t directly sell the technology, “It’s the duty of the researcher to promote the well-being and safety of the individual in the community,” said Thomas Vaughn, a Northeastern engineering ethics professor, adding, “And non-malfeasance is an obligation on the part of the researchers to avoid causing harm by their discoveries.” Selling robots to ICE goes against that ethical principle, he said.

It’s unclear how ICE plans to implement the robots in their operations, but the agency is known to rely on technology, from facial recognition to spyware, for its surveillance and enforcement efforts. Congressional funding in 2026 also allowed ICE to purchase a device meant to stop and capture a moving car, and battery powered electric shock gloves for agents to wear during arrests.

“I think it is a trend of dehumanizing conflict, kind of turning conflict into some kind of video game that I think makes it even easier to take life without thinking about it,” Hoffecker said.

Building momentum

This month’s protests are not the first time the local groups have mobilized. Don’t Mourn Organize and De-Ice Action Network held their first protest back in September at the Museum of Science, where a SPOT robot was on display. Protesters dressed up in dog outfits and held signs decrying the original sale.

De-Ice Action Network also has previous experience with protests — and with success. Its campaign against Citizens Bank saw dozens of rallies around the country and the bank ending its financial support of private prisons used by ICE to detain immigrants.

Hoffecker, who was part of the Citizens Bank Coalition, said IW and other local activists aim to bring awareness to such issues that people may not be aware of.

“Ultimately, if we’re going to shift course, it’s going to come down to just regular people in large enough numbers changing who gets elected and also changing … the dynamics of all these businesses that are propping up the current system,” she said.

title: ICE pursued Houston suspect who died in 2017, family says - USA Today
description:

The man's daughter provided a Mexican death certificate to the group and an attorney representing the injured worker, FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said Oct. 16.

text:
The man U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said it was pursuing when an agent struck and seriously injured a Houston construction worker had been dead for nine years, according to his family and an immigration advocacy group, raising new questions about the agency's account of the Oct. 10 incident.

The family identified the man in an ICE-released photograph as Jose Hector Jimenez Mendoza, who died in 2017, according to FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights organization. The man's daughter provided a Mexican death certificate to the group and an attorney representing the injured worker, FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said Oct. 16.

The Harris County District Attorney's Office has received the documentation, Espinosa said. A spokesperson for the office also told The Associated Press that Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, the name ICE gave for its target, was not in the vehicle with the injured worker.

The incident left Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, with multiple leg fractures and an injured ankle. He remains hospitalized in federal custody and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to AP News.

USA TODAY reached out to ICE, as well as the Harris County District Attorney's Office for additional comment.

Family disputes ICE's identification of suspect

ICE said its agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Mendoza-Cervantes when Parra Hernandez and another man fled on foot. The agency previously said Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.

But the family recognized the photograph ICE released as that of Jimenez Mendoza, who died while attempting to reenter the United States, according to The New York Times.

In a statement published Oct. 15, Espinosa accused ICE of providing a false account and called on the agency to tell the truth.

"How can they have seen a dead man getting into a car? How could they have seen a dead man run?" Espinosa said in the statement.

The death certificate lists the man's name as J. Hector Jimenez Mendoza, his year of death as 2017 and the location as Laredo, Texas, NBC News reported. His daughter, Jamie Jimenez, told The New York Times that her father used aliases, including the name ICE provided.

USA TODAY reached out to FIEL Houston for additional comment on how the group verified the death certificate, the family's identification of the photograph and efforts to secure Parra Hernandez's release from ICE custody.

Video raises questions about ICE's account

Surveillance footage reviewed by authorities appears to contradict ICE's claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle. The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median toward a man running away. Although another vehicle blocks the camera's view of the collision, the man is seen on the ground moments later, AP News reported.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare is investigating the incident and considering whether the ICE officer who drove the vehicle could face an aggravated assault charge involving a deadly weapon, NBC News reported. Teare has said the footage indicates the officer intentionally struck Parra Hernandez. ICE has denied that allegation.

A senior Department of Homeland Security official told NBC News that the officer had been placed on administrative leave and that the agency was reviewing body-camera footage internally.

Worker remains hospitalized in ICE custody

Parra Hernandez's attorney, Kim Bruno, told The Associated Press he was experiencing depression in federal custody, particularly after learning that he may not have been the target of the operation.

FIEL is seeking his release before he is transferred from the hospital to a federal detention center.

Bruno also represents Luis Enrique Delfin Martinez, one of two men who had been detained in a separate operation and were handcuffed in the back of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra Hernandez. Bruno said Martinez suffered soft-tissue injuries after being thrown around inside the vehicle

FIEL has called on ICE to release body-camera footage and provide a fuller account of the incident as the district attorney's investigation continues.

Reporter Anthony Thompson can be reached at ajthompson@usatodayco.com, or on X @athompsonUSAT.

title: Trump's Big Bend Border Wall Faces Legal Setback as Judge Finds DHS Likely Exceeded ...
description:
Although federal officials cited more than 89,000 apprehensions between 2021 and 2025, the judge found that Big Bend ranked last among southern border sectors in both total apprehensions and apprehensions per mile.
The order also suspended three DHS waivers affecting Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and surrounding public and private lands while litigation continues.
Congress granted the DHS secretary broad authority under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 to waive legal requirements for expedited border construction.
Evidence showed that Big Bend accounted for approximately 1% of non-marijuana drug seizures during the period reviewed.
Federal officials are seeking to lift the restrictions.
text:
A federal judge has found that the Trump administration likely exceeded its authority when it waived dozens of federal laws to build border barriers in Texas's Big Bend region, citing evidence that the sprawling sector has the lowest migrant apprehension rates along the U.S.-Mexico border.

In a 14-page opinion issued October 14, 2026, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone challenged the Department of Homeland Security's justification for bypassing environmental and other legal protections across the 517-mile sector. Although federal officials cited more than 89,000 apprehensions between 2021 and 2025, the judge found that Big Bend ranked last among southern border sectors in both total apprehensions and apprehensions per mile.

The opinion explains Cardone's October 2 preliminary injunctionA preliminary injunction is a temporary court order issued before a case is finally decided that requires a party to take or stop an action while the litigation continues. Federal courts generally consider the likelihood of success, irreparable harm, the balance of equities, and the public interest before granting one.Read more →, which halted border barrier construction and other ground-disturbing activities unless the administration complies with applicable laws. The order also suspended three DHS waivers affecting Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and surrounding public and private lands while litigation continues.

Congress granted the DHS secretary broad authority under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 to waive legal requirements for expedited border construction. However, the statute ties that power to efforts to deter unlawful crossings in areas of high illegal entry, a limitation at the center of Cardone's findings.

Big Bend accounts for more than a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border but represented only 0.3% to 2.2% of apprehensions along the southern border annually over the past 30 years. Federal officials argued that apprehension figures provide an incomplete measure of illegal crossings, while Cardone found that the comparisons remained relevant to determining whether the sector met the law's requirements.

The judge reasoned that accepting DHS's interpretation would effectively erase Congress's geographic restriction. If the sector with the lowest apprehension rate qualified as an area of high illegal entry, the same authority could extend across the entire southern border.

Cardone also examined the administration's reliance on drug smuggling to justify construction. Evidence showed that Big Bend accounted for approximately 1% of non-marijuana drug seizures during the period reviewed. The judge found that a significant portion of seizures likely involved drugs already moving within the United States, weakening the government's argument that the figures established a need for barriers in the sector.

The findings supported the challengers' claim under the major questions doctrine, which requires clear congressional authorization when federal agencies exercise powers of major economic or political significance. Cardone ruled that the doctrine could support a constitutional challenge to the waivers and that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in showing DHS had exceeded the authority Congress granted.

The lawsuit was filed April 16 by the Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church and river guide Danny William Miller Jr. They contend that the construction threatens protected wilderness, historic sites, religious practices and livelihoods tied to the Rio Grande.

Testimony at an October 2 hearing detailed the potential consequences. Miller described how proposed barriers could prevent him from launching river tours, while rancher Bill Guerra-Addington warned that losing access to the Rio Grande would leave him without the water needed to grow crops.

An ecologist and soil scientist also testified that construction could disrupt natural water systems, damage vegetation and affect wildlife, with recovery potentially taking decades. Cardone cited that evidence in finding a substantial threat of irreparable harm, a legal standard covering injuries that a later court ruling or financial compensation could not adequately remedy.

The construction plans have also drawn opposition from Texas Republicans, including ranchers, local officials and longtime Trump supporters concerned about potential federal land seizures. Some property owners have received survey-access notices warning that the government could pursue eminent domain proceedings if agreements cannot be reached.

Federal officials are seeking to lift the restrictions. On October 8, the administration asked Cardone to suspend her injunction while pursuing Supreme Court review, arguing that the construction delays impose substantial financial costs.

The government estimated that the order is costing Customs and Border Protection at least $462,800 daily, with another $7 million needed to remove workers and equipment from five projects.
