title: They free immigrants from ICE in hours. S.F. says wait a year. - Mission Local
description:
The delay means Bay Area immigrants will languish in detention because the network cannot meet demand.
The Bay Area Habeas Network, which consists of nine Bay Area legal nonprofits and public defenders’ offices, aims to file emergency habeas corpus petitions for every immigration arrest in the area.
The Bay Area Habeas Network, which has freed at least 49 Bay Area residents arrested by ICE in the last five months, asked San Francisco for $250,000 in August to contribute to this work.
“ICE is weaponizing geography against immigrants,” said Jordan Weiner, an immigration attorney at La Raza Centro Legal and one of the founding members of the Bay Area Habeas Network.
The network has filed 49 petitions total for 57 Bay Area residents since the network began on May 1.
text:
The Bay Area’s network of pro-bono immigration lawyers won’t receive needed city funding to release people from detention until late next year, according to Hillary Ronen, director of La Raza Centro Legal. The delay means Bay Area immigrants will languish in detention because the network cannot meet demand.

The Bay Area Habeas Network, which consists of nine Bay Area legal nonprofits and public defenders’ offices, aims to file emergency habeas corpus petitions for every immigration arrest in the area. Those petitions can quickly release someone from detention, often within hours.

On Tuesday in Santa Rosa, for example, three vehicles surrounded a Mexican-born father and tow-truck driver as he sat in his car in a parking lot. About half-a-dozen masked officers in vests marked “POLICE ICE” exited their cars, drew their guns, pulled him out and handcuffed him, according to his attorney and court filings.

The man was taken to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s San Francisco holding cells at 630 Sansome St., where a group of attorneys filed a habeas petition seeking his release.

A federal judge ordered his release the same day. He is now back home with his 18-year-old daughter and wife, a U.S. citizen.

But those petitions require a team of round-the-clock attorneys to interview immigrants in detention and write legal arguments. They monitor arrests and quickly step in to file petitions.

The Bay Area Habeas Network, which has freed at least 49 Bay Area residents arrested by ICE in the last five months, asked San Francisco for $250,000 in August to contribute to this work.

After inquiries from Mission Local, the mayor’s office said the request will be considered as part of next year’s budget process. But that funding would not arrive until September 2027, said Ronen, the former District 9 supervisor.

“The emergency is now,” she said. “We need to challenge every illegal arrest of our neighbors by ICE, today.”

The demand is significant: 116 habeas petitions have been filed in San Francisco’s Northern District court between the start of President Donald Trump’s term and July 1, 2026. But according to federal data from the U.C. Berkeley’s Deportation Data Project, 3,870 immigrants were arrested across 18 major Bay Area cities in that time, meaning thousands likely went without a petition to challenge their detention.

Santa Clara County has already committed $250,000 to hire one more attorney, according to the network. San Francisco’s contribution would also mean an additional lawyer.

San Francisco already funds several nonprofits that are members of the network directly, but not the network itself.

The request comes as immigration arrests surge in other parts of California. Though there has not been a surge locally, arrests across major Bay Area cities rose 81 percent between July 2025 and July 2026, according to a Mission Local analysis of federal data released by U.C. Berkeley.

How does the Habeas Network respond to arrests?

A habeas petition asks a federal judge to decide whether the government is holding someone lawfully. Attorneys argue that ICE arrested people without a warrant, for example, and subsequently win their release from detention.

While winning doesn’t end a person’s immigration case, it does let them fight from home instead of a detention center.

Speed is everything when it comes to filing habeas petitions: If a petition is not submitted quickly, ICE can move a detainee out of Northern California. Once that happens, a petition can no longer be filed in San Francisco’s federal court.

“ICE is weaponizing geography against immigrants,” said Jordan Weiner, an immigration attorney at La Raza Centro Legal and one of the founding members of the Bay Area Habeas Network.

One immigrant with pre-existing medical conditions was arrested near the Highland Hospital in Oakland, for example, and lawyers were unable to find him in the ICE locator before he was transferred to Texas and then deported.

When someone calls one of the regional Rapid Response Networks to report an arrest, the network sends an attorney to the San Francisco ICE field office. The attorney then interviews the detained person and gathers facts about their case.

Meredith Sullivan, an attorney with Centro Legal de La Raza in Oakland, spent last Tuesday on the sixth floor of that office sitting across a glass wall from her clients and interviewing them, including the tow-truck driver from Mexico.

“It’s very sobering, and it’s extremely unfair. You’re trying to get as much info as possible with a time crunch,” she said.

Sullivan then shared those facts with the network of attorneys, who wrote up a habeas petition with a legal argument pushing for release. Once the petition is filed, a federal judge reviews it and, if they accept it, orders the immigrant released, usually within hours.

The network has filed 49 petitions total for 57 Bay Area residents since the network began on May 1. Over 90 percent of them were ordered immediately released, according to materials shared by the creators of the network.

“If we didn’t get to these individuals, then they would be in a detention center in the middle of a desert, or deported to a third country,” Ronen said.

The network says it needs more funding

Ali Saidi, who leads immigration work at the Contra Costa County Public Defender’s Office, said the network does not have the lawyers to meet demand. The attorneys writing habeas petitions need to be “cranking out a complex legal motion” and cannot also be at the court gathering facts.

“We’re not able to cover them all,” said Jennifer Noris, an immigration defense attorney in the same office.

Ronen said she met with Supervisor Jackie Fielder’s office, the Office of Civic Engagement and Immigrant Affairs and Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office on Aug. 26 to make the request.

Ronen said the city’s contribution would likely come as a budget supplemental, a one-time bucket of funding that must be approved by the Board of Supervisors.

City staff was receptive, Ronen said, but she heard nothing until Oct. 15, after Mission Local inquired about the funding. The mayor’s office then said it would consider it, but only next year.

What the network truly needs, said Shira Levine, co-founder of the network and former immigration judge, is a regional response. Santa Clara has funding through June 2027 at least, and San Mateo has almost finalized its own contract. Napa and Sonoma counties both made “soft commitments,” according to the network.

But “were there to be greater levels of enforcement,” as threatened last year during President Trump’s aborted immigration surge in October, the network would be critical, Levine said.

“It’s impossible to flip a switch” and quickly hire the needed lawyers, she added.

“Because we are doing the legal process.
We are here legally, with documents from USCIS, the federal government that allow us to be here while our case is in process,” Eduardo said.
He called his wife to confirm that ICE arrested him, and that he was taken to the detention center in Batavia.
In the last year, ICE arrested five other SUNY employees and a University of Buffalo researcher.
text:
BATAVIA, N.Y. — The son of a SUNY Brockport IT worker spoke out after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents took his father into custody Tuesday morning.

German Machado, an IT tech at SUNY Brockport, was arrested by ICE after officials said he overstayed his visa, which allowed him to stay in the United States from August 2016 until February 2017. His son Eduardo Machado told News10NBC’s Erin Mahon that the family came from Venezuela and is seeking political asylum after his mother received threats for her work as a journalist.

“The process takes a very long time. And in that time, you are provided with a work authorization card to legally work and live while the process is ongoing,” Eduardo said.

Eduardo said he and his brother now hold the same work permit as their father and both have entered the workforce. “It’s nothing different from an American. I, they asked me for my social security number, which I have. They ask for a document from the federal government that states that you are allowed to work with — which is that work authorization card. And then your background check. Just like any other American,” Eduardo said.

Eduardo said the family is afraid but believes they deserve due process. “Because we are doing the legal process. We came the right way. We came legally. We are here legally, with documents from USCIS, the federal government that allow us to be here while our case is in process,” Eduardo said.

Eduardo’s brother Sam said the family filed their asylum and withholding removal application in September 2016, before their initial visas expired the following February. Since then, their application status remained pending, and they had not yet received a hearing date. ICE officials said that work authorization or a pending application does not confer legal status.

“We’ve been following every recommendation,” Sam said. “We’re grateful to the United States for the opportunity to seek asylum, and still trust the legal process while waiting for a determination,” he continued.

The family said they have only heard from German once since his arrest, during a brief phone call just after 9 a.m. Tuesday when he arrived at the detention facility. He called his wife to confirm that ICE arrested him, and that he was taken to the detention center in Batavia. The family has not received updates regarding the next step in his legal proceedings.

In the last year, ICE arrested five other SUNY employees and a University of Buffalo researcher. SUNY employees included Yan Vazquez Hidalgo, Alex Ramirez Gonzalez, Mohamed Fofana, Dane Ka and Ibrahim Halil Topkaya. All of the SUNY employees, with the exception of Topkaya, and the UB researcher, Dr. Shovgi Huseynov, were released.

News10NBC will continue to follow developments in this case.

text:
A Texas Department of Public Safety official warned troopers against using third-party messaging applications to communicate with other law enforcement agencies after body camera footage showed a trooper using Signal to help coordinate the detention of an 18-year-old high school student by federal immigration authorities.

The warning followed the publication of a video showing the trooper sending information about the teenager to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement through the encrypted messaging app. An ICE agent responded with one word: “Detain.”

Emails obtained by KPRC 2’s investigative team show that concerns about Signal and other messaging platforms were not new. DPS leadership had previously warned officers that communications related to investigations must be preserved and, when required, submitted as evidence.

The latest disclosure raises questions about how law enforcement agencies document communications between officers and federal immigration authorities, particularly when those exchanges help facilitate an arrest or detention.

According to the investigation, a 28-minute body camera video recorded during a May 1 traffic stop in Austin shows a trooper pulling over a teenager who was returning home after working a night shift at a fast-food restaurant.

The student was a high school senior. During the stop, the trooper used Signal on a personal phone to send a photograph of the teenager’s identification to federal immigration authorities.

The messages shown in the footage indicate that the trooper shared information identifying the teenager as 18 and as a Mexican national. An ICE agent responded by sending information about the teen, including a federal identification number, and the message “Detain.”

Federal immigration authorities subsequently arrived and took the teenager into custody.

The trooper’s communications were visible in the body camera footage, which later became central to questions about the agency’s use of messaging apps and its record-preservation procedures.

The teenager was released in time to attend his high school graduation after his attorney filed a habeas corpus petition seeking his release. U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat representing Austin, also pushed for the teenager’s release.

A habeas corpus petition allows a person to challenge the legality of their detention before a court.

Within five days of Austin NBC affiliate KXAN publishing the footage, DPS Deputy Director of Law Enforcement Operations Lt. Col. Jason Taylor sent an email to agency chiefs warning that officers continued to use third-party messaging applications.

In the email, Taylor referenced applications such as Signal and emphasized that officers should use agency-approved platforms instead. He identified Bridge4PS as the agency’s primary messaging application.

Taylor explained that the approved platform allows officers to preserve and transfer communications into PDF documents, making it easier to maintain records that could be subject to public information requests.

Signal is known for its end-to-end encryption and features that allow messages to disappear automatically. Those features can create challenges for agencies that must retain communications in accordance with public records requirements or preserve evidence for legal proceedings.

The emails obtained by KPRC 2 also show that Taylor had raised similar concerns in March 2024. At that time, he warned that communications exchanged through Signal, WhatsApp and other third-party apps during joint investigations could be subject to evidence-preservation requirements.

Taylor said messages involving multi-agency task forces and operations may need to be included in case files provided to prosecutors, even when other participating agencies do not submit them.

The agency’s concerns, therefore, extend beyond which messaging app officers use. They also involve whether law enforcement communications are documented and retained in accordance with applicable requirements.

In September, DPS released a redacted screenshot of the Signal exchange between the trooper and ICE agents after a public records request.

The screenshot included portions of the conversation captured on body camera footage, as well as additional messages from individuals identified as ICE agents. Some messages included requests for status updates and instructions such as “stand-by” and “release.”

The release of those messages offered another view of the communications between state and federal officers. However, questions remain about whether similar exchanges are consistently preserved across the agency.

Tom Gregor, a Houston trial lawyer and board member of the Freedom of Information Foundation of Texas, told reporters that the preserved messages were an encouraging sign but did not establish whether all officers were following the required procedures.

He emphasized the importance of establishing mechanisms to ensure communications are retained, rather than relying solely on individual officers to preserve them.

Texas law and applicable public records requirements govern how government agencies maintain and disclose records. Whether a particular message must be retained or produced depends on the applicable legal requirements and circumstances.

The Texas Department of Information Resources also confirmed that a state contract allows multiple agencies to use Bridge4PS at a pre-negotiated price. DPS had not provided details about how much the agency pays for the service.

The incident comes amid broader scrutiny of cooperation between Texas law enforcement and federal immigration authorities.

Texas has expanded coordination between state agencies and federal immigration enforcement, including through programs that authorize certain trained state and local officers to perform specified immigration enforcement functions under federal agreements.

The trooper involved in the Austin stop had received limited immigration authority through the federal 287(g) program, according to reports.

The program allows participating law enforcement agencies to enter into agreements with ICE under which designated officers receive authority to perform certain immigration enforcement duties. The scope of that authority depends on the specific agreement and training.

The use of traffic stops in immigration enforcement has also drawn attention from other Texas news organizations. In March, KUT and The Texas Newsroom reported on a separate Austin traffic stop in which a DPS trooper contacted federal authorities during an encounter that led to the detention of five men.

That case involved a different incident and does not establish that the same procedures or circumstances applied to the teenager’s detention. It does, however, provide additional context for ongoing reporting about how state traffic enforcement can intersect with federal immigration operations.

text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a rising star in the Democratic Party who captured the governor's office last year by a large margin, will deliver the Democrats' response Tuesday night to President Donald Trump's State of the Union address, focusing on affordability and the chaos she believes the Trump administration has caused at home and abroad, her team told reporters.

Spanberger, who was inaugurated in January after serving three terms in the House of Representatives, will discuss lowering the persistently high costs of housing, health care, energy and groceries despite the administration's insistence that some of these costs have come down.

LIVE UPDATES: Pres. Trump to deliver State of the Union address on ABC

The daughter of a law enforcement officer and a nurse, Spanberger focused relentlessly on affordability throughout her 2025 gubernatorial campaign. Despite the economy being the top issue Trump ran on in the 2024 election, it's been one of the issues he's struggled with the most during his second term, as Americans still haven't felt the "Trump boom" they were promised.

In an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, 57% of Americans disapprove of how Trump's handling the economy, and 64% disapproved of how he's handling tariffs on imported goods.

Spanberger, a former CIA officer, will also address how the Trump administration is contributing to greater worldwide uncertainty.

Trump and his team have spent a large portion of his second term so far focusing on foreign policy, including Trump going head-to-head with some U.S. allies and becoming more aggressive on the world stage. A former federal law enforcement officer who worked on narcotics and money-laundering cases for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Spanberger will also address what critics call the chaos caused by the Trump administration, which continues its immigration enforcement efforts that Americans are seeing in their communities.

RELATED: How to watch Trump's 2026 State of the Union address

She is also expected to challenge Republicans in Congress for not standing up to Trump.

Several Democrats have invited survivors of late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to attend Trump's address, while others plan to skip the event altogether in protest.

The governor will give her speech live from Colonial Williamsburg, the restored 18th century capital where Virginian representatives voted for its delegation to Congress to propose independence for all 13 colonies from Great Britain, and later adopted the Virginia Declaration of Rights -- which influenced the Declaration of Independence and Bill of Rights.

Spanberger has been able to appeal to both Democratic and Republican voters. She won the governor election in November by more than 15% -- the largest margin for a Democrat in the state since 1961 -- winning counties that voted for Trump in 2016, 2020, and 2024.

There are at least two major counter events that several Democrats plan to attend, including MoveOn's People's State of the Union, which is promoting the participation of more than 20 members of Congress; and the "State of the Swamp" event by Defiance.org that features a handful of celebrities appearing by video or in person, such as Robert De Niro.

Spanberger prepared for her remarks by watching speeches other Democrats have delivered in response to Trump's previous addresses to Congress.

title: It wouldn't be easy to strip Rep. Ilhan Omar of her citizenship, legal experts say | Politics
description: (CNN) — The search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, home by federal law enforcement earlier this week was an extraordinary legal step taken against a sitting congresswoman who is
text:
(CNN) —
The
search
of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, home by federal law enforcement earlier this week was an extraordinary legal step taken against a sitting congresswoman who is facing reelection.
The Justice Department pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Omar’s home while the congresswoman has said she believes the administration is ultimately seeking to intimidate her.
The government has not yet indicated it will take steps to attempt to strip Omar of her citizenship. But the president himself has said he’d like to see Omar sent
to Somalia
.
“Fake “Congresswoman” Illhan Omar, a constant complainer who hates the USA, knows everything there is to know. She should be in jail, or even a worse punishment, sent back to Somalia, considered one of the absolutely worst countries in the World,” President Donald Trump posted on Truth social earlier this year. “She could help to MAKE SOMALIA GREAT AGAIN!”
Omar has not been charged with a crime, and the Justice Department has not revealed any evidence against her.
But the path for the federal government to attempt
denaturalization
wouldn’t be an easy one, legal experts told CNN.
Citizenship has long been considered “a kind of a safe harbor,” said Daniel Kanstroom, a Boston College professor who teaches immigration law. “It’s hard to get, but once you get it, the standard for the government to take it away is really, really high.”
Challenges ahead
Sources told CNN the search was related to an immigration-fraud probe investigating whether Omar’s father lied about her age when she obtained her citizenship in 2000.
Omar maintains she was born in Somalia in 1982 and spent the first years of her life in that country as it was embroiled in a deadly civil war. She has said she came to the US around age 12, and about five years later, she became a US citizen.
The federal investigators are looking at whether Omar lied about her age of 17 when she was applying for citizenship, and potentially whether that may have been a false statement repeated in recent years that could be prosecuted now.
Denaturalization, the process of stripping a naturalized citizen of their citizenship, is an arduous and, until recently, relatively rare process typically reserved for extraordinary lies or omissions made during the naturalization process.
It was used frequently to strip the US citizenships of former Nazis who lied about their wartime activities — the Department of Justice had a unit called the Office of Special Investigations that was formed specifically for this purpose — and has also been used against naturalized members of terrorist and other criminal organizations.
Since Trump took office last year, the Justice Department has said it would prioritize some denaturalization proceedings, which take place as lawsuits filed against citizens in federal court.
Between 2008 and June 12, 2026, 166 denaturalization complaints were filed, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, an annual average of less than 10, and a miniscule fraction compared to the hundreds of thousands of people who became newly naturalized every year.
But the second Trump administration has sought to ramp up those numbers as part of its efforts to curb and repeal nearly all forms of immigration — legal and illegal — into the United States. Earlier this month, the government announced it was moving to strip citizenship from 40 naturalized citizens through cases filed since August 21.
Under recent previous administrations, civil denaturalization cases were relatively rare. Between 2008 and 2024, 116 civil denaturalization lawsuits were filed, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, an average of less than seven cases a year.
But the second Trump administration has significantly ramped up those numbers as part of its efforts to curb immigration, filing more than 160 civil denaturalization cases this year alone as of September 28, according to TRAC’s analysis.
“It’s a significant increase,” said Texas-based attorney Dan Gividen, a former Immigration and Customs Enforcement attorney during the Obama administration who is currently defending about 10 clients from denaturalization.
“For the government to go forward on either a criminal or civil denaturalization back then, the person had to warrant that kind of attention,” Gividen said.
The government could seek to denaturalize someone either through civil proceedings, or by obtaining a criminal conviction for naturalization fraud.
There is no statute of limitations for civil denaturalization proceedings.
The criminal offense, however
,
is generally subject to a 10-year window where it can be brought after a person becomes a citizen, so it would likely not be applicable in a case against Omar, who obtained her citizenship more than two decades ago.
A case against Omar
Omar has been under criminal investigations in recent years, including before Trump took office last year.
The current federal investigation is looking at whether Omar could have committed immigration fraud, and repeated false statements when filling out government documents, such as a passport, in recent years, and that could be considered a continuation of any suspected fraud.
Further detail of what prosecutors have gathered about Omar’s immigration and government records so far have been presented to a court confidentially and aren’t yet available to the public. However, more than a dozen media organizations and the right-leaning transparency advocacy group Judicial Watch asked a court this week to release more of investigators’ records that supported the search.
While the judge will hear from the Justice Department next week about those transparency requests, the criminal investigation continues.
Federal investigators gaining access to records found in Omar’s DC home is likely to progress slowly, as federal investigators could spend weeks or months trying to obtain some of the congresswoman’s documents.
If Omar were ever to be charged with a crime related to alleged immigration fraud, the Justice Department would have to prove that any misleading statements in immigration documents were made intentionally.
Process that could take years
The question of a possible deportation or denaturalization for Omar would also likely loom far in the future, even if there was evidence found of an immigration fraud crime.
Contested denaturalizations typically take between one to three years to process in district court, not including appeals, said Peter Loblack, an Orlando-based immigration attorney.
Even if a person has their citizenship stripped, deportation is not an immediate given.
A denaturalized citizen would revert to their most recent status — typically, a lawful permanent resident or green card holder — and then the government would have to seek to have them deported through an entirely different proceeding.
That also means that someone who is denaturalized could, theoretically, be renaturalized at a later date and under a different administration.
CNN’s Priscilla Alvarez and Catherine Shoichet contributed to this report.

text:
BURLINGTON, Mass. —

Vermont congresswoman Becca Balint and several other members of Congress made a surprise visit to New England's largest regional Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility on Friday.

Balint, who is the Vice Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, visited the ICE facility in Burlington, Massachusetts, on Friday. She and several other committee members showed up unannounced.

After waiting at the door for a moment, the group was allowed inside the building. After about an hour, they came back out and spoke to reporters.

"They understand that the eyes of the nation are on them," Balint said. "They understand that Americans don't like what they've been seeing."

Balint and fellow lawmakers said the facility holds about 12 detainees for about 5 to 7 days on average. They said the facility is not meant for such long holding periods.

"The fact of the matter is, people are here too long, especially women, " said Rep. Gabe Amo, D-RI-01.

Rep. Jake Auchincloss, D-MA-04, had previously visited the facility. He said that conditions have improved, but sleep and food accommodations are not ideal.

"I think the food situation is modestly improved from what I saw six months ago," Auchincloss said. "I don't think it's acceptable yet."

An ICE spokesperson sent NBC5 the following comment following the visit:

"The ICE Burlington field office complies with all required state and local laws.

"This is a processing facility, not a detention facility. Illegal aliens are quickly processed and transferred to permanent housing at a detention facility. ICE is regularly audited and inspected by internal and external agencies and is committed to transparency.

"Claims of inadequate conditions at the Burlington facility are FALSE. The ICE Burlington facility has an abundance of supplies, including food, assorted snacks, water, personal hygiene, and bedding materials. Detainees have access to a shower. In fact, ICE has higher detention standards than most US prisons that hold actual US citizens. All detainees are provided with proper meals, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with lawyers and their family members. Men and women are processed separately."

title: NYT reporter explains records behind questions about ICE target photo in Houston operation
description:
FOX 26 has not independently verified the identification of the man in the photograph or the reported alias connection.
DHS separately confirmed to FOX 26 that the agent is on leave during an active internal investigation.
What they're saying: DHS confirmed to FOX 26 that the agent involved in the incident is on leave.
FOX 26 also asked what supports the agency’s conclusion about intent while its internal investigation remains active.
The family’s account and the documents described by Ulloa raise questions that federal officials have not addressed in their response to FOX 26.
text:
A New York Times reporter whose work raised questions about the photograph ICE released after a Houston-area enforcement operation told FOX 26 her team reviewed multiple documents to corroborate a family’s account that the pictured man died nearly a decade ago.

In an interview Friday, Jazmine Ulloa described the reporting behind her story about Jamie Jimenez, a Dallas woman who identified the man in the photograph as her father, Jose Hector Jimenez Mendoza.

ICE identified its intended target as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes. Jimenez told the Times that her father used aliases, including that name.

The photograph was released following the Oct. 10 operation in northwest Harris County that left Miguel Parra-Hernandez hospitalized after an immigration agent struck him with an SUV.

FOX 26 has not independently verified the identification of the man in the photograph or the reported alias connection.

Ulloa, a national reporter for the Times, is also the author of El Paso, a book examining the history of the Texas border city through stories of migration, race and power. PenguinRandomHouse.com: Books

What we know:

The incident occurred near Clay Road and Highway 6. According to the Harris County Sheriff’s Office, two men left a truck and fled on foot. One escaped, while Parra-Hernandez was struck by an ICE vehicle.

Surveillance footage captured the SUV striking Parra-Hernandez as he ran through a parking lot. He was hospitalized and underwent surgery for a broken leg.

ICE said agents were attempting to arrest Mendoza-Cervantes, whom the agency described as having a final removal order and prior arrests.

Parra-Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, has said her client does not know Mendoza-Cervantes and that the wanted man was not in the truck with him.

The Harris County District Attorney’s Office and sheriff’s office are investigating the incident. DHS separately confirmed to FOX 26 that the agent is on leave during an active internal investigation.

What The Times Examined:

Ulloa said Jimenez recognized her father in the photograph DHS released and initially contacted FIEL, the immigrant rights organization assisting Parra-Hernandez’s family.

Jimenez later contacted Ulloa.

"She wanted to come forward and clear his name," Ulloa said.

Ulloa said the Times sought multiple sources of evidence to corroborate Jimenez’s account. The materials included family photographs, a Mexican death certificate recording Jimenez Mendoza’s death in Laredo in October 2017, and Jimenez’s own birth certificate identifying her father.

"We wanted to compile as much evidence corroborating her account as we could," Ulloa said.

Jimenez told the Times her father died during a separate immigration pursuit near the southern border. That account of the circumstances of his death remains attributed to the family.

Ulloa said her team also searched court records and found a criminal history consistent with the charges ICE attributed to its intended target.

"We also did many court record searches, compiled documents showing that the charges that ICE attributed to the men that they were targeting matched those of Mr. Jimenez Mendoza," Ulloa said.

She said those records included driving-under-the-influence and unlawful-possession-of-a-weapon charges.

What Records Establish:

Asked whether the court records appeared under Jimenez Mendoza’s given name or the name ICE released, Ulloa said her team found records under his given name.

"Yeah, we saw the name, his given name," she said.

Ulloa also acknowledged the difficulty of searching a common name, saying multiple people in Texas have variations of the name released by ICE.

She said Jimenez provided additional information that helped the Times distinguish her father’s records from those of other people.

The distinction matters: the court records Ulloa described were under Jose Hector Jimenez Mendoza’s given name. The connection to Jose Mendoza-Cervantes came from his daughter’s account of his aliases.

In the interview, Ulloa did not identify a court record independently establishing that alias connection.

Questions also remain about whether ICE distributed an incorrect photograph, confused identities or had another explanation for the discrepancy.

Ulloa said the Times asked federal officials whether an error occurred, whether someone else could have assumed the deceased man’s identity and how agents identified their target.

She said the agency had not answered those specific questions as of the interview.

What they're saying:

DHS confirmed to FOX 26 that the agent involved in the incident is on leave. The agency said the action is standard practice and does not establish wrongdoing.

A DHS spokesperson provided the following statement:

The statement did not address the photograph, Jimenez’s identification of her father or the reported death certificate.

FOX 26 asked DHS whether the photograph accurately depicts its intended target and what evidence led agents to identify someone in Parra-Hernandez’s truck as that person.

FOX 26 also asked what supports the agency’s conclusion about intent while its internal investigation remains active.

What the family told Ulloa

Ulloa said seeing the photograph circulated as an image of a wanted man was painful for Jimenez and her relatives.

Jimenez described her father as a pool plumber who had built a life in Dallas and encouraged her to attend college, Ulloa said.

The two had become estranged before his death, but Jimenez had been considering inviting him to her college graduation as a way to reconnect.

He died before she had that opportunity, Ulloa said.

Jimenez and other relatives felt compelled to speak because they believed the public was receiving an incomplete and inaccurate picture of him.

"They wanted to give a fuller picture of who he was and his life," Ulloa said.

What's next:

The local and federal investigations into the incident remain ongoing.

Identifying the man in the photograph and establishing whom agents actually encountered are separate questions. The family’s account and the documents described by Ulloa raise questions that federal officials have not addressed in their response to FOX 26.

Ulloa said Jimenez’s family is seeking answers about both the circumstances of her father’s death and why his photograph is now connected to the Houston operation.

"She still has so many questions about the day her father died under pursuit of immigration authorities," Ulloa said, "and now she has even more questions about why he’s being linked to this new incident."

description: NorCal Resist Migra Watch observers said they confirmed ICE officers were staying at the Home2Suites Hilton in Woodland and that an incident occurred near Empower Yolo early morning, Friday, Oct.
text:

The state of California filed a federal lawsuit against the National Archives an…



NorCal Resist Migra Watch observers said they confirmed ICE officers were staying at the Home2Suites Hilton in Woodland and that an incident occurred near Empower Yolo early morning, Friday, Oct. 9.

NorCal Resist says the incidents show an increase in immigration enforcement presence — a growing trend the nonprofit has tracked since the first Trump administration. “Since January of last year there has been a complete increase in enforcement, but within the last week, we will say it's likely doubled,” NorCal Resist programs director  Giselle Garcia, J.D., told the Enterprise on Thursday.

Garcia said NorCal Resist has documented detainments in areas of Butte, Colusa, El Dorado, Nevada, Placer, Sacramento, Sutter and Yolo counties, every day since the Thursday before the interview.

The uptick follows direction from the Department of Homeland Security from two weeks ago directing ICE to continuously target sanctuary cities. “We are absolutely going through a really critical time right now.”

However, Garcia said NorCal Resist does not confirm “Operation Safe California,” a viral 45-day plan showing increasing ICE activity in the state close to the general election. She points out: “Viral because we haven't seen any official memo from DHS or an ICE directive.”

About 40 people joined an emergency protest organized by Moms Against ICE outside the Hilton calling for the hotel not to house ICE agents on Tuesday .

Casa del Pan business owner Maria Olmedo has been collecting cash, gift cards, groceries, self-help items, and cleaning supplies for the family related to the incident near Empower Yolo. “I don't have to see the family to help out. We know they've been affected, so I'm just doing my part and collecting the items for the family.”

“They're scared, and there are kids involved, so we didn't want to put their names out there or anything that could make them visible to the community. It was a safe way to take donations and go through people who have that direct contact with them. I'm not asking questions. The goal is just for them to be a part of our community, regardless, and they don't have to explain anything.”

Garcia says NorCal Resist has also seen a general increase in city enforcements, like code enforcement on street vendors. “When we have policies that create a subclass of workers, they are more vulnerable to exploitation and use the system to abuse and target them, whether through code enforcement, ICE enforcement, not paying them for their labor.”

At Casa del Pan, Olmedo says the “sun shines for everyone,” calling it a safe space. She also supports other small businesses by letting them sell their items there.

She’s heard about restaurants calling code enforcement on street vendors. “That's not right. Let the sun shine for everyone.”

Honored by the Hispanic Chamber of Commerce for Small Business of the Year at the 54th annual SALUD! Business Awards, Olmedo also serves as a Trustee for the Yolo County Board of Education.

As the Woodland community comes together to support families targeted by ICE, the city of Davis is finalizing its street vendor ordinance, prompting some to urge the city council to slow down and consider the voices of the vendors.

As reported in the Enterprise earlier this year, Davis city staff expects to bring a sidewalk ordinance before the city council this fall for vendors operating in the public right-of-way. The sidewalk vendor ordinance does not require review by the Planning Commission.

“So far, the conversation appears to have centered on brick-and-mortar businesses and business associations. Their concerns matter, but they're only one part of the picture,” said Deema Tamimi, Davis human relations commissioner, during public comment at the Oct. 6 city council meeting.

Noting that street vending is often how entrepreneurs get started, especially those without significant capital, Tamimi said it’s not an “either-or” situation:  “Davis can have strong storefronts and a thriving, fairly treated street food scene, and the two can strengthen each other. So please take more time, broaden who you're listening to, and get this right.”

Tamimi cited the 2019 “Food and Economic Development (FED) in Davis” report that she co-authored with current planning commissioner and professor of community development Catherine Brinkley, Grace Perry, and former Davis Mayor Ann Evans. The report calls for policies that enable mobile food vending to succeed in Davis. Then-Davis Mayor Brett Lee, current executive director of the Davis Downtown Business Association, even wrote the foreword.

“Make it right the first time,” agreed street vendor Gustavo Landeros Mireles, speaking as a father of three children, whose business is his livelihood. He suggested to the council sending the drafted ordinance to city commissions.

He says brick and mortars are pressuring the city to restrict street vendors. He suggested the city gathers advice from food experts, street vendors, and a street vendor attorney to “educate the city council and the city on what the city can do and cannot do regarding this important issue.”

“Today, the community of Davis feels that Davis is for everyone, unless you're a Taco vendor. Please help us change this perspective. This is my full-time job,”  Mireles said.

He said that if he drew a map highlighting where they cannot sell, it would push most street vendors to the outskirts of the city. “That is something the community will not like, and that is an attack on my community, my values, and my culture. I am desperate because this ordinance will cause an economic hardship towards me and my family.”

“Everybody loves churros” - Mireles quoted in the California Aggie

In April 2025, the California Aggie student newspaper featured Mireles as the owner of the popular Churros El Rey in E Street Plaza, who shared his love of the business and plans to be an attorney to “protect those whose food, culture and labor have contributed immensely to the vibrancy of California’s streets.”

“Just imagine how terrifying it could be for undocumented people to be harassed,” Mireles told the Aggie. “That motivated me to go to law school and fight for everybody, because we have to fight for a better world.”

text:
Ilhan Omar’s attorneys have asked the US Department of Justice to return property that federal agents removed days earlier from her home during a search.

The lawyers for the Minnesota Democrat contended that the seizure as “neither justified nor lawful”, according to a letter that the Associated Press reported on Friday.

The federal investigation into Omar was launched just weeks ahead of the 3 November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot. Democrats accused Donald Trump, a Republican, of abusing his power as president to target a political opponent.

Omar’s attorneys wrote that there is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, according to the Wall Street Journal, which first reported on the lawyers’ letter.

“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the president’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” the congresswoman’s attorneys wrote.

The federal government has issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives, and seized her phone in its investigation of the congresswoman.

A justice department spokesperson said the letter from Omar’s defense team was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”, according to the AP.

“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” the spokesperson, Emily Covington, wrote in a text message on Friday evening.

The letter from Omar’s lawyers also accused the justice department of violating the agency’s longstanding policy aimed at avoiding potentially influencing an election. And they raised concerns about whether the investigators followed instructions from the magistrate judge who approved the search.

The attorneys demanded in the letter that the justice department preserve any audio and video taken during the search on Monday.

The justice department launched the investigation after years of Trump and conservative media figures promoting unsubstantiated rumors that Omar’s ex-husband is actually her brother – and that she married him so that he could obtain immigration status.

Omar, the most prominent Somali American in the US, has denied that allegation.

Citing sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News reported that the search on Monday was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork. Omar’s father filled out that paperwork when she was a child.

“I’m ok,” Omar posted on X after the raid. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

Omar also said the search was “just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation”.

The president has consistently launched racist attacks against Omar and other Somali Americans in Minnesota.

In December, he described them as “garbage” who “come from hell, and they complain, and do nothing but bitch”.

He said Omar “should be thrown the hell out of our country”.

After Monday’s search, Trump denied being involved in the investigation.

“I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

text:
Laramie County District Court Judge Robin Cooley is deciding whether to hold Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak in contempt of court on claims his office disobeyed the judge’s earlier order to produce documents pertaining to the case of a Cheyenne man taken into Immigration Customs and Enforcement custody after a traffic stop.

Cooley will issue a written decision “as quickly as possible,” she said during a hearing Friday morning in Cheyenne.

Cooley heard arguments both for and against holding Kozak in civil contempt.

Drake Hill urged the court to issue the contempt finding.

Hill said that in response to the plaintiffs’ requests for documents about the Mexican national Mario Fabian Valenzuela Robles, the sheriff’s office produced conflicting accounts of his April 23 encounter, didn’t produce any communications with ICE about it though ICE was involved, and handed over a messy tranche of documents containing unreadable computer code on Aug. 7, two days after the deadline Cooley set.

Hill alleged that his clients needed to obtain these documents for Valenzuela Robles in a timely fashion to fight the man’s federal and immigration court cases, but the sheriff’s office has a pattern of not producing necessary documents until Hill’s team takes court action against it.

“We have no communications – those communications with ICE are missing,” said Hill. “We’d like to know where those are. If there are none then certify that there are none. I can’t believe there are none, but we have none.”

Producing 7,700 documents

Hill represents Colorado-based firm Lichter Immigration, which represents Robles in a federal immigration case. Hill also represents Kevin Lewis, who is an investigator for Lichter and is Hill’s business partner.

Laramie County Attorney Mark Voss argued on Kozak’s behalf that what Hill calls unreadable computer code opened readably on the county’s devices. He conceded he was two days late producing documents, but said that’s because the search terms agreed upon produced 7,700 documents and he and others had to review those for privileged information, and he also combed through them for relevance.

Voss said he sympathizes with Valenzuela Robles’ plight and appreciates Hill’s concern over it.

The county attorney also conceded that an early attempt to hand over the case records “was disordered at best.”

But he emphasized that the Friday hearing was about whether Kozak’s office “willfully” disobeyed the court’s order – and he said it did not.

“Mr. Hill, who writes very well, basically spends a great deal of time (in his contempt motion) essentially engaging in derogatory comment about the sheriff, and very little time arguing about the law in regard to the Public Records Act,” added Voss.

Judge Grapples With ‘Additional Information’

Cooley’s decision is pending.

“I thought I had the pretty full picture walking into the proceeding this morning,” she said, “but with a little bit of additional information, the court is going to take this under advisement; and will issue a written decision as quickly as possible.”

Civil contempt cases tend to involve a judge ordering some ongoing penalty against a party until that party does what the court originally ordered.

Cooley didn’t specify what “additional information” gave her pause, but earlier in the hearing Hill produced a copy of the sheriff’s office’s 287g agreement with ICE, which Hill said specifies that the sheriff’s office should keep records and have a record-keeping policy.

Cooley had called that agreement “additional information.”

Background Now

Lichter Immigration and its investigator Lewis filed this lawsuit against Kozak and his office June 30.

The lawsuit complaint accuses Kozak’s office of wrongly withholding body camera video and information that Valenzuela Robles needed for his ongoing immigration case.

The sheriff’s office detained Valenzuela Robles on April 23 “as part of a wider effort directed by Defendant Kozak,” says the complaint.

An order in Valenzuela Robles’ federal wrongful-detention case says he was detained starting about April 23 through at least May 27, after a Cheyenne police officer initiated a traffic stop on him because his taillights were “kind of dark” and his truck had “tinted windows.”

ICE agents were on scene within the span of time Valenzuela Robles took to provide his ID to the officer, the order says, adding that Valenzuela Robles asserts he was given a choice between $2,600 to return to Mexico or face ICE detention. He opted for detention, the order says.

The order recounts assertions by Valenzuela Robles that he’s lived in the U.S. for 20 years and has no criminal history, plus has three children who are U.S. citizens.

Voss noted in court Friday that Valenzuela Robles is “not a criminal.”

Hill said Valenzuela Robles’ children were in Cooley’s courtroom Friday.

Hill filed the motion asking Cooley to hold Kozak in contempt Aug. 6, after a back-and-forth over how the county should search and provide documentation to Hill’s clients.

Hill alleged that Kozak’s office disobeyed Cooley’s order to turn over documents pertaining to Valenzuela Robles.

Kozak bristled at the filing and cast the case’s motivation as politically motivated, pointing Cowboy State Daily to Hill’s tangential connections to a gubernatorial candidate whom Kozak is investigating for alleged bribery.

Kozak said his office turned over the body camera video, which he indicated was initially withheld to ensure it could be released according to the narrow provisions allowed in public-records law.

In Court

In court Friday, Voss said body camera is difficult to vet for privileged information such as people giving their driver’s license numbers, Social Security numbers, or mental-health diagnoses. If a law enforcement encounter lasts 30 minutes but three deputies capture it via body cam, that’s an hour and a half through which records staff must scour to edit out confidential information. That duration expands if dash cameras also capture the encounter, he said.

Plus, Voss noted, Wyoming law applies much narrower grounds for releasing officers’ video than other documents.

Voss cast the records search and demands as an information technology (IT) nightmare, repeatedly conceding to Cooley that these efforts were messy. He said the sheriff's office is inundated with records requests, and the sheriff may have to request a budget boost to get more staffers to field them.

Voss said he should thank Hill for prompting the formation of a new records policy at the sheriff’s office, as this case marked the "first meaningful request for records regarding ICE detention that we had received."

The sheriff’s office sent Cowboy State Daily its new records policy in a Friday email.

Hill, conversely, read dubious behavior into the sheriff’s office’s responses.

“I believe these delays do mean that they are not honoring the court’s order and that it’s intentional,” said Hill. “You cannot know about a court deadline and not meet that deadline without intentionality.”

He noted that the earliest released report about Valenzuela Robles’ arrest was, in the words of one Cheyenne Police Department staffer, a “complete fabrication.”

Voss countered, saying one of the deputies had conflated the traffic stop with another later but similar one, but that was corrected.

Hill also said the body camera video his team ultimately obtained doesn’t match the deputy reports.

“I’m sure the defendants disagree,” said Hill.

He added that the deputy who made the stop said, “Well, I pulled you over for failure to use your turn signal, but I really couldn’t see it.”

Other aspects of the body camera are “very concerning,” said Hill.

ICE’s main report of the incident, according to Hill, claims Valenzuela Robles didn’t have a current registration or tags on his vehicle, nor current insurance.

“Well, the body camera video shows that he did. And they had it in their possession,” said Hill.

Hill asserted that deputies didn’t have probable cause for the initial stop.

Voss urged Cooley to rein Hill back to the hearing’s purpose, of a proposed contempt finding.

Cooley agreed.

“I find the background information is peripherally important,” said Cooley over Hill’s due process concerns for Valenzuela Robles.

“But the standard here really is whether there was a clear and effective order, the defendants knew of that order and they did not comply with that deadline – and that their failure to comply was willful or intentional,” said Cooley, listing the basis of the contempt hearing.

Privileged

Hill also took issue with Voss saying 40 emails were deleted, and contained privileged communications between his office and other county agencies, not the sheriff’s department.

Hill said descriptions of those should rather have been listed in a “privilege” list.

Cooley asked Voss about that.

Voss agreed he hadn’t provided the privilege log, saying “I guess maybe I misunderstood the instruction in the order.” But he emphasized that he explained to Hill why he withheld those emails, and said none of them were communications with the sheriff’s office.

text:
SANFORD, Maine —

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducted an enforcement operation Thursday in Sanford, after which, the Department of Homeland Security shared the following message with Maine's Total Coverage: "If you are here illegally, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you."

That appeared to be the case on Brook Street just after 9 a.m., as two ICE vehicles stopped Manucho Nseka, an immigrant from Angola who had his 1-year-old child in the backseat of his SUV.

"The baby was in a car seat in the backseat of the car, but the car seat wasn't properly installed," said Sanford Police Chief Eric Small.

Small was on the scene Thursday morning, as Sanford police officers responded because Nseka had backed into an ICE vehicle that approached his SUV from behind.

The toddler was taken to a local hospital as a precaution and was not injured, Small said.

Social workers and others assisting the family said the mother of the child was working and that Nseka took the 1-year-old with him to run an errand while two other children, ages 2 and 11, were left home alone. Police had said members of the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) responded to the home to ensure the children's safety and welfare.

"The children have returned home to their mother," Small said.

Small also addressed questions about the Maine law that states local authorities should not cooperate with ICE in regard to immigration issues. The police chief said his department uses common sense.

"We follow the state law. We don't participate in any searches for people, for immigration violations. We don't provide ICE with any non-public information," Small said.

Small said when it comes down to public safety, in this case, a crash with a child involved, Sanford police can and will respond, as well as cooperate.

"If something happens in Sanford that we become aware of, the officers are going to go there and make sure that our public, the people that live on the street, the people who live in the city, are safe," Small said.

Homeland Security said ICE initiated the targeted enforcement operation because Nseka failed to show up for a mandatory immigration proceeding. It is unclear where Nseka is being held.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security said Nseka will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the United States.

text:
LAS VEGAS (KTNV) — Las Vegas taxpayers are footing the bill for yet another payout stemming from the June 2025 ICE protest in downtown Las Vegas — this time, $20,000 to settle a claim against a city corrections officer accused of using religion to threaten and intimidate people held in jail.

Our previous reporting detailed Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department payouts to protesters totaling nearly half a million dollars. But this settlement involves the City of Las Vegas directly, not Metro police. It centers on City Corrections Officer Bernabe Ibarra, who is accused of preaching a six-minute religious sermon to detainees — even after at least one tried to opt out.

Watch the Channel 13 investigation:

Las Vegas pays $20,000 after officer preached to ICE protest detainees

Kathleen Cavalaro attended the protest that night carrying a sign that read "Love Thy Neighbor As Thyself." Body camera video shows how the sign became a shield against pepper balls — 48 of them, according to court records — fired by SWAT Officer Mark Eshe and then-Deputy Chief Bryan Peterson. Court records also say Peterson shot her in the back as she was following orders and walking away.

As officers moved to arrest her, Cavalaro can be heard on body camera video asking:

"You're shooting me? What am I under arrest for? Because I called you a fascist?"

She was zip-tied and arrested, then taken to the Las Vegas City Jail.

Federal lawsuit filed

Cavalaro later filed a federal lawsuit against LVMPD, the City of Las Vegas, Peterson, Eshe and Officer Joel Tomlinson. The suit accuses Tomlinson of falsifying the declaration of arrest by backdating the time and moving the location into the dispersal zone to "manufacture" probable cause for a "failure to disperse" arrest.

The city declined to prosecute. Her lawsuit says Tomlinson filed a second declaration that still contained false or misleading information, omitted Peterson's role, and conflicted with body camera video. No charges were filed after that, either.

Cavalaro cannot discuss that portion of her federal case because it remains pending. But she can speak to the part that was settled in her favor on Oct. 7.

13 Investigates

Metro police rewrite protest policy after anti-ICE demonstration lawsuits

Darcy Spears

Overcrowded cells and an unexpected sermon

"There were approximately 100 of us that were put in holding cells in rooms that were over capacity," Cavalaro said. "And they held us pretty close to the 24 hours that they could."

Despite a Las Vegas Municipal Court order requiring protesters to be released on their own recognizance, her lawsuit says the city kept her in custody at least nine more hours. Jail security video she obtained through her lawsuit shows what happened after she was finally moved from her cell.

"They released about 20 of us together, and they brought us down and sat us at the tables," Cavalaro said. "And that's when the correctional officer came in and started preaching a sermon to us, and brought in a jail chaplain and two church volunteers."

Her lawsuit accuses Ibarra of delivering the six-minute sermon even after she tried to opt out.

"I thought I made it pretty clear that I was uncomfortable and did not want to participate, but it happened anyway," Cavalaro said.

The jail footage has no audio, but it does show Ibarra delivering the sermon.

"It was very strange religious language to me, because it was a lot of, like, 'I rebuke you in the name of Jesus,'" Cavalaro said. "But the general message was that we had misbehaved, and Jesus would be disappointed in us, and that there is nothing we could do to change the system, that we should all go home and we should pray instead."

Implying the language of prayer is OK, but the language of protest is not.

"And that we were on a pathway of spending the rest of our life in prison if we continued to go to protests," Cavalaro said.

13 Investigates

Videographer arrested at Las Vegas ICE protest prepares to sue Metro

Darcy Spears

ACLU warns of First Amendment fallout

Nevada ACLU executive director Athar Haseebullah warned that protests are likely to increase, and that aggressive law enforcement responses risk putting agencies in unnecessary legal jeopardy.

"In some of these protests, local law enforcement is not the target of the protest, so by sort of responding in an incredibly aggressive way — in a harmful way — in a way that violates the First Amendment and violates civil liberties and civil rights more broadly," Haseebullah said, "they will unnecessarily make themselves a part of the story."

And part of Kathleen's federal lawsuit.

Watch the body camera footage obtained by Channel 13 in January as federal lawsuits challenge police tactics against protesters:

Federal lawsuits challenge Las Vegas police tactics against protesters

'Using Jesus as a weapon'

"I think that using Jesus as a weapon against people in custody is harmful," Cavalaro said. "Because if you're a Christian, it's taking something that is sacred and turning it into a tool of intimidation. And if you are not a religious person, it's imposing a religious message onto people who, at that moment, are under complete government control."

After accusing the city and Ibarra of weaponizing religion against detainees, Cavalaro received an offer of judgment. The city called it "not an admission of liability," but "an offer of compromise."

The payout was $20,000 of taxpayer money.

"It's just time for people to actually open up their eyes and see that there are no consequences, and it's costing them money," Cavalaro said. "So, whatever side you're on: if you believe police should be able to act however they want with no consequences, I think everyone agrees that at some point we should stop paying for this behavior."

The city has no policy addressing religious sermons delivered by corrections officers to inmates. An on-camera interview with city officials was requested, but the city declined and would not make Ibarra available. He remains employed as a city corrections officer.

title: Federal Judge Throws Out Trump's Bid to Overturn NYC Sanctuary Laws | Law Commentary
description:
A federal judge has thrown out the Trump administration's lawsuit against New York City's sanctuary laws, rejecting its attempt to force local authorities to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement.
The decision leaves New York City in control of how its police officers, jail officials and other municipal employees assist federal immigration authorities.
Reyes found that state restrictions already prevent local authorities from detaining individuals solely at the request of federal immigration officials.
Federal immigration officers can continue conducting operations within the city, while local authorities generally retain discretion over whether to participate.
A federal judge in Rochester dismissed another Justice Department challenge in September 2026, rejecting the government's arguments that the city's sanctuary policies were overridden by federal law or unlawfully discriminated against federal authorities.
text:
A federal judge has thrown out the Trump administration's lawsuit against New York City's sanctuary laws, rejecting its attempt to force local authorities to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. The October 15, 2026, ruling preserves city restrictions on assisting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

U.S. District Judge Ramón E. Reyes Jr. of the Eastern District of New York found that the Justice Department lacked standing to challenge the city's policies and rejected its argument that federal immigration law overrides local restrictions. The decision leaves New York City in control of how its police officers, jail officials and other municipal employees assist federal immigration authorities.

New York state law proved to be a central obstacle to the administration's case. Reyes found that state restrictions already prevent local authorities from detaining individuals solely at the request of federal immigration officials. Striking down the city's provisions would leave those independent protections intact, depriving the Justice Department of the legal standing needed to pursue that challenge.

The administration filed its lawsuit on July 24, 2025, seeking to invalidate municipal policies that prosecutors argued obstructed immigration enforcement and violated the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, which gives valid federal law precedence over conflicting state and local laws.

At issue were restrictions governing when city agencies can honor immigration detainers, share custody information or dedicate public resources to federal deportation operations. Immigration detainers are requests from ICE asking local authorities to hold individuals temporarily so federal officers can assume custody.

Federal prosecutors argued that New York City's policies interfered with immigration operations by limiting access to people in local custody and forcing ICE agents to conduct arrests after their release. The Justice Department maintained that federal law superseded the municipal restrictions and sought to have them struck down.

Reyes rejected the government's challenge to city rules limiting the disclosure of release dates, whereabouts and other detention information. The federal statutes cited by prosecutors address the exchange of citizenship and immigration-status information, rather than requiring local authorities to provide the broader custody details sought by ICE.

The judge also invoked the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine, which generally prohibits the federal government from forcing state and local officials to administer federal programs or carry out federal enforcement duties.

Under that principle, New York City retains authority over how it uses municipal personnel and resources. Federal immigration officers can continue conducting operations within the city, while local authorities generally retain discretion over whether to participate.

Together, the standing and constitutional findings defeated the Justice Department's attempt to dismantle the challenged sanctuary provisions, preserving the city's existing limits on cooperation with ICE.

The dismissal follows similar legal defeats for the Trump administration in cases involving Boston and Rochester, New York, where federal judges also rejected challenges to local immigration policies.

In May 2026, U.S. District Judge Leo T. Sorokin dismissed the administration's lawsuit against Boston's Trust Act, finding that Massachusetts law independently restricted the police cooperation federal prosecutors sought to compel.

A federal judge in Rochester dismissed another Justice Department challenge in September 2026, rejecting the government's arguments that the city's sanctuary policies were overridden by federal law or unlawfully discriminated against federal authorities. Unlike the standing issue in New York City, that decision addressed the merits of the administration's claims.

The rulings form part of a broader dispute over how far Washington can go in requiring state and local governments to assist with immigration enforcement. Although the decisions concern different municipal laws, they underscore the constitutional limits courts have applied to federal efforts to compel local cooperation.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani welcomed the dismissal, calling it a victory for New Yorkers and defending the city's authority to determine how municipal employees and resources are used.

description:
Thousands of demonstrators are expected to gather in downtown Los Angeles Saturday for a “No Kings” rally and march protesting President Donald Trump’s administration, federal immigration enforcement policies and what organizers describe as threats to voting rights ahead of the November midterm elections.
Organizers said the Los Angeles event will focus on opposition to federal immigration enforcement actions, concerns about potential election interference and efforts to encourage eligible voters to participate in the upcoming midterm elections.
