title: The Hidden Immigration Risks of Automatic Voter Registration | Dickinson Wright - JDSupra
description:
Why This Matters Under U.S. immigration law, falsely claiming U.S. citizenship or voting unlawfully carries severe consequences.
USCIS closely examines voter registration and voting activity when adjudicating applications for adjustment of status, naturalization, and other immigration benefits.
How Automatic Voter Registration Works Under the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), many states offer voter registration through motor vehicle agencies, and a growing number now use automatic voter registration (AVR) during driver’s license or identification card transactions.
If You Receive a Voter Registration Card Do not ignore it — but speak with an immigration attorney before taking any action.
If You Have an Immigration Case Pending Inform your immigration attorney immediately if: You have received a voter registration card; You believe you may have been registered to vote; You have answered questions about voter registration during a DMV transaction; or USCIS asks about your voting or voter registration history.
text:
Many foreign nationals are surprised to learn that a routine visit to the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) or other motor vehicle agency can create serious immigration problems. Across the country, many states have integrated voter registration into driver’s license and identification card applications. In some cases, noncitizens have found themselves registered to vote without realizing it — and years later must explain that registration to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) during adjustment of status or naturalization. Employment- and family-based immigrants and their families should take this risk seriously.

Why This Matters

Under U.S. immigration law, falsely claiming U.S. citizenship or voting unlawfully carries severe consequences. USCIS closely examines voter registration and voting activity when adjudicating applications for adjustment of status, naturalization, and other immigration benefits. The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) makes a false claim to U.S. citizenship both a ground of inadmissibility (INA §212(a)(6)(C)(ii)) and a ground of deportability (INA §237(a)(3)(D)), and separately penalizes noncitizens who vote in violation of any federal, state, or local law (INA §§212(a)(10)(D), 237(a)(6)). Unlike many other grounds, a false claim to U.S. citizenship generally cannot be waived. A narrow statutory exception applies only to certain individuals each of whose natural or adoptive parents is or was a U.S. citizen, who permanently resided in the United States before age 16, and who reasonably believed at the time that they were a U.S. citizen. Voting by noncitizens in federal elections and falsely claiming citizenship to register or vote, are also federal crimes (18 U.S.C. §§611, 1015(f)).

What makes these cases particularly troubling is that many people never intended to register to vote and never voted at all. Instead, the registration occurred during a driver’s license application or renewal, often through a state’s automatic voter registration system — and sometimes at the very agency to which the person had just disclosed their foreign citizenship.

How Automatic Voter Registration Works

Under the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), many states offer voter registration through motor vehicle agencies, and a growing number now use automatic voter registration (AVR) during driver’s license or identification card transactions. AVR generally registers eligible individuals unless they decline or are screened out — even though federal law requires applicants to attest to their citizenship and eligibility. Procedures vary, and weak safeguards can result in noncitizens being prompted to register or inadvertently registered. As of 2026, AVR has been adopted in approximately 24 states and the District of Columbia, including California, Colorado, Michigan, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Virginia, and Washington. Some states, including New Jersey, have considered reforms to keep applicants who present proof of non-citizenship from being prompted to register.

Why This Is Getting More Attention Now

Since 2025, the federal government has expanded the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program so that state election officials can check voter rolls against federal citizenship and immigration records — and, in some cases, Social Security data. That expanded use was challenged in court. In September 2026, after a federal district court had found the revamped system unlawful, the U.S. Supreme Court issued an emergency order allowing the program to be used while the litigation continues. Separately, because federal law limits systematic removals from the voter rolls in the 90 days before a federal election, large-scale roll actions are more likely after the November 2026 midterm elections. The practical effect is that voter registrations created years ago — including registrations a person never knew about — are more likely to be flagged and referred to immigration or law enforcement authorities, rather than surfacing only at a USCIS interview.

The Growing Immigration Consequences

Employment-based immigrants are particularly vulnerable because many will eventually apply for permanent residence or U.S. citizenship after years of living and working in the United States. Lawful permanent residents face the same risks, and more: many green card holders mistakenly assume they may vote, and a registration or vote discovered at the naturalization stage can lead not only to denial of the application but also to removal proceedings.

During these applications, USCIS often asks whether the applicant has ever:

Registered to vote in the United States;

Voted in any federal, state, or local election; or

Claimed to be a U.S. citizen.

If government records show a voter registration, USCIS may issue a Request for Evidence (RFE), Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID), or raise questions during an interview, even if the person never voted and never intended to register.

Under policy guidance that took effect in August 2025, USCIS treats a false claim to U.S. citizenship as a basis for inadmissibility regardless of intent, knowledge, or willfulness. Where USCIS finds a voter registration record, the analysis often turns on whether the person affirmatively indicated U.S. citizenship — for example, by attesting to citizenship on the registration form — so whether a particular form required that attestation could matter a great deal. USCIS has also stated that it will issue Notices to Appear (NTAs), which begin removal proceedings, against individuals found to have falsely claimed citizenship or voted unlawfully. This approach reflects the Board of Immigration Appeals’ holding that a specific intent to deceive is not required to find a false claim to U.S. citizenship (Matter of Zhang, 27 I&N Dec. 569 (BIA 2019)). While the analysis is highly fact-specific, responding to these issues can be costly, time-consuming, and stressful, often requiring extensive documentary evidence and legal argument.

How Inadvertent Registration May Occur

A typical sequence may unfold as follows:

A foreign national renews a driver’s license and completes electronic prompts without realizing that a voter registration option was presented.

The DMV processes the transaction, and its system generates a voter registration record.

The person later receives a voter registration card and assumes it was sent in error.

Years later, USCIS discovers the voter registration during adjustment of status or naturalization and requests an explanation.

In this situation, the person may never have voted, completed a stand-alone voter registration application, or believed that they were eligible to participate in U.S. elections.

What Noncitizens Should Do

If you are not a U.S. citizen, consider the following precautions when visiting the DMV:

Carefully read every screen (if online filing) and document before signing.

Do not assume the system will screen you out because you are not a citizen; read and answer every voter registration prompt yourself.

If asked about voter registration, clearly indicate that you are not a U.S. citizen and are not eligible to vote.

Never register or vote in any election — even a local election that permits noncitizen voting — without first consulting an immigration attorney.

Be equally careful with other forms that ask about citizenship, such as jury questionnaires, Form I-9, student financial aid applications, and job or benefit applications.

Keep copies of any driver’s license application records if possible.

If You Receive a Voter Registration Card

Do not ignore it — but speak with an immigration attorney before taking any action. Cancellation forms often ask why you are ineligible, and that statement may be shared with immigration or law enforcement authorities. Your attorney can help you contact the appropriate election office to determine whether you are actually registered, how the registration occurred, and what steps are available to cancel or remove it if you are not eligible. Keep written confirmation of any cancellation.

If You Have an Immigration Case Pending

Inform your immigration attorney immediately if:

You have received a voter registration card;

You believe you may have been registered to vote;

You have answered questions about voter registration during a DMV transaction; or

USCIS asks about your voting or voter registration history.

Early investigation is critical. In many situations, obtaining relevant records before a USCIS interview can make a substantial difference. Never deny or minimize a voter registration on a USCIS form or at an interview; a misrepresentation can create a separate and more serious problem.

What Employers Should Know

Employers that sponsor foreign national workers have a direct stake in this issue. An unexpected voter registration record can delay or derail a green card case the company has invested in for years and can disrupt workforce planning. Practical steps include:

Adding a brief voter registration warning to global mobility and onboarding materials, particularly when an employee relocates to a state with AVR;

Adding questions about voter registration and voting history to green card intake questionnaires so that issues surface early;

Making sure that any company “get out the vote” or civic engagement campaign clearly states that only U.S. citizens may register and vote; and

Reminding HR and managers not to advise employees on their registration status, but to refer those questions to immigration counsel.

Employers should also keep in mind that Section 1 of Form I-9 asks employees to attest to their citizenship status. An employee who incorrectly checks “A citizen of the United States” may have made a false claim to citizenship. Employers should encourage employees to complete Section 1 carefully and accurately, but must not tell employees which status to select or request specific documents.

Key Takeaway for Employment-Based Immigrants

For H-1B, L-1, TN, E-2, O-1, and other employment-based visa holders — as well as their spouses and children, and lawful permanent residents preparing to naturalize — voter registration issues are no longer rare. What seems like a routine driver’s license renewal can create immigration complications years later when applying for a green card or citizenship.

The safest approach is to review every DMV transaction carefully, never assume that a voter registration prompt does not apply to you, and address any questionable registration records as soon as they are discovered. A mistaken voter registration does not automatically mean a person intentionally claimed U.S. citizenship or voted unlawfully. But because USCIS may closely examine these issues, foreign nationals should take them seriously and seek legal guidance whenever questions arise. While every case is fact-specific, early investigation and proactive corrective action can often make a significant difference.

*This article reflects developments as of October 2026.

text:
A Biden-appointed judge dismissed former CIA Director John Brennan's lawsuit against President Donald Trump and senior administration officials, ruling that his concerns about the potential destruction of evidence needed for a future criminal defense were too "speculative."

The dismissal comes as Brennan faces two federal investigations, including a Justice Department probe into whether former intelligence officials conspired to violate Trump's civil rights through investigations into alleged ties between his 2016 presidential campaign and Russia.

A separate investigation is examining whether Brennan made false statements during 2023 congressional testimony about the Steele dossier's role in a 2017 intelligence assessment of Russian interference in the presidential election.

FORMER CIA DIRECTOR BRENNAN SUBPOENAED TO TESTIFY IN FEDERAL TRUMP CONSPIRACY CASE

Trump has repeatedly accused Brennan, President Barack Obama and other former intelligence officials of orchestrating the "Russia collusion hoax," but they have rejected those accusations, claiming that the administration is attempting to discredit legitimate intelligence findings about Russian interference in the 2016 election.

While Judge Jia Cobb called Brennan’s allegations that the Trump administration was targeting him for opposing the president "deeply concerning," she ruled that he lacked standing to sue because he had not shown that officials were likely destroying records relevant to a potential defense, and the injury he feared depended on a series of events that had not yet occurred.

"For Brennan’s constitutional injury to actually accrue, a series of dominoes must fall, and Defendants’ deletion of records is just one of those dominoes," Cobb wrote.

"There is no dispute about this: Defendants describe this domino chain in their motion to dismiss ... and Brennan accepts it in his response."

Brennan has been identified as a target in two federal investigations that have involved three grand jury inquiries — two in the Southern District of Florida and one in Washington, D.C. — but he has not been charged with a crime. The former CIA director was subpoenaed to testify before a federal grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida, Oct. 15, though his scheduled appearance was postponed.

Brennan filed his lawsuit naming Trump, FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and other officials July 1, 2026. The 46-page lawsuit accused the Justice Department of handling its investigation into Brennan with "unprecedented, irregular conduct" that was driven by the "president’s retribution agenda."

DELETED EMAIL DETAILS ALLEGED TRUMP-TARGETING PUSH INSIDE LETITIA JAMES’ OFFICE: ‘FIND AND PURSUE CRIMES’

Brennan argued that key evidence could disappear before he had a chance to challenge any future indictment. He pointed to deleted social media posts, the administration’s use of Signal and other messaging tools with auto-delete features, unpreserved texts and direct messages, AI queries, Microsoft Teams chats and alleged failures to preserve discovery in other cases, including the prosecution of Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J.

He said the loss of those records could make it harder to determine whether the investigations were based on legitimate law enforcement concerns or political retaliation.

"With this lawsuit, Director Brennan has served notice that the government’s conduct and its document preservation will be carefully scrutinized in the event of any future indictment," Brennan’s lawyers, Ken Wainstein and Dan Gelber, told the AP.

"Director Brennan will continue to vigorously defend himself against these baseless investigations, and he will challenge any attempt to use the criminal justice system for personal and political retribution."

The lawsuit also pointed to what it described as irregularities in the Justice Department’s handling of the investigation.

It cited the removal of longtime DOJ prosecutor Maria Medetis Long, who was reportedly taken off the Brennan investigation in April 2026 after expressing doubts about the strength of the case, as evidence of what it described as irregular conduct. She was replaced by Trump ally Joseph diGenova, who later resigned from his role overseeing the investigation amid reported internal disagreements over the handling of the case.

TRUMP SAYS HE WILL NOMINATE ACTING AG TODD BLANCHE TO PERMANENTLY LEAD JUSTICE DEPARTMENT

Brennan’s attorneys accused the Justice Department of "judge-shopping" by trying to steer grand jury proceedings toward Trump-appointed Judge Aileen Cannon in Fort Pierce, Florida, rather than allowing the case to proceed through the court's normal assignment process. They also questioned why prosecutors were pursuing the investigation in Florida when much of the allegations occurred in Washington, D.C.

The complaint also accused DOJ and FBI leaders of improperly discussing details of the investigations publicly, raising questions about whether officials disclosed information that should have remained confidential.

It cited Attorney General Todd Blanche’s statements that DOJ had issued "200 grand jury subpoenas" and was investigating a "pattern of behavior" to "destroy" Trump, as well as FBI Director Kash Patel’s public discussion of the investigations and their targets.

description:

text:
On Monday, federal agents searched the Washington home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar and confiscated her phone, her personal computers, her notebooks and passport. The search, conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), is the opening move in an effort by the Trump administration to strip a sitting member of Congress of her citizenship and deport her.

The immigration Gestapo has been deployed against an elected representative over paperwork filed when she was a child three weeks before an election in which she is all but certain to win a fifth term. The first Somali elected to Congress, Omar won her last two elections with 74 percent of the vote and her August primary with 81 percent.

The Trump administration is asserting the power to overturn the election and drive a political opponent out of Congress and out of the country. This is an attack on democratic rights that must be opposed by the entire working class.

To obtain a search warrant, prosecutors must persuade a judge that there is probable cause to believe a crime was committed and that evidence of it will be found. What is this supposed crime? Investigators working for Trump claim that Omar or her late father misstated her age by one year on the paperwork through which she became a citizen in 2000, when she was 17. Her father died in 2020. The same allegation was examined in 2019 and again under the Biden administration, and both reviews found insufficient evidence to proceed.

Denaturalization cases ordinarily proceed as civil lawsuits based on the government’s own records. Former immigration officials told Reuters that it is “extremely unusual for them to involve search warrants.” No raid was needed to read a 26-year-old immigration file. The administration is searching for a basis to impose the punishment Trump has repeatedly demanded, deportation.

On the evening of October 12, hours after the raid, Trump took the stage at a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio and delivered a fascist diatribe against Omar. “She’s a disaster,” he said. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military. All they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’” The crowd answered with chants of “deport.”

On the same day his administration raided her home, the president mocked the idea that a Somali-born member of Congress had constitutional rights at all.

Omar is a member of the Democratic Party, and the Socialist Equality Party has fundamental political differences with her politics. But she is being targeted for definite political reasons.

Omar came to the United States as a child refugee from the civil war in Somalia and has represented Minneapolis in Congress since 2019. She was an original member of the “Squad” of four “progressive” Democratic women first elected to Congress in 2018, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ayanna Pressely and Rashida Tlaib.

Omar and Tlaib are in the crosshairs of the Trump administration due to their characterization of Israel’s war on Gaza as a genocide. Omar has also called Trump’s war against Iran an “unlawful operation” that “must end immediately.” In January, at a town hall in her district, she declared, “We must abolish ICE for good.”

The persecution of Omar is also bound up with a fascistic and racist campaign against Somali immigrants. At a cabinet meeting last December, Trump called Somali immigrants “garbage,” and said, “Their country stinks.” That month, ICE launched Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis, which spread across Minnesota and produced more than 3,000 ICE abductions, along with the murders of US citizens Renée Good and Alex Pretti.

The administration has ended Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Somalis and opened a review of naturalization cases from Somalia and 18 other countries for possible denaturalization. On October 8, four days before the raid on Omar’s home, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Minnesota “is being taken over by Somali Immigrants,” and urged, “Fight back Minnesota, fight back!”

The fusion of anti-immigrant agitation with the persecution of left-wing opposition has a long history in the United States. Between 1917 and 1921, as the United States entered the First World War and the ruling class reacted with fear to the Russian Revolution, the American state waged a war against democratic rights at home.

Victor Berger, the Socialist Party congressman from Milwaukee and himself an immigrant, was convicted under the Espionage Act for opposing the war. On November 10, 1919, the House voted 311 to 1 to bar him from his seat. His constituents elected him again, and on January 10, 1920, the House excluded him again, 330 to 6.

The anarchist Emma Goldman’s citizenship derived from her marriage to Jacob Kershner, and in 1908 the government revoked his naturalization. When it moved to deport her in 1919, officials ruled that the revocation of her husband’s citizenship had annulled hers as well. On December 21, 1919, Goldman and 248 others were put aboard the Buford, the “Soviet Ark,” and deported to Russia. J. Edgar Hoover, then 24, was on board to see them off.

This was part of a broader assault on all political opposition. Opponents of the war were jailed under the Espionage Act, socialist newspapers were barred from the mails, and the Immigration Act of 1918 authorized the deportation of immigrant anarchists, socialists and labor organizers. Joe Hill, singer, song writer and labor activist, was executed at the Sugar House Prison in Utah in 1915 after being framed for murder. Frank Little, like Hill a member of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), was brutally lynched by Pinkertons in Butte, Montana in 1917.

The lesson of that period is that the attack on immigrants and the attack on left-wing politics form a single operation. Opposition to war and exploitation is branded the work of foreigners, and foreign birth is made grounds for silencing it.

In the current situation, the stakes extend far beyond one Democratic Party congresswoman. Some 26 million naturalized citizens live in the United States, according to the Congressional Research Service. The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse counted at least 105 civil denaturalization suits in the first seven months of 2026, including 50 in July alone. In the entire period from 2008 through 2025, it counted 125.

The attack on Omar is also part of a conspiracy against the elections themselves. On October 15, the Justice Department sued California to block the counting of mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it claims are likely noncitizens. A similar claim of nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada’s rolls collapsed when the state’s review did not establish a single one.

The aim is not to purge the rolls of a handful of ineligible voters. The administration is laying the basis for declaring the results of the November 3 election fraudulent, for throwing out ballots in states it does not control, and for treating any outcome it rejects as the product of “alien” voting.

The response of the Democratic Party establishment is virtual silence. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) Democrat and fellow “Squad” member Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez does not have so much as a press release on her congressional web site denouncing the fascistic campaign against Omar. While Ocasio-Cortez’s Instagram is filled with daily updates on the congresswoman's’ efforts to freeze her eggs, there is nothing about ICE and the Trump administration’s attempt to denaturalize and deport her colleague.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, an ardent supporter of the genocide in Gaza, has said nothing during the more than five days since Omar’s home was raided.

The Democrats’ sharpest attacks on Trump are reserved for his policy toward Russia, not for his assault on democratic rights. What they fear is not dictatorship, but a movement of the working class they cannot control. A party that answers the persecution of one of its own office-holders with nothing more than a mildly worded press release will not defend the rights of workers.

Trump is the personification of a financial oligarchy that confronts a deepening economic and geo-political crisis. It is waging an escalating global war and faces growing resistance from the working class at home. The unprecedented concentration of wealth in the hands of a small group of billionaires is incompatible with democratic forms of rule, and the ruling class is turning to dictatorship. As was the case a century ago, the scapegoating of immigrants serves to divide the working class and prepare repression against every form of opposition.

The defense of the democratic rights is a class question. Native-born and immigrant workers must unite in rank-and-file committees in every workplace and neighborhood to oppose the raids, deportations and denaturalizations. This fight must be connected to the struggle against war, the capitalist oligarchy and the system that give rise to them.

text:
A new lawsuit filed by an Arizona legal-aid group alleges the Trump administration is fast-tracking deportations for immigrant children alone in the U.S.

In July, the Trump administration ended its contract with legal-aid groups part of a federally-funded program to ensure unaccompanied children have access to legal counsel. The program was enacted almost two decades ago by Congress in the wake and underpinned by federal anti-trafficking laws.

More than 20,000 children could now face court alone, unless their lawyers stay on pro-bono.

In the lawsuit, Arizona’s Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project and other plaintiffs say the government is sending children into speedy asylum proceedings — sometimes within 24 hours — leaving no time to prepare, even with attorneys. They also say requests from attorneys to reschedule proceedings in order to gather more evidence are being routinely denied.

Another policy, they say, pushes immigration judges to close cases for children in custody by January. The process normally takes years.

In legal filings, the group says the U.S. immigration system is built for adults, "with one caveat."

"When a child under the age of 18 presents at the United States border without a parent or legal guardian and without lawful immigration status, a cluster of federal laws ensure the child — deemed an unaccompanied child, 6 U.S.C. § 279(g)(2) — is treated differently than an adult," the complaint reads.

The groups argue the new practices violate due process and the Administrative Procedures Act. They're asking the judge to intervene.

More Immigration News

Activists started occupying the cottonwood tree at the end of July, hoping to save it after the other three were felled. They hoisted a wooden platform high into its branches, and camped on private land right next to it.

Arizona has for a long time been one of the leading states for refugee resettlement, but now with the numbers cut so low, refugees in our state and the resettlement agencies that are built up to help them adjust are feeling the impact.

The standoff began Oct. 5, when Border Patrol agents swarmed a protest camp situated in and around a cottonwood tree slated for removal to make way for two steel border walls — the last of a border-hugging grove on the U.S. side that was estimated to be as much as 250 years old.

His comments come after the Arizona Sheriff’s Association accused his office of refusing requests for assistance from Border Patrol.

The Arizona Sheriff’s Association issued an open letter calling out the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office over its response to the public safety concerns surrounding the border wall construction in that area.

text:
Addressing the man in handcuffs, a woman speaking in the video calls out in Spanish to offer help as three masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents lead the man into an unmarked SUV at Gates Avenue and Union Street in Montclair Tuesday evening.

It was one among a spate of recent ICE detentions that have prompted community members to connect on encrypted chats and respond in coordination to help detainees and their families, residents and officials said in interviews with Montclair Local.

Among the local responders at the scene Tuesday was Michelle Ashley, a Montclair resident who said she had attended a training at Unitarian Universalist Congregation of Montclair earlier in the year during which she learned how to help when ICE comes. She pivoted from walking her dog to the scene.

Community Responder

“I went to that corner and they were all gone. I just stood there and waited to see if someone would come and they did come and they knew the person who had been taken,” Ashley, 45, said. “And other responders were able to connect as well, exchange information and give him information to give to the wife.”

The detained man, she said, is the father of two children.

His arrest followed the ICE detentions of five men who agents arrested from a pickup truck in the same neighborhood on Bloomfield Avenue last month, something Ashley said she had witnessed while on her way to work and reported to the Deportation & Immigration Response Equipo. DIRE is a New Jersey nonprofit that supports undocumented individuals and their families facing immigration and detention crises.

Ashley’s one action — calling the hotline — was the key to getting local “rapid responders” to connect families with legal aid and other key supports, Jill Beckman-Gaynes, co-lead of the Immigration Action Team at Unitarian Universalist, said in an interview.

‘Number one thing that people can do’

“The number one thing that people can do to help is to put the rapid response phone number in their contacts on their phone — the DIRE phone number,” which is 888-347-3767 (888-DIRE-SOS). “If they could just take out their phones, the minute that they’re reading this, and add it as a contact, that would be the most helpful, given that these abductions, unfortunately, seem to be ramping up in Montclair. You just never know when you’re going to be the person who sees the ICE activity.”

Mayor Dr. Renee Baskerville confirmed Friday that ICE detained people in the township Tuesday, Thursday and Friday, as well as in previous weeks.

“The sight of aggressive, masked agents taking people away from their jobs, daily activities, and families, and removing them from town, has created fear, uncertainty, and distress among many residents, their families and friends,” Baskerville said in a statement. “We cannot ignore the lasting human consequences of these actions.”

She said Montclair is paying attention, “even though there are some things we cannot discuss publicly in detail.”

“This is not because we are standing still or turning away from the chilling and inhibitory impact of the reported ICE incidents, but rather because some of this work must remain confidential to protect the people involved and preserve our ability to respond effectively,” Baskerville said. “Please do not mistake our discretion as inaction.”

ICE Won’t Confirm

The mayor’s statements come amid limited information from the federal authorities conducting the detentions. A spokesperson for ICE did not confirm reports on social media of detentions in Montclair, West Orange and Orange this week. The spokesperson, Christine Cuttita, requested a reporter provide the names of the detainees for her to track down their information. Cuttita did not answer questions seeking to know how many people were detained, where they were being held and how federal agents identified them for detention.

Ellen Whitt, the hotline coordinator for Deportation & Immigration Response Equipo, which supports people and their families facing immigration detention, described a significant rise in ICE sightings and encounters, including calls from the families and friends of people ICE picked up in several Essex County towns this week.

“A father and son were arrested by ICE in West Orange while walking down the road to work,” Whitt told Montclair Local. “People walking on the way to work are typically random arrests. Another was from Orange who originally arrived in the U.S. as a child with his parents and now has a small U.S. citizen child and pregnant wife.”

A person detained in Orange was on their way to work, she said.

“Many in general lately are people who have lived here for a long time with no prior contact with immigration and ICE doesn’t seem to know who they are when they stop them,” Whitt said. “That indicates that it was random because ICE doesn’t know who they are stopping. They especially target people who appear to be in vehicles related to construction and just people in a neighborhood where many immigrants are living or working.”

Taking Note

Whitt said DIRE encourages people reporting to their hotline to get license plate numbers so they can determine if they are other government vehicles that may have no relationship to ICE. This way, she said, they can let people know the arrest was not an ICE detention. DIRE also tries to help communities know if a vehicle has been left on the road due to an ICE arrest so that families can pick them up, she said.

“It would be great if more people could organize more rapid response teams in the Oranges,” Whitt added. “This is a volunteer operation dependent on local community members who organize themselves.”

Baskerville highlighted the coordinated community response.

“The team is trained in how to respond and help to identify where individuals are taken, connect affected families with appropriate legal assistance and ensure that potential violations of the law are brought to the attention of the appropriate authorities,” she said.

‘The Community is Watching’

Among residents organizing in Montclair is Greg Pason. Along with other organizers, he leads regular community walks supplementing the work of the teams that respond to document ICE detentions and assist families.

“We just want to get our neighbors aware of what’s going on in the community to talk to people as we’re walking through the street, to see if there are any random SUVs that are parked in public lots or where we think they’re staging,” Pason said in an interview. “It’s a way for the community to meet other people and raise awareness of ICE activity, especially now in Montclair.”

The walks typically begin between 7 and 9 a.m. in the morning, he said. They’ve been focusing on Pine Street, the area of Lackawanna Plaza and Walnut Street — the area of recent ICE arrests, Pason said.

“We take a look at the surroundings to see if anything is changing or if there are people who may be undocumented and they gather at a certain place, just to make them aware that the community is watching out for them,” he said. “We hope that this strengthens the community so we’re not just constantly reacting to news about ICE kidnaps randomly.”

Several houses of worship, he said, have formed the Montclair Emergent Coalition, a broader project working in coordination with AAPI New Jersey and other organizations in town working in immigrant advocacy.

The walking group on Friday announced an email at which volunteers can reach the group. It is Walkinggroupsmontclair@gmail.com.

Surveilling ICE

Joe Fortunato, a Montclair attorney, has offered his services to help secure the release of people detained by ICE. Of the five men detained in Montclair last month, Fortunato said, he has secured the release of two and is working on the other cases. He described his role in the context of other residents supporting immigrants.

“That’s really the story — the organization of Montclair people walking and driving to try to surveille ICE,” Fortunato said. “It’s really nothing short of amazing. I’ve been an activist for a long time. Montclair residents are motivated to protect their neighbors.”

“We think that they’re valued members of our community whether documented or not,” Fortunato added. “I’m Italian American, and I don’t forget that my grandparents came over here as immigrants under difficult conditions. We should be trying to support the people who are coming here to our township for a better life.”

Food Service Workers

Many of the people detained have been food service workers, including two kitchen staff from the restaurant Raymond’s who ICE detained in August.

Karen Schloss Diaz, the owner of a food and hospitality public relations firm that represents many Montclair restaurants, is among a group of industry insiders who have been notifying each other about ICE activity in private chats.

“I am thinking that it’s time for those of us who are white and older and ‘safe’ to consider driving restaurant kitchen staffs’ home at night,” Schloss Diaz said. “Let’s say I volunteer to do Thursday nights at, say, Faubourg. I can drive three kitchen guys home safely in my car.”

She said she emailed her local elected officials seeking action.

Deputy Mayor Susan Shin Andersen said township police should not be cooperating with ICE.

“We put that into policy,” Shin Andersen said in an interview. “What else can the town do? From my perspective what the town can do is make sure it is providing information on rights and resources as well as how to report incidents.”

The township, she said, cannot stop ICE detentions, which is why it is important for people to know what their rights are. Although it is not under the auspices of the township, Shin Andersen said she is working with the New Jersey Alliance for Immigrant Justice to bring a “Know Your Rights” training to the township. It follows an immigration issues panel the Montclair Civil Rights Commission held in April.

Politics

However, not everyone in Montclair feels the same way about immigrants and ICE enforcement.

“Limousine liberals in Montclair are not ‘neighbors’ of immigrant workers,” Michael D. Byrne, chairman of the Montclair Republican County Committee, said in an emailed statement.

“The best thing Montclair residents can do is demand that our virtue-signaling town council end its illegal Trust Act and direct Montclair Police to help facilitate orderly ICE operations so that citizens, bystanders, officers and detainees are safe throughout the process,” Byrne said.

In contrast, the township’s mayor spoke directly to the immigrant community. No government agency is above the law, and no person’s rights should be disregarded, Baskerville said.

“To our immigrant residents, families and visitors, I know that many of you are frightened and worried about going to work, to school, and carrying out ordinary daily activities,” she said. “No family should be insecure or abandoned by our township. We are working with people who are committed to helping and we will continue to do everything within our authority to support each and every member of our community.”

text:
Yesterday, in United States v. City of New York, yet another federal court ruled against the Trump administration in a sanctuary city case. "Sanctuary" jurisdictions are state and local governments that restrict their law enforcement agencies and other employees from assisting federal immigration enforcement and deportation efforts in various ways. In this case, Judge Reyes of the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York upheld New York City laws restricting local law enforcement information-sharing and other assistance to federal immigration enforcers.

The court ruled that federal law does not preempt these policies, and that if if it did, there would be a violation of the anti-commandeering requirements of the Tenth Amendment:

Even were the Court to find that the United States has standing and the challenged provisions are preempted—both answered in the negative above—United States' claims would still fail because the anticommandeering doctrine of the Tenth Amendment to the Constitution of the United States precludes relief.

"The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." U.S. Const. amend. X….

The United States argues it is "not seeking to compel participation in immigration enforcement … but rather to remove Defendants' express and implicit obstacles to the Executive's duty to carry out its immigration enforcement duties…." New York City replies "if accepted, [the United States' claims] would require the City to affirmatively assist the federal government in enforcing immigration laws in violation of the Tenth Amendment's anticommandeering doctrine…." New York City is correct, at least partially.

The United States seeks injunctive and declaratory relief to preempt the challenged provisions… If the challenged provisions were struck, while New York City would not be obligated to carry out federal immigration enforcement, they would be barred from prohibiting their agencies and employees from engaging in federal immigration enforcement by expending personnel, property, and other resources to (1) detain individuals and (2) implement inter-agency information-sharing, including disclosing personally identifiable information, all potentially in violation of state law. And of course, there is nothing within federal law that obligates states to participate in federal immigration enforcement or compels states to comply therewith.

The United States' preemption arguments amount to nothing more than a backdoor around the Tenth Amendment and rest on a false distinction between (a) compelling local governments' participation in federal immigration enforcement and (b) prohibiting local governments from dictating how their personnel and other resources may be utilized towards federal immigration enforcement….. "

The basic principle—that Congress cannot issue direct orders to state legislatures—applies" to commands for "affirmative action" and the imposition of "prohibitions." Murphy [v. NCAA], 584 U.S. at 455 (citation modified). If states cannot remain free to control their agencies and employees to resist federal immigration enforcement, which is within states' constitutional prerogatives, the Tenth Amendment anticommandeering doctrine means nothing.

This reasoning is correct. And it is notable that this ruling - like many others protecting sanctuary cities - relies heavily on the Supreme Court's 2018 anti-commandeering decision in Murphy v. NCAA, written by Justice Samuel Alito (probably the Court's most conservative justice), and joined by all the other conservatives then on the Court. In that case, the Court emphasized that the anti-commandeering doctrine bars Congress from dictating the actions of state and local legislatures, regardless of whether the dictation takes the form of an affirmative mandate, or a prohibition against legalizing or barring something under state law.

Judge Reyes also rejects the administration's argument under the "intergovernmental immunity" doctrine, which bars states and localities from directly regulating federal agencies or "discriminating" against them. Like the court in the recent case of United States v. New Jersey, he correctly emphasizes that there can be no discrimination when there is no other comparable activity that gets more favorable treatment under the sanctuary jurisdiction's policies:

"Differential treatment is critical to a discrimination-based intergovernmental immunity claim." New York, 814 F. Supp. 3d at 282….; "[A] comparator is necessary." New York, 810 F. Supp. 3d at 353. The United States discrimination claim fails for lack of a comparator.

The United States does not and cannot identify a similarly situated entity. State and local agencies and their officers do not enforce immigration law, nor do members of the public… As the United States concedes, the Federal Government holds the "exclusive charge of enforcing immigration law…." Not only are other federal law enforcement agencies with different charges differently situated, "[f]or a state law to unconstitutionally discriminate against the federal government, it must treat comparable classes of federal and non-federal employees differently, not different classes of federal employees." Illinois, 796 F. Supp. 3d at 534

I would add that, as I explained in a recent post, the entire antidiscrimination element of the intergovernmental immunity doctrine is dubious, and should probably be overturned by the Supreme Court:

[T]he whole doctrine of intergovernmental immunity strikes me as bogus, judge-made law. There is no provision in the Constitution requiring it. And the federal government is not some historically oppressed minority group protected by the antidiscrimination provisions Fourteenth Amendment. Where state and local governments are otherwise free to refuse to help the feds, that autonomy should not be forfeited merely because they choose to support potentially similar activities by state or local governments, or by the private sector. Obviously, a district court cannot refuse to obey Supreme Court precedent in this field. But I hope the Supreme Court might someday reevaluate that precedent.

This is just the most recent of a long line of defeats for Trump in sanctuary city cases, in both his first and second administration. Judge Reyes cites close to a dozen such cases over the last year alone. I summarized this jurisprudence more fully in a post covering three other recent sanctuary cases, last month:

In cases where the administration has tried to directly coerce states and localities into cooperating, courts have rightly ruled this violates the Supreme Court's "anti-commandeering" precedents, a series of decisions reached primarily by conservative justices, which hold that the federal government may not force state and local governments to help enforce federal law or carry out under federal purposes. In cases where Trump has sought to withhold federal funds from sanctuary jurisdictions, courts have (also rightly) ruled that the executive cannot impose conditions on federal grants that were not authorized by Congress and (in some cases) that the Trump conditions are unconstitutionally coercive. For my analyses of Trump II court decisions on these issues, see here, here, and here.

My 2019 Texas Law Review article surveying and assessing litigation arising from Trump's first-term attacks on sanctuary jurisdictions. There and in other writings, I also explain why immigration sanctuaries (and conservative gun sanctuaries) are beneficial, and help protect our constitutional system. See also my February 2026 Dispatch article, "In Defense of Sanctuary Cities," which provides an overview of these issues, and defends sanctuary jurisdictions on both constitutional and policy grounds.

Yesterday's ruling may be appealed. But if so, it is unlikely to be overturned.

Trump has posted a few rare wins in sanctuary cases with unusual facts, such as in the Contracts Clause case I analyzed in the September post. But, such cases are highly exceptional. And, as explained in the September post, the Contracts Clause decision has various flaws, and would not greatly impede sanctuary jurisdictions even if it survives on appeal.

Overall, Trump has been losing these kinds of cases so much that he might even get tired of losing.

text:
The Trump administration informed Congress in September that it will once again reserve its refugee admissions “primarily” for white South Africans and set a limit of just 17,500 for fiscal year 2027. The determination extends White House refugee policy established last year that has all but closed the program to people fleeing war and persecution anywhere else.

The move provoked concern from Catholic leaders who advocate for more merciful treatment of refugees.

“This announcement comes as no surprise,” Mario Russell, the executive director of the Center for Migration Studies of New York, wrote, responding to an email from America. “The administration’s mass deportation of law-abiding, working migrant families and barring of refugees—with the exception of a few pre-selected thousand—are distorted and inhumane policies.”

“When today’s U.S. Refugee Admissions Program reflects an 80 percent decrease from the historical average across decades of both Republican and Democratic presidential administrations alike, we should ask ourselves whether the current approach is truly living up to our history and values,” David Spicer, the director of policy and engagement for migration at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, wrote in an email to America.

The U.S. Refugee Admissions program historically has accepted about 80,000 refugees each year, allowing admissions from around the world, often from nations stricken by humanitarian crises or conflict. The president annually sets a threshold for total refugee admissions.

During his first administration, President Donald Trump dramatically reduced the refugee threshold to just 15,000, and in the first days of his second administration he effectively shut the refugee resettlement system altogether. In the fall of 2025, Mr. Trump set the refugee ceiling for fiscal year 2026 at 7,500—the lowest on record.

Admissions in FY 2026 were primarily reserved for Afrikaners, white South Africans who descended mainly from Dutch settlers. In May, invoking a law that allows a midyear change for emergencies, he raised the cap to 17,500.

Washington media reports that in a letter to Congress arguing for the prioritizing of white South African farmers, the State Department repeated administration claims that the group faced “the seizure of agricultural property without compensation; government policies designed to dismantle equal opportunity in employment, education, and business; and hateful rhetoric fueling disproportionate violence against racially disfavored minorities.”

Those charges and other allegations of “white genocide” in South Africa have been repeatedly challenged by the nation’s leaders.

The president has insisted on a course of “America First” in his domestic and international policymaking, but for Catholics, a focus on the homeland need not and cannot correspond with a neglect of all other people, Mr. Spicer said.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church states that “more prosperous nations are obliged, to the extent they are able, to welcome the foreigner in search of the security and the means of livelihood which he cannot find in his country of origin.”

“Our Catholic faith simply does not accept the false premise of choosing between two goods when it comes to doing what is right,” Mr. Spicer said. “Meanwhile, the demonstrated contributions to American communities of past refugees, economic and otherwise, show this is not merely one-sided charity.”

And “as the most prosperous and powerful country in the history of the world,” the United States must accept a role as a global paragon, Mr. Spicer added.

If its policies have the power to influence other nations, then the example set by the Trump administration on refugees is a dangerous one, Mr. Russell said.

The administration’s stance on immigration and refugee welcome comes “from a distorted perception of human experience,” he said. “They ignore facts, they dismiss history, and they are, sadly, indifferent to suffering and basic human dignity.”

Mr. Russell shared a hope “that in time the United States will be able to reaffirm its commitment to protection and the fair and compassionate treatment of migrants.”

“As the U.S. bishops have long said, we can continue to be a beacon of hope and defender of those who are persecuted, including our brothers and sisters in Christ, while also addressing the challenges faced by everyday Americans,” Mr. Spicer said. “The Refugee Admissions Program offers a lawful, secure and proven way to do that.”

text:
On a bright, breezy Saturday morning in late September, Eliott Rodriguez, a congressional candidate in Florida’s Twenty-seventh District, walked the streets of Little Havana with two of his campaign volunteers. They were in the throes of a debate over the best translation for “Sorry I missed you,” an essential phrase in the door-knocking lexicon, eventually settling on “Perdona que no nos vimos” (“I’m sorry we didn’t see each other”). Nearby, roosters scampered along the edge of Cuba Memorial Boulevard Park. Rodriguez, a trim, seventy-year-old Cuban American, is a Democrat and former local news anchor, which makes him a well-known figure in the area. Predictably, he has spent much of the lead-up to Election Day working to win over Latino voters in the majority-Hispanic district, which covers much of central Miami—a group that, in recent years, has moved to the right. In 2020, despite voting for Joe Biden, the district narrowly elected Republican María Elvira Salazar, who had been endorsed by Donald Trump, to Congress. In 2022, she was reëlected, and, in 2024, Trump carried the district, and Salazar cruised to victory, winning by more than twenty points. But Salazar, who, amazingly, is also a Cuban American former news anchor, is now reckoning with her district increasingly turning on the President amid economic pressure and an immigration crackdown that is extremely unpopular among Latinos.

At the onset of the race, it seemed as if Salazar’s campaign strategy was to continue her embrace of Trump and the MAGA movement, even alongside a surge in deportations in Miami, the nation’s leader in ICE arrests. Last year, she declared that the facilities at Alligator Alcatraz, the infamous immigrant-detention center in the Everglades, met the “highest standards,” and she avoided criticizing the Trump Administration when it announced the terminations of Temporary Protected Status for Venezuelans, Haitians, and Nicaraguans, upending countless lives and businesses in her district.

But, a few weeks ago, Salazar released an ad breaking with Trump over immigration enforcement and warning him that the Latino voters who helped him win in 2024 felt betrayed—“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far.”—joining the ranks of several G.O.P. candidates nationwide attempting to distance themselves from the President. As Election Day approaches, Trump’s approval rating has hit a record low, currently hovering in the mid- to low thirties, and a recent poll from NBC News showed that a higher percentage of voters consider their vote this November to be a signal of opposition to the White House than in any other midterm in nearly thirty years. Perhaps because of this, Salazar’s ad seemed to barely make a dent. In fact, as Rodriguez explained, Salazar’s turnabout had seemed to spark a fund-raising windfall for his campaign from national donors, who saw the dysfunction as a sign that the seat was potentially flippable. Shortly after, their premonitions were borne out: political forecasters shifted the seat from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican,” whereas other pollsters even went as far as to call it a toss-up.

We crossed Calle Ocho, where tourists milled around Domino Park and perused souvenir shops selling rooster T-shirts and Cuban-flag magnets, before eventually making our way a few blocks north, to a neighborhood of modest, low-slung apartment buildings. With a little more than a month to go, Rodriguez’s campaign was relentlessly targeting voters with no party affiliation (N.P.A.s, as his staffers called them), who make up thirty per cent of the district and more than twenty-four per cent of Florida’s registered voters. The canvassers were in high spirits: in contrast to the district’s more affluent neighborhoods, where they were often met with silence and Ring cameras, they told me that people in Little Havana still opened their doors, and, more often than not, they were excited to see Rodriguez at their doorstep.

“Rodriguez is essentially a household name for Miamians of a certain age,” Carlos Odio, a researcher focussing on Latino voter sentiment who grew up in Miami, told me. “I remember him being on television as a kid.” When I asked Rodriguez if it felt like he was back on the local-news beat, he smiled and nodded. “Same skill, talking to people.” As a campaign volunteer filmed with an iPad, Rodriguez introduced himself in his mellifluous anchorman’s voice to residents and passersby, asking how they were doing. “La situación está difícil, no?” he said. (“Things are hard, right?”) Fidelia, a woman in her sixties who had arrived in the U.S. from Cuba seven years ago, mentioned how difficult life was for her family back on the island but wasn’t critical of the Trump Administration, or of Salazar. “This country has been a blessing for me,” she said. At Rodriguez’s pitch, one older man in a fedora and sunglasses held up his hands as if it had nothing to do with him: he was only a resident. Another Cuban woman was more forthcoming. “I don’t like her,” she said when I asked about Salazar. “I don’t think she’s sincere.”

As the South Florida heat intensified, we passed a pair of Jehovah’s Witnesses across the street. “We got some competition,” Rodriguez murmured. When Rodriguez approached Melba, a middle-aged Nicaraguan woman walking her dog, she told him that she had swum over the southern border with her son in the eighties but proudly declared herself a Republican, mainly owing to her Christian values. She had voted for Trump but wasn’t happy with the state of the country. “The things that he’s doing, or the things that ICE is doing, that’s sad,” she said, also mentioning the Iran war and gas prices. She liked the Democrats but was turned off by the “gender stuff,” adding that she was too old to change her beliefs. “I’m with you on that,” Rodriguez replied. After he moved on, I asked if Melba knew who she’d be voting for, and she said that she’d have to think hard about it.

The Twenty-seventh District has been referred to as the at-large seat of the Americas, and, increasingly, the matchup between Rodriguez and Salazar has taken on an international dimension. During that morning’s canvassing shift, Rodriguez and several campaign volunteers walked by a monument to the Bay of Pigs invasion, and a member of the group mused that Trump and the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio (a native of the Twenty-seventh), seemed to be plotting a repeat of the operation. The notion isn’t far-fetched. Recently, a Wall Street Journal report revealed that, in June, a group of wealthy Cuban Americans met at a mansion in the district, just a few miles south of Little Havana, to plot Cuba’s post-Communist future. Meanwhile, Rubio has openly discussed direct intervention, threatening that the Cuban regime would “learn the lesson the hard way” if it didn’t capitulate to American demands.

The current Administration’s crushing sanctions and blockade on oil shipments to the island have made Trump popular among Miami Cubans. And some right-wing politicians in Latin America allied with the White House have endorsed Salazar, including María Corina Machado, the exiled Venezuelan politician who won the Nobel Peace Prize, and the Colombian President, Abelardo de la Espriella. But, in this election, both candidates have attempted to claim the mantle of anti-communism. Rodriguez, in addition to covering Miami’s biggest stories, such as the Mariel boatlift and Hurricane Andrew, had also reported from inside Communist regimes such as Venezuela, Nicaragua, and Cuba, once even interviewing Fidel Castro, and recently attacked Salazar in a Spanish-language social-media post over the Trump Administration’s partnership with the socialist government in Venezuela. (He isn’t a fan of Zohran Mamdani’s plan for government-owned bodegas, either.)

In a reflection of the race’s tricky political balancing act between long-term and more recent exiles, Rodriguez said that he still has family in Cuba and believes that the Administration’s economic strangulation of the island is hurting citizens more than the government. “I think people have opened their eyes that Trump’s policy toward Cuba is not about restoring democracy—it’s about enriching himself,” Rodriguez told me. In response to de la Espriella’s and Machado’s endorsements of Salazar, he said that he was more focussed on families struggling to make ends meet in Miami.

After all, the campaign would need more than Little Havana. Though Rodriguez’s campaign has gained momentum, fuelled by the same anti-Trump resentment that has powered the Republican-turned-Democrat former congressman David Jolly’s run for governor and the Democratic state legislator Angie Nixon’s Senate campaign, Republicans maintain a strong grip on the district and have been significantly outpacing Democrats in voter registration throughout the state. Since 2020, national Democrats and their allies have all but abandoned Florida financially. Susan Whitman-Helfgot, the co-finance chair of Democratic Hispanic Caucus of Florida, was motivated to get involved anyway. She helped found the West Miami Dems, a voter-registration group, after the 2024 Presidential election, newly determined to make Florida a swing state again. “You need to pull in the no-party voters. It’s not an easy sale, but it can be made,” she told me.

The stakes for voter engagement are particularly high for this year’s elections in Florida, she explained, in the face of recent Republican-led changes to state election laws that will de-register voters who do not participate, as well as a swell of disinformation aimed at disenfranchising Latino voters. Some Latinos told her that they thought they weren’t allowed to vote in congressional elections as independents. Others mentioned hearing at church that they simply couldn’t vote this year. She was also quick to point out that, although Latino voters were not a monolith, the Trump Administration’s immigration crackdown had increasingly become a political wake-up call for those affected by it. “It changes when it’s personal,” she said. “When you’re Venezuelan, and you’ve had a family member thrown out, it’s a whole different ballgame.”

That sentiment dovetailed with a 2025 poll of mostly long-term Venezuelan immigrants in Florida by Florida International University’s Latino Public Opinion Forum, which found that thirty-five per cent of respondents had family or a close friend affected by the termination of T.P.S. Of all the poll’s participants, a fifth of those who had voted for Trump now regretted it. Trump, for his part, did not seem concerned. After initially shrugging off questions about Salazar’s ad, he reposted more than a dozen posts attacking her on Truth Social: “She is nothing but a back stabber,” one post read. “I’m glad Latino support hasn’t wavered.” Another read, “So we need a NEW Republican to Replace Salazar.”

In the days after the ad, Salazar appeared on CBS News’ “Face the Nation,” saying that she spoke with Trump and had a “fantastic conversation” with him, adding that he was “courteous” and “very receptive.” It was unclear whether her ad was a reaction to any new voter data, but, since its release, she had been keeping a relatively low profile in Miami. Shortly after meeting with Rodriguez, I reached out to Salazar’s spokesperson for an interview, even visiting her office on Eighth Street, where a Cuban flag emblazoned with the word “Libertad” hung on the wall, but my repeated requests were unanswered. Then, a few days later, I received a tip that the congresswoman would appear at a Mass at Our Lady of Lebanon, a Maronite Catholic church back in Little Havana that serves a diverse community of Lebanese and of Latino descent. At the conclusion of an English-language service interspersed with hymns in Arabic, the priest introduced Salazar, who stood up in the front row, smiling and waving. She walked with him into an adjoining banquet hall, where she shook hands and posed for pictures. As I approached Salazar, a young woman stepped in front of me and began addressing her as a bearded man beside me filmed the exchange.

“You were talking about enforcement,” the woman said. “I wanted to interrupt. My name is Arianne Betancourt. My father was in Alligator Alcatraz. Myself and several of the people here went to your office several times. Your staff told us you were in full support of this Administration and its policies.”

Salazar nodded in response, a tight smile across her face as a small crowd formed around us. “Wait a minute, who did you talk to?” she said, glancing over her shoulder as two staffers approached. She began to introduce Reidel Nabut, her deputy district director. “This is, uh . . .”

“Yes, that’s who I spoke to,” Betancourt said. “But, you know, it’s been six months since that happened. And you really let the community down.” After some back and forth, with Salazar’s spokesperson looking on uneasily, the congresswoman turned to the priest. “Are they part of this community?” she asked him, indicating Betancourt and the man who was filming. “No,” he said.

“We are part of the community, and I’m one of your constituents,” Betancourt replied. Salazar smiled and nodded, pointing at the man who was filming, an activist named Thomas Kennedy. “Sí, that’s why you’re taping.”

Eventually, the priest and a few parishioners intervened, and Betancourt left. Salazar’s team told me that she wouldn’t be taking questions. I spoke briefly to the priest, Manuel Rahmeh, a native of Lebanon, who told me that the majority of his church congregants are immigrants. “They should be treated in a different way.”

A few days later, I met Betancourt for coffee in North Miami. The video of her exchange with Salazar had been posted online and had gone viral, so much so that Salazar had been forced to issue a statement, telling a local news station she believed that the encounter was politically motivated and that Betancourt had a “clear agenda.” Betancourt, who is half Cuban but also has Honduran and Salvadoran roots, told me that before her father was detained she wasn’t a political person at all—she had even voted for Salazar. She had worked as a tour guide in Little Havana and other parts of Florida before quitting her job to focus full time on getting her father released from detention and had been among the first to document human-rights abuses at the facility. Her father’s case was complicated; he had a criminal record, but she told me he had been following immigration protocol.

He was detained at a routine check-in at ICE’s Miramar field office. She had sat outside in her car all day waiting for him and finally received a call at 9 P.M. with his voice on the line telling her that he was in Alligator Alcatraz, shackled to a bed.

When she tried to get help from Salazar’s office, she said members of the staff told her that there was nothing they could do and that the congresswoman supported immigration enforcement. Eventually, with help from the Community Justice Project, Betancourt was able to get her father out. The congresswoman’s office disputed her account, saying that her team had met with Betancourt and claimed they had offered to help with her father’s case. A spokesperson for the congresswoman also said that her office has resolved many immigration-related cases for its constituents.

Betancourt now works for an immigrant-rights group called the Workers Circle, and she said that she’d confronted Salazar on behalf of nearly eight hundred families with loved ones detained in other South Florida facilities, such as Krome. Her phone was constantly pinging throughout our conversation, and at one point she received a call from a detention center. She showed me a WhatsApp group for Cubans who had been deported to Africa.

Later, Betancourt told me that advocating on her father’s and other detainees’ behalf had made her a target of far-right Cuban American influencers. It had also caused tension in her family. She’d been renting from her father’s sister, a Trump supporter, who she said called her a communist and kicked her out after seeing her attend a vigil. But she added that, over the past couple of months, she had felt a shift in her critics. “Some of the people who were against the work I was doing are now, like, ‘You know what, maybe you were right.’ ”

It echoed what I’d heard from others in the city. Although no one I spoke to in the Twenty-seventh District predicted a stampede of Republicans running to vote for Rodriguez, one longtime local politician told me that even his most vociferous MAGA friends had become quieter, steering their conversations away from politics. A lawyer I met related the story of a Republican colleague who had remained a Trump supporter until a few weeks ago, appalled by the lack of due process in immigration court. She asked her colleague if she planned to vote for Salazar.

“She told me she would probably stay home,” she said. ♦

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement has never issued a written reprimand to a single officer for failing to turn on a body camera — and the Trump administration this week dismissed the one safeguard that would have removed that choice from officers' hands entirely. The decision, formalized in a federal watchdog's report released publicly on Wednesday, deepens an accountability crisis at an agency where cameras were not recording during any of at least six fatal shootings involving ICE officers since President Trump's return to the White House.

A Federal Watchdog Finds a System Built Entirely on Officer Discretion

The October 14 report from the Government Accountability Office — conducted at the request of Democratic members of Congress — examined body-worn camera programs at ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection covering the period from February 2025 through September 2026. At its core, the audit concluded that neither agency had built the institutional controls needed to guarantee that agents actually press record when required.

Under current ICE policy, individual officers retain full discretion over when their cameras activate. Agency rules require recording during arrests, searches, and pre-planned enforcement operations — but without any automated enforcement mechanism, compliance rests entirely on human judgment during high-pressure encounters. ICE has not implemented the controls needed to ensure its own camera policies are being followed, the watchdog concluded — a finding the agency's zero-reprimand record makes difficult to challenge.

Same Hardware, Completely Different Rules: The CBP Divide

Among the GAO's most pointed observations: both ICE and CBP carry Axon body cameras that natively support automatic activation under preset conditions — when a firearm clears its holster, when emergency vehicle lights engage, or when a nearby camera begins recording. CBP deploys those features as standard practice. ICE does not.

In its formal response, DHS argued that extending auto-activation to ICE "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement." The department also raised privacy concerns, warning that accidental recording could capture sensitive conversations with informants or victims, or document bystanders engaged in First Amendment-protected activity. Critics note that CBP agents operate the identical Axon hardware in the field every day — making the gap between the two agencies less a technological problem and more a reflection of institutional resistance to being on the record.

Fatal Shootings Without Footage Drove the Congressional Probe

Democratic lawmakers launched the GAO review against a backdrop of deaths that drew national attention. Federal immigration agents have killed at least nine people and injured more than a dozen others in at least 30 shootings since Trump began his second term, according to a CBS News independent review — among them two people shot dead in Minneapolis: Renée Good on January 7 and Alex Pretti on January 24. Two more men were killed later in the year during immigration enforcement vehicle stops — Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 8, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, roughly a week later. In each high-profile case, no cameras were running.

The program's funding history tracks the political turbulence surrounding those deaths. The Trump administration's fiscal 2026 budget had proposed cutting ICE's camera program funding by roughly 75 percent, from approximately $20.5 million down to $5.5 million. After the Houston and Maine shootings triggered protests across the country, Congress reversed that course and directed $20 million specifically toward the procurement, deployment, and operation of body cameras for immigration enforcement officers. DHS confirmed to the GAO that all ICE field offices had received their devices by August 5 — a distribution milestone that resolves the hardware gap but does nothing to enforce activation once the cameras are in agents' hands.

Zero Reprimands, No Performance Standards, Plans Years Out of Date

The GAO's criticism reaches well beyond the auto-activation dispute. Neither ICE nor CBP had updated its body camera management plan since the programs were first established — ICE's dated to 2024, CBP's to 2022 — even as both agencies substantially expanded their workforces in the intervening years. At multiple ICE field offices reviewed by auditors, officers reported confusion about basic activation requirements, including whether cameras had to be on during vehicle searches or when transporting detainees.

Most critically, neither agency has established any measurable performance standards by which to gauge whether its camera program is delivering the transparency and public trust it was designed to produce. Tens of millions in federal dollars have been allocated, but no formal benchmarks exist to determine whether that investment is working. DHS accepted six of the GAO's seven recommendations. The sole rejection was the only one that would have taken the activation decision entirely out of individual officers' hands.

Legislation Promised, but Its Path Through Congress Remains Unclear

Rep. Thompson chose direct language after the report's release. "This is completely unacceptable," he said in a statement, pledging to introduce mandatory auto-activation legislation "in the coming days." Whether that bill can advance in a divided Congress remains an open question. What the GAO report and DHS's response make clear is where the line has been drawn: agents will carry cameras into every enforcement encounter, but the choice to actually roll footage — even when drawing a weapon — will remain, for now, theirs alone.

Last week I drove to Edinburg in the Rio Grande Valley and back in one day.

I was shocked at the number of patrol cars, representing multiple law enforcement agencies, positioned on the side of the highway. I counted five within a 1-mile stretch.
